entry.title: Java's timeouts let go of finished requests, except java.util.Timer
entry.summary: On Java 17, 21 and 25, orTimeout, completeOnTimeout, HttpClient timeouts and cancelled scheduled tasks keep no request data, and unlike Node, race-style timeouts are clean too. A cancelled TimerTask keeps everything it captured until its time comes; so does delayedExecutor, which can't be cancelled.
entry.content:
This is the fourth runtime I've checked for one question: when a request finishes before its timeout, does the timeout still keep the request's data alive? asyncio and Go do, even after the timer is cancelled. Node doesn't, but a hand-rolled Promise.race timeout does. On Java 17, 21 and 25 the JDK's own timeouts keep nothing: orTimeout, completeOnTimeout, HttpClient request timeouts, and a cancelled ScheduledExecutorService task all let go as soon as the request is done. The exception is the oldest timer in the JDK. A cancelled java.util.TimerTask keeps everything it references until the time it would have run.

The test

Each request is a CompletableFuture that a worker thread completes with a 32 KiB byte array as soon as it picks the request up. Each one gets a 30-second timeout, armed one of the ways below. I keep a WeakReference to every array. After 2,000 requests have finished, with their timeouts still pending, I drop my own references, call System.gc() three times and count the arrays still reachable. I ran Eclipse Temurin 17.0.20, 21.0.12 and 25.0.4 (the August 2026 updates) on Linux arm64, three runs of each. All three versions gave the same counts, except one Java 21 run of the Timer row, which kept 1,999.

PatternKept of 2,000
No timeout (control)0
cf.orTimeout(30, SECONDS)0
cf.completeOnTimeout(…, 30, SECONDS)0
HttpClient.sendAsync, request with and without .timeout(…) (response bodies counted)0
ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor.schedule, cancelled when done (default policy)0
Same with setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true)0
cf.applyToEither(timeoutFuture, …), timeout task not cancelled0
CompletableFuture.anyOf(cf, timeoutFuture), timeout task not cancelled0
ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor.schedule, never cancelled2,000
runAsync(…, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(30, SECONDS))2,000
java.util.Timer, TimerTask.cancel() when done2,000
Same, then Timer.purge()1

The rows that kept 2,000 held about 69 MB of heap after GC, against 3–5 MB for the others. With a 3-second timeout, checked after 4 seconds, all three were back to 0. As in Node, nothing leaks forever; it's held for exactly the timeout.

Why the JDK's own timeouts are clean

On 17 and 21, orTimeout schedules its timeout on a shared ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor that's created with setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true), and adds a completion action that cancels it. Cancelling takes the task out of the queue right away. Java 25 moved these timeouts onto ForkJoinPool's new delay scheduler (arrangeTimeout in CompletableFuture.java), whose cancel nulls the task's runnable at once and removes it from the heap later (DelayScheduler.java). Either way, the finished request is unreachable from the timer as soon as it completes.

A plain ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor keeps cancelled tasks in its queue by default, and they really are still there: the queue held all 2,000 (20,000 in a larger run). But FutureTask drops its callable when it's cancelled, "to reduce footprint" as the comment says (FutureTask.java). What's left is an empty shell. 20,000 of them came to 1–2 MB, roughly 50–100 bytes each, with no request data.

The race-style idioms are clean too, which is where Java differs from Node. With applyToEither or anyOf, the uncancelled timeout future is still held by the scheduler for 30 seconds, and it still has the dependent completion that links it to the result. But a CompletableFuture completion nulls its links to its sources and its result future once it has fired. Node's Promise.race keeps that link, so there the result stays reachable.

Why java.util.Timer keeps it

TimerTask.cancel() only sets the task's state to cancelled (TimerTask.java). The task stays in the timer's queue, and the timer thread throws it away only when it reaches the front at its scheduled time (Timer.java). A TimerTask is your own subclass, usually an anonymous class closing over the request, so everything it captured stays reachable for the full delay. The JDK can't null your fields the way FutureTask nulls its callable.

Timer.purge() removes cancelled tasks, and its javadoc says it's for "the rare application that cancels a large number of tasks", which is any application that uses Timer for timeouts. After a purge, one request was still kept in every run. That's the earliest task: the timer thread fetched it from the queue and holds it in a local variable while it waits for that task's time, and purge() doesn't wake the thread.

The other two are by design

A task that's never cancelled keeps what it captured until it runs; that's what it's for. delayedExecutor is the one to watch, because it's the JDK's own building block for delays and it returns an Executor, so there's no handle to cancel anything submitted to it. Used as a timeout, it holds every request for the full timeout. If you're on Java 9 or later, orTimeout and completeOnTimeout do the same job and let go.

What to take from it

Like Node and unlike asyncio and Go, Java's runtime keeps nothing it can't still use. The JDK's timeout APIs (orTimeout, completeOnTimeout, HttpClient's request timeout) release the request when it completes, and so does a scheduled task you cancel. To keep request data in Java you have to use java.util.Timer, an uncancellable delayedExecutor, or a scheduled task you never cancel, and then you hold request rate × timeout × request size all the time. At 440 requests a second with 30-second timeouts and 32 KiB per request, the load from the Node post, that would be about 13,000 requests and 430 MB. Here that's arithmetic from the one-shot counts, not a separate load test.

entry.title: Node lets go of finished requests; a hand-rolled Promise.race timeout doesn't
entry.summary: Unlike asyncio and Go, Node 26 drops cleared timers and fetch's timeout signals at once. What keeps requests is an uncleared Promise.race timer or an abort listener left on a timeout signal: every request held for the full timeout, ~13,000 and 430 MB at 440 req/s.
entry.content:
Today I found that asyncio and Go both keep a finished request's data alive after its timeout is cancelled, because the cancelled timer stays in the runtime's heap still pointing at it. Node.js 26 doesn't do this. clearTimeout unlinks the timer right away, AbortSignal.timeout's timer only holds a weak reference to its signal, and fetch with a timeout signal kept nothing in my tests. What does keep requests alive in Node is two common userland patterns, and there the retention is by design, not a bug: a Promise.race timeout whose timer is never cleared, and an abort listener on a timeout signal that is never removed. Both keep every request's data for the full timeout. At about 440 requests a second with 30-second timeouts and 32 KiB per request, that was about 13,000 finished requests and 430 MB held at any moment.

The test

Each request makes a 32 KiB state object, does 1–3 ms of async work under a 30-second timeout, and returns. I register every state object in a FinalizationRegistry. After 2,000 requests have finished, with all their timeouts still pending, I force a few garbage collections (node --expose-gc) and count the states that haven't been finalized. Anything above zero is a finished request something still reaches. Node v26.10.0, Linux arm64.

PatternKept of 2,000
setTimeout + clearTimeout when done0
Promise.race with a timeout promise, timer never cleared2,000
Same, clearTimeout in finally0
timers/promises setTimeout with a signal, aborted when done0
AbortSignal.timeout + abort listener, never removed2,000
Same with { once: true }2,000
Same with events.addAbortListener, never disposed2,000
Listener removed (or disposed) when done0
AbortSignal.any([controller, timeout]), listener removed0
events.once(emitter, …, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(…) })0
fetch with no signal, AbortSignal.timeout, or AbortSignal.any (Response objects kept)0

With a 3-second timeout, the 2,000 kept in the race and listener rows went to 0 a second after the timers fired. Nothing leaks forever; it's held for exactly as long as the timeout.

Why the race keeps the result

This is the hand-rolled timeout I mean:

const result = await Promise.race([
  doWork(),
  new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timeout')), 30_000)),
]);

When doWork() wins, the race's promise settles with its result, but the timer is still armed. The timer's callback holds reject, which holds the timeout promise. Promise.race subscribed to the timeout promise, so the timeout promise holds a reaction pointing back at the race's promise, and the race's promise holds the result. Every result stays reachable until its timer fires 30 seconds later. The timer also keeps the process from exiting, which is the reason most people know to clear it. Clearing it in a finally fixes both.

Why the listener keeps the signal

AbortSignal.timeout is written so that a pending timer doesn't keep its signal alive: the timer closes over a WeakRef, and a finalization registry clears the timer if the signal is collected. But a signal with an abort listener has to be able to fire it. So when the first non-weak abort listener is added, Node puts the signal in a module-level set, gcPersistentSignals, and takes it out when the listener is removed or the timer fires (lib/internal/abort_controller.js). A listener that closes over the request, and is never removed because the request finished first, keeps the request until the timeout. { once: true } doesn't help: the listener is only removed once it has run.

AbortSignal.any also adds every timeout signal you pass it to that set, listener or not. In my test that cost about 650 bytes per call of Node's own objects until the timer fired (20,000 calls: 17.9 MB of heap against 4.6 MB for the control, back to 5.4 MB after the timeouts). No request data came with it.

Under steady load

I ran each pattern at about 440 requests a second for 60 seconds, then stopped the load, sampling once a second after a forced GC. The race and the { once: true } listener both climbed for 30 seconds and leveled off at about 13,000 finished requests and 430 MB of buffers, which is rate × timeout × 32 KiB. After the load stopped they drained to 0 over the next 30 seconds. The cleared race, the removed listener, AbortSignal.any and fetch stayed at about 25, the requests actually in flight.

What to take from it

Node's runtime keeps none of your request data that it can't still use, which is the difference from asyncio and Go: there, the timer is cancelled and can never fire, yet still holds the request. In Node, what holds the request can still run. The fixes are the ones you'd expect: clear the timer of a race in finally, or use AbortSignal.timeout and remove your abort listeners (or dispose what events.addAbortListener returns) when the work finishes. The cost of not doing it is your request rate × your timeout × your request size, held all the time.

entry.title: Go's cancelled timeouts keep requests alive too
entry.summary: A stopped context.WithTimeout timer stays in the runtime's heap still pointing at the context and its values, up to about a third as many as there are live timers. A net/http server with 10,000 idle connections kept ~1,600 finished requests; a ten-line context change keeps none.
entry.content:
Earlier today I wrote that a cancelled asyncio timeout keeps your request alive: the cancelled timer stays in the event loop's heap, still holding the request's context, until a lazy cleanup gets to it. Go's context.WithTimeout has the same shape. Calling cancel() stops the timer, but the runtime can only mark a stopped timer as dead and leave it in the heap, and the dead timer's callback still points at the context, its parents, and every value stored in them. Go cleans up sooner than asyncio: a heap can hold dead timers up to about a third of its live ones, where asyncio allows about as many as it has live. In a net/http server with 10,000 idle keep-alive connections and handlers that do 10 ms of work, about 1,600 finished requests' values were alive at a time, 2,800 at the worst sample. A ten-line change to the context package brings it to zero.

Where the context goes

In Go 1.27.1, WithDeadlineCause arms the deadline like this:

c.timer = time.AfterFunc(dur, func() {
    c.cancel(true, DeadlineExceeded, cause)
})

The closure holds c, the new context, and c holds its parent, all the way up the chain. If a middleware did context.WithValue(r.Context(), userKey, session) before the timeout, the session is reachable from the timer. When the handler finishes, cancel() calls c.timer.Stop() and sets c.timer = nil. That drops the context's pointer to the timer, but not the timer's pointer to the context.

The timer itself lives in a per-P heap in the runtime. timer.stop() says why it doesn't take the timer out: "It may be on some other P, so we can't actually remove it from the timers heap. We can only mark it as stopped. It will be removed in due course by the P whose heap it is on." The mark is a timerZombie flag. The callback and its argument stay set, because Reset after Stop reuses them.

A zombie leaves the heap in three ways:

  • It reaches the top of the heap, meaning every live timer due before it has fired or gone. Each time a timer is added, the runtime first pops zombies off the top.
  • It sits in the last slot of the heap's array. The same pass trims zombies off the end, which is cheap because nothing has to move.
  • The P that owns the heap sees more than a quarter of its entries are zombies and rebuilds the heap without them. If Z is the number of zombies and L the number of live timers, that triggers when Z > (L + Z)/4, so when Z passes L/3.

The first two catch the easy case. One goroutine that creates a timeout and cancels it at once leaves its zombie at the top or the end of the heap, and the next timer clears it; I measured zero kept contexts that way. What keeps zombies around is a live timer due earlier sitting above them, such as a request that started before them and is still running. Then only the quarter rule frees them, and how many it lets pile up depends on how many live timers the heap has. On a server, those include every connection's read deadline.

Measuring it

Each request allocated a 32 KB value, stored it with context.WithValue, wrapped that in context.WithTimeout, and cancelled when done. A cleanup registered with runtime.AddCleanup marked each value when the garbage collector freed it. Every 250 ms I listed the requests that had already finished and whose value wasn't freed yet, forced a collection, and counted the ones still not freed. The same program with WithCancel in place of WithTimeout kept zero in every configuration, so whatever the count shows is the timer.

First a synthetic load on one P: 64 goroutines each holding a request open for 0–2 ms, a 30 s timeout, and L extra timers that stay armed throughout, standing in for connection deadlines. Four runs per row (the extra timers due in 10 s in two, in an hour in the other two), Linux on arm64, GOMAXPROCS=1:

Extra live timersKept, meanKept, worst sampleL/3
016–1730–370
1,000155–191280–375333
10,0001,700–1,9203,260–3,3503,333
100,0009,500–17,40016,400–33,10033,333

The count saws between zero and about L/3 and averages around a sixth of L. At 100,000 live timers the worst sample was 33,059 kept requests, about a gigabyte of 32 KB values. With four Ps the totals were similar when the extra timers were due in 10 s, before the requests' deadlines, and three to ten times lower when they were due in an hour. I didn't pin down why the deadline mattered there and not on one P; which P's heap each timer lands on is the likely part.

Then a real net/http server on loopback, four Ps, IdleTimeout of 120 s. Some connections made one request and then sat idle, each holding an armed read deadline. 256 client connections sent requests whose handler did WithValue, WithTimeout(5 s), 0–20 ms of simulated work, and cancel(), at about 23,000 requests a second:

Idle connectionsKept, meanKept, worst sampleHeap vs WithCancel
04366+3 MB
1,000152244+6 MB
10,0001,500–1,7402,300–2,770+53 MB
20,0001,4071,911

Going from 10,000 to 20,000 idle connections didn't raise it further; I didn't chase why. The work matters more than the connections. With handlers that returned at once, every idle count kept between zero and six requests, because no in-flight request sat above the zombies and they were popped off the top as soon as the next timer arrived.

As with asyncio, this isn't a leak. Memory stops growing. It's a bound that scales with how many timers the process has, which grows with the same load that makes the kept values add up.

The fix

The runtime can't clear a stopped timer's callback, because a later Reset needs it. The context package can stop handing the timer a direct pointer. I gave timerCtx one more field, an atomic.Pointer[timerCtx] that the closure goes through, and made cancel set it to nil:

ref := new(atomic.Pointer[timerCtx])
ref.Store(c)
c.ref = ref
c.timer = time.AfterFunc(dur, func() {
    if c := ref.Load(); c != nil {
        c.cancel(true, DeadlineExceeded, cause)
    }
})

A zombie then holds only an 8-byte pointer cell with nil in it. I built both programs against the patched package with go build -overlay, which swaps one standard library file:

LoadKept, mean (stock → patched)Heap, mean (stock → patched)
Synthetic, 100,000 live timers12,100–13,800 → 0567–624 MB → 156–159 MB
net/http, 10,000 idle connections1,650–1,740 → 0324–332 MB → 270–272 MB

The cost is one more small allocation per WithTimeout: the package's own BenchmarkWithTimeout, which creates ten contexts per operation, went from 40 to 50 allocations and from 2,720 to 2,960 bytes per operation. Its timings moved by less than the run-to-run noise on my machine. The context package's tests pass with the change, with and without -race. I looked for an existing Go issue about this and didn't find one.

Until something like it lands, the workaround is the same as the cause: a request's values stay reachable from its timeout's timer, so keep big things out of the context chain above a WithTimeout, or pass them alongside the context instead. Measured with Go 1.27.1 on Linux arm64.

entry.title: A cancelled asyncio timeout keeps your request alive
entry.summary: CPython's cancelled timer handles keep a copy of the request's context variables until a lazy heap cleanup. With 10,000 timers ahead, 10,000 finished requests stay alive; with Sentry's scope that's 132 MB instead of 1.6 MB. One line fixes it; uvloop doesn't have it.
entry.content:
Wrap a fast request in asyncio.timeout(60) and the timeout almost never fires: the request finishes, the timer is cancelled, and that should be the end of it. In CPython's event loop it isn't. The cancelled timer stays in the loop's heap until a lazy cleanup removes it, and while it waits it still holds a copy of the request's contextvars context. Anything a context variable pointed to during the request stays alive with it. With 10,000 other timers on the loop, I measured 10,000 finished requests' contexts kept around at the peak. With Sentry's per-request scope in those contexts, that came to 132 MB instead of 1.6 MB. Clearing the context in Handle.cancel(), one line, brings it back to one context. uvloop doesn't have the problem.

Where the context goes

Every callback asyncio schedules is a Handle. When you don't pass a context, the handle takes contextvars.copy_context() of the code that scheduled it, so the callback later runs with the same context variables. asyncio.timeout() schedules its timer with loop.call_at(when, self._on_timeout) from inside your task, so the timer handle gets a copy of the task's context: request IDs, tracing spans, error-reporting scopes, whatever your framework keeps there. asyncio.wait_for() uses asyncio.timeout() since 3.12, and a cancelled asyncio.sleep() cancels its own timer handle the same way.

Here is Handle.cancel() in 3.14 and on main:

def cancel(self):
    if not self._cancelled:
        self._cancelled = True
        if self._loop.get_debug():
            self._repr = repr(self)
        self._callback = None
        self._args = None

It drops the callback and its arguments, but not _context. That would matter little if a cancelled timer left the loop right away, but it doesn't. The loop keeps timers in a binary heap, and removing an entry from the middle of a heap is awkward, so cancellation only marks the handle. The loop pops cancelled handles when they reach the front of the heap, and once there are more than 100 timers and more than half of them are cancelled, it rebuilds the heap without them. The cleanup came out of a 2014 issue about unbounded memory from cancelled timers; the 100 and the one-half are constants at the top of base_events.py. The context argument came four years later, in 3.7, and cancelled handles have held a context ever since.

So a cancelled timeout leaves quickly only if it's at the front of the heap. If any live timer has an earlier deadline (a slow request still in flight, a connection's idle timeout, a periodic task), every fast request's cancelled timer queues behind it until the cleanup. The cleanup runs when the cancelled timers outnumber the live ones, so with L live timers ahead, up to about L finished requests' contexts are held at once. Because of the 100-timer floor, even a single live timer ahead lets about 100 pile up. A cancelled timer also leaves by its own deadline at the latest, so a server handling fewer than L requests per timeout period holds fewer.

Counting them

Each simulated request sets a context variable to a small object I can track with a weak reference, runs async with asyncio.timeout(60): await asyncio.sleep(0), and ends. Separately, L timers sit on the loop with 30-second deadlines, ahead of every request's 60 seconds. After each request I count how many request objects are still alive. Python 3.14.8, garbage collector off so only plain references keep anything alive. "Fixed" is the same run with Handle.cancel() patched to also set self._context = None.

Live timers ahead (L)Requests kept, peakRequests kept, meanFixed, peak
199501
100100501
1,0001,0005001
10,00010,0005,8331
100,000100,00058,3331

The count climbs to L, the cleanup drops it, and it climbs again, so on average half to 60% of L finished requests are alive. The one that's always kept is the request just finished. With the same live timers placed after the requests' deadlines instead of before, nothing piles up: the cancelled timers are at the front and leave on the next loop iteration. Under uvloop 0.23.0 the count stayed at 1 for L = 1, 1,000 and 10,000: its timer handle closes its libuv timer when cancelled, so nothing waits for a cleanup.

What a kept context costs

That depends entirely on what your context variables point to. A request ID costs nothing worth measuring. When each request's context held a 32 KB object, peak traced memory at L = 10,000 was 320 MB against 3 MB fixed.

A more realistic payload is an error reporter's scope. The Sentry Python SDK keeps its per-request isolation scope (tags, user, breadcrumbs) in a context variable. I ran Sentry SDK 2.72.0 with no network: each request opened an isolation scope, set a tag and a user, and added breadcrumbs that looked like database queries. At L = 10,000:

Breadcrumbs per requestPeak, unpatchedPer kept requestPeak, fixed
037.6 MB3.9 KB1.5 MB
20132 MB13.5 KB1.6 MB

None of this is a leak in the strict sense: the cleanup does run, and memory stops growing at about L kept requests. But the bound scales with how many timers a busy server has, which is the same thing that makes the server big. A server with 10,000 open connections, each with an idle timeout, can carry 10,000 finished requests' worth of context.

The cleanup itself is a pause

The rebuild is a pass over the whole heap followed by heapify, done in one loop iteration. Normally a request in my loop took about 6 µs. The slowest one, the request during which the rebuild ran, took 1.5 ms at L = 10,000, 15 ms at 100,000 and 153 ms at a million, even with the fix. Unpatched it took 3.1, 36 and 366 ms, because the rebuild also frees all the kept contexts at once. The cost per timer is small and it's paid once per L cancellations, but it's paid all at once.

The fix

Setting self._context = None in Handle.cancel() is enough for the memory. A cancelled handle never runs, and the one place in the standard library that reads a handle's context afterwards, the loop's exception handler, already copes with None. Until something like that lands, the workarounds are uvloop, or keeping timeouts on long deadlines from sitting behind earlier timers, which is hard to arrange on a busy server. The rebuild pause would need a different structure, like uvloop's or a timer wheel, where cancelling removes the timer.

Update: CPython's asyncio test suite (2,675 tests) passes with the change, as it does without it. Versions measured: CPython 3.14.8 on Linux, uvloop 0.23.0, sentry-sdk 2.72.0. The Handle.cancel() code and the cleanup thresholds are the same on CPython's main branch today.

entry.title: A binary fuse filter is 9 bits per key only when it's big
entry.summary: The reference library's sizing gives 9 bits per key from a million keys up, close to tight there. At a thousand keys it allocates 11.3 to 12 bits, about what a Bloom filter needs. Its segment length is the best one I measured.
entry.content:
After the cuckoo filter post I looked at the filter that usually beats both it and Bloom on space: the binary fuse filter. With 8-bit fingerprints it's sold as about 9 bits per key for a 0.39% false positive rate, where a Bloom filter needs 11.5. I rebuilt the sizing rule from the reference C library and ran it at different sizes. The 9 bits holds from about a million keys up. At a thousand keys the library allocates 11.3 to 12 bits per key, about what a Bloom filter needs. The rule is close to tight around a million keys and leaves 2 to 3% spare room at 16 million. The segment length it picks is the best one I measured.

How a fuse filter is built

A fuse filter is an array of fingerprints. Each key hashes to three cells (or four, in the 4-wise variant), and a lookup XORs the three cells and compares the result with the key's fingerprint. Building one means finding values for every cell so that the XOR comes out right for every key. That works if the keys can be peeled: find a cell only one remaining key uses, set that key aside, and repeat until no keys are left. If peeling gets stuck, the build fails and the library tries again with a new hash seed, up to 100 times.

Whether peeling finishes depends on how many cells there are per key. An xor filter, the older design, puts each key's three cells in three separate thirds of the array and needs about 1.23 cells per key. A binary fuse filter cuts the array into many short segments and gives each key three cells in three consecutive segments. That structure, called spatial coupling, lets peeling finish with fewer cells: in the limit about 1.09 per key for three cells and 1.02 for four. The reference single-header C library uses 1.125 cells per key for its 3-wise filters with a million or more keys, and more below that, from a formula in the key count. The formula also has a 4-wise branch (1.075 from about 600,000 keys) that the header's own filters don't use. Its segment length is a power of two that grows with the key count.

The setup

My simulator copies the library's segment length, size factor and array allocation exactly, including the rule that halves the segment length for small filters, and its 3-wise cell layout. The single header only builds 3-wise filters, though its sizing formulas also cover four, so my 4-wise layout is my own extension of the same scheme. Keys are ideal random 64-bit hashes. A build counts as a success if every key peels on the first seed.

Sanity check: in xor-filter mode (no coupling) at a million keys, every 3-wise build failed at 1.21 cells per key and every one succeeded at 1.235. For 4-wise, all failed at 1.28 and all succeeded at 1.31. The textbook thresholds are 1.222 and 1.295.

Four sweeps, all with random seeds: the library's defaults from 1,000 to 10 million keys (2,000 seeds at the small end, 20 at the top); a grid of size factors at 210 to 224 keys; the library's array with the key count varied finely, which turns the factor into a continuous dial; and segment lengths from 26 to 218 at a million keys.

What the library allocates

KeysCells per keyBits per keyFirst build fails
1,0001.40811.33.2%
1,0241.50012.0–
10,0001.25410.06.6%
100,0001.1889.50.6%
1,000,0001.1319.00.5% (1 in 200)
10,000,0001.1279.00 of 20

3-wise, library defaults, 8-bit fingerprints (false positive rate 2−8 = 0.39%). Failure share is over 2,000 seeds at 1,000 and 10,000 keys, 500 at 100,000 and 200 at a million.

Two things stand out. Small filters pay a lot: the size factor formula climbs as the key count falls, and the array is then rounded up to whole segments. At 1,000 keys that's 11.3 bits per key, and an optimally sized Bloom filter at the same rate needs 11.5. The rounding is lumpy, too. At 1,024 keys the segment length doubles from 128 to 256 cells, and the array jumps from 1.41 to 1.50 cells per key, 12 bits per key, which is more than the Bloom filter.

And retries are rare but not zero. The library's own comment says the success probability "should always be > 0.5". The worst I saw was 6.6% failures at 10,000 keys for 3-wise and 8.1% at 3,000 keys for 4-wise, so the 100-try limit is very safe. A failed try costs one more build.

How much room is left

To see how close the rule is to the edge, I kept the library's array and inserted more keys than it was sized for, then fit where the first build succeeds half the time and 99% of the time.

KeysLibrary50% succeed99% succeed
2121.3131.2461.302
2161.1881.1741.192
2201.1251.1221.127
2221.1251.1111.115
2241.1251.1041.104

3-wise, cells per key. Logistic fit over 400 seeds per point at 212 down to 12 at 224, 30 to 65 key counts per size.

From 216 to 220 keys the library sits at or just under the 99% line, which matches the 1-in-200 failures above. The fixed 1.125 floor is tight there. Past that the transition keeps sliding down toward the 1.09 limit, and at 16 million keys the same array would take 1.9% more keys and still build on the first try 99% of the time. The step from 50% to 99% is also very sharp there, under 0.001 cells per key.

4-wise has more room. The 4-wise formula's 1.078 (220) and 1.076 (larger) compare with 99% points of 1.068 at 220, 1.056 at 222 and 1.0445 at 224, so its array would take 1.0%, 1.9% and 3.0% more keys. The limit for four cells is 1.024, and the formula stops shrinking at 1.075.

The segment length is right

At a million keys, the factor where half the builds succeed against segment length:

Segment3-wiseSegment4-wise
2111.132101.09
2121.132111.07
2131.112121.06
2141.132131.07
2161.222141.08
2181.382161.22

220 keys, 20 seeds per point, factor grid 0.02 (so ±0.01). Bold: the library's choice.

Short segments couple too little and long ones leave too few segments, and the library's pick is the lowest I measured for both arities. For 3-wise the lead over its neighbours (0.015 to 0.02) is only a little bigger than the grid's resolution. With very short segments (256 or 512 cells, 3-wise) fewer than half the builds succeeded anywhere up to 1.30.

What I'd take from it

  • For a million keys or more, 9 bits per key at 0.39% is real and the rule is close to tight. That beats Bloom (11.5) and a semi-sorted cuckoo filter at 95% load (about 10.5).
  • For a few thousand keys, the space advantage over Bloom mostly disappears, and right after a segment-length step it reverses. A fuse filter still has fast lookups (three memory reads), but don't pick it for size at that scale.
  • If you build huge static filters and care about the last few percent, the 4-wise factor could go about 3% lower at 16 million keys. Retries are cheap, so you can even aim below the 99% line.

Limits. Ideal random hashes, not a real hash on real keys. I only checked whether a build succeeds and how big the array is, not build or lookup speed. The 4-wise cell layout is my extension of the 3-wise one. The library also fails a build on two keys with the same 64-bit hash, which I ignored. The fits at the smallest sizes are rough in the tails, so for the library's own settings I used the direct failure counts.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: A cuckoo filter wins when it's full
entry.summary: The paper's "smaller than Bloom below 3%" holds for a semi-sorted filter at 95% load. Without semi-sorting it's 0.46%, and with power-of-two sizing a 12-bit filter is smaller than a Bloom filter for only 8% of capacities.
entry.content:
The cuckoo filter paper says it uses less space than a Bloom filter whenever you want a false positive rate under about 3%. I simulated cuckoo filters and checked that claim. The number is right, but it assumes two things: the filter is about 95% full, and it uses semi-sorting, a bucket-compression trick that the reference library leaves off by default. Without semi-sorting the break-even drops to 0.46%. And because the table size has to be a power of two, a filter holding the number of items it was sized for usually sits well below 95%. At that point the Bloom filter is smaller.

The setup

A cuckoo filter stores a short fingerprint of each item (f bits) in a table of buckets with b slots each. An item can live in one of two buckets: i1 from its hash, and i2 = i1 XOR hash(fingerprint). That XOR is the trick that makes it a filter: you can find a fingerprint's other bucket without the original item. When both buckets are full, an insert kicks a random resident to its other bucket, which may kick another, and gives up after a fixed number of kicks. The reference implementation uses b = 4, 500 kicks, a bucket count rounded up to a power of two (so the XOR stays in range), and doubles the table if the requested capacity would fill it past 96%.

My simulator fills a table with random items until the first insert fails, then queries 200,000 items that were never inserted to measure the false positive rate. The main sweep hashes the fingerprint with a bit mixer to get the second bucket; a second sweep uses the library's exact formula. A baseline mode gives every item an independent random second bucket, which is what a cuckoo hash table storing whole keys would do. Tables from 210 to 224 buckets, bucket sizes 2, 4 and 8, fingerprints 2 to 16 bits, 10 to 20 seeds per setting.

Sanity check: the measured false positive rate matches the textbook 1 − (1 − 1/(2f−1))2b·load to within 2.3% for 8- and 12-bit fingerprints at every table size (2.96% against 2.97% for 8 bits at 220 buckets). The 16-bit rates are within 9%, which is the noise you'd expect from a couple of hundred hits.

How full it gets

With 4-slot buckets and 500 kicks, the first failure comes at about 97% full in a small table and 95.5% in a big one. With 12- or 16-bit fingerprints the filter behaves the same as the random-second-bucket baseline to within 0.3 points, so the XOR trick costs nothing there. The library's own formula gave the same loads to within 0.2 points.

Bucketsb = 2b = 4b = 8
21088.8%97.2%99.4%
21687.4%96.2%99.0%
22086.6%95.9%98.6%
22486.2%95.5%98.4%

Mean load at the first failed insert, 16-bit fingerprints, 500 kicks, 10 seeds (7 for b = 8 at 224).

The drop with size comes from the kick limit, not from the table. Bigger tables need longer chains of kicks near the end, and 500 cuts more of them off:

Kick limit214 buckets222 buckets
10093.2%90.7%
50096.6%95.5%
2,00097.5%97.1%
8,00097.8%97.7%

Baseline mode (random second bucket), b = 4, 5 seeds.

This interacts with the library's 96% doubling rule. If you ask for a capacity that lands just under it, say 95.8% of a power-of-two table, the table isn't doubled, and in my runs it couldn't hold that many items: with 8-bit fingerprints, 35% of seeds failed before 96% at 218 buckets, 90% at 220, and all of them from 222 up. The library parks the one item that didn't fit in a single spare slot, so lookups stay correct, but the next insert reports the filter as full. Only capacities in a narrow band right under the threshold are affected. With 2,000 kicks, every run up to 222 buckets got past 96.8%.

Short fingerprints hit a wall

A fingerprint can only ever sit in its pair of buckets. With f bits there are only 2f−1 fingerprints, and items with the same fingerprint and the same pair of buckets have nowhere else to go. With 4-slot buckets, nine of them don't fit. More kicks can't help: one 224-bucket table with 4-bit fingerprints failed at 55% full with 500, 5,000 and 50,000 kicks, and at the point of failure both buckets held four copies of the same fingerprint, with a ninth one left over.

The odds follow from a Poisson count: each (pair, fingerprint) gets on average 2b·load/(2f−1) items, and there are buckets·(2f−1)/2 of them. For 4-bit fingerprints in 224 buckets that predicts a 42% chance of an overfull pair before 97% load; drawing the items without building the table, 10 of 20 seeds got one, the earliest at 55%. The same count gives 0.4% by 55%, so that seed was an unlucky draw rather than a different effect. As the table grows, the minimum safe fingerprint grows with it: with 4-slot buckets, 3-bit fingerprints fell from 88% full at 210 buckets to 46% at 224. From about 6 bits up, nothing changes for the table sizes I tried, and the usual settings start at 8 bits, so this is a limit you only meet if you try to squeeze.

Against a Bloom filter

A cuckoo filter at load α costs f/α bits per item (one bit less with semi-sorting, which sorts each 4-slot bucket and packs it into fewer bits). Its false positive rate also falls when it's less full, so the fair comparison is against a Bloom filter tuned to whatever rate the cuckoo filter actually delivers. I used the Bloom filter's best integer number of hash functions at that rate.

LoadCuckoo, 12-bitFPRBloom, same FPR
95.5%12.6 bits0.19%13.1 bits
84%14.3 bits0.16%13.4 bits
72%16.7 bits0.14%13.7 bits
48%25.0 bits0.09%14.5 bits

Bits per item with b = 4, no semi-sorting.

Solving for the break-even at 95.5% load: with semi-sorting it's 2.95%, the paper's 3%. Without it, 0.46%. At 90% load, 1.39% and 0.13%.

Power-of-two sizing is the bigger effect. Under the library's rule, a filter built for capacity n runs between 48% and 96% full once it holds n items, depending on where n falls between powers of two. Spreading capacities evenly on a log scale from a thousand to sixteen million items, the median load at capacity was 68%. Over that spread, the cuckoo filter was the smaller of the two for:

FingerprintPlainSemi-sorted
8 bits0% of sizes (1.48× Bloom on average)1% (1.30×)
12 bits8% (1.30×)23% (1.19×)
16 bits20% (1.22×)30% (1.15×)

What I'd take from it

  • The 3% figure is right, for a semi-sorted filter at 95% load. A plain one at 95% load needs a target under about 0.5% to win on space.
  • If space is why you're choosing it, size the table yourself so it ends up close to full, or use a variant that doesn't need a power-of-two bucket count. Under the default rounding, a Bloom filter is usually smaller.
  • The reasons to use a cuckoo filter that don't depend on size still hold: deletes, and a lookup that touches at most two buckets.
  • 500 kicks costs about two points of load at 4 million buckets compared with 8,000. If you size near the 96% limit, raise it.

Limits. Ideal random hashes, not a real hash on real keys. I counted space as bits per item and didn't measure speed, where cuckoo filters usually do well. The Bloom side is the textbook formula with an exact, freely sized bit array, so it's the best case for Bloom. I took the first failed insert as "full", ignoring the library's one spare slot. Eight-slot buckets at 224 buckets ran out of memory for some seeds, and the 16-bit runs with the library's formula at that size didn't finish.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: A count-min sketch is right where it matters
entry.summary: On skewed streams, a second row cuts a count-min sketch's worst overcount from 10,931 to 226, and conservative update takes the top 100 items from off by 119 to exact while the average error only halves.
entry.content:
A count-min sketch counts how often each item appeared in a stream using a fixed grid of counters. It only ever overcounts. I ran one on skewed streams and found two things worth knowing: depth buys you the worst case rather than the average, and a one-line change to the update rule (conservative update) makes the most frequent items come out exact, even though the average error only halves.

The setup

The sketch is d rows of w counters. Each item hashes to one counter per row; an update adds 1 to each of those, and a query returns the smallest of the d counters it maps to. Collisions only add, so the answer is never too low. Conservative update changes the add: it raises only the counters that equal the current minimum, up to minimum + 1.

The stream: 500,000 events over 100,000 possible items, drawn from a Zipf distribution with exponent 0.8, 1.1 or 1.4 (bigger is more skewed). Widths 256 to 16,384, depths 1 to 8, five seeds each, hash ((a·x+b) mod p) mod w with a 61-bit prime. After the stream I queried every item that appeared and compared with the true count.

One sanity check on the harness: with d = 1, an item's error is just the other events that landed in its counter, about N/w on average. Measured at exponent 1.1: 1,954 against 1,953 predicted at w = 256, 485 against 488 at 1,024, 115 against 122 at 4,096, 25 against 31 at 16,384. The measured value runs slightly under the prediction at wide settings; I didn't chase why.

Depth is for the worst case

At exponent 0.8 and 16,384 counters per row, a single row had a mean error of 26.7 but a maximum of 10,931: some item shared its counter with the most popular one. Two rows (so twice the memory) brought the mean to 12.8 and the maximum to 226. At exponent 1.1 the single-row maximum was 67,325 against 296 for two rows. Going from two rows to eight only shaved the mean from 12.8 to 7.2 at exponent 0.8. A second row is the large win, and it is a win against a rare large miss, which the average hides.

With one row the mean error scales with width: it fell about 4× for each 4× in width, as the N/w formula says.

Width or depth, at the same memory

The grid above grows memory along with depth, so it can't say how to spend a fixed budget. A follow-up run did: total counters fixed at 2,048, 8,192, 32,768 or 131,072, split as 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 8 rows (width = total ÷ depth, rounded down), the same three exponents, eight seeds each.

Rows × widthMean error99th percentileMax error
1 × 8,19256.149467,323
2 × 4,09629.51152,234
4 × 2,04851.3109367
8 × 1,024106.7169301

Plain update, exponent 1.1, 8,192 counters in total, mean over eight seeds.

Each metric wants a different depth. The mean is lowest at two rows; past that, going from four rows to eight halves the width and roughly doubles the mean. The maximum keeps falling until six or eight rows. The 99th percentile sits in between, best at two to four. At exponent 1.1 that held at every budget; at 1.4 the best depth for the mean and the 99th percentile crept up to three or four rows (and deeper once errors fell below one count), while the maximum was still lowest at six or eight. At exponent 0.8 (flatter traffic) one wide row had the lowest mean at the three smaller budgets (57.1 against 76.5 for two rows at 8,192), but its maximum was 10,936 against 1,214, and two rows still won the 99th percentile everywhere.

Conservative update pays less for extra rows. At exponent 1.1 and 8,192 counters, going from two rows to four raised its mean 44% (20.7 to 29.8) against 74% for plain update, and its maximum still fell from 284 at four rows to 168 at eight. At exponent 0.8 it took the best mean from one row to two at budgets of 8,192 and up. With conservative update the top-100 error was 0.1 or less at every depth from two to eight once the budget reached 8,192 counters.

Conservative update makes the top exact

Width × depthMean error, plainMean error, conservativeTop-100 error, plain → conservative
1,024 × 4130.777.3118.8 → 0.0
4,096 × 420.111.018.3 → 0.0
16,384 × 42.10.91.8 → 0.0

Exponent 1.1, mean over five seeds. "Top-100 error" is the mean overcount of the 100 most frequent items.

The average error roughly halves, which is nice but not the story. The top 100 items went from an average overcount of 118.8 to 0.0 (to one decimal) at 1,024×4. My reading, which I didn't test separately: a heavy item's counters sit well above most others, so a light item's update, which only lifts the counters at its own minimum, rarely touches them. At exponent 0.8, 1,024×4: 316 plain against 0.3 conservative. Even at 256 counters wide, the top-100 error at exponent 1.1 with four rows dropped from 668 to 1.5.

The catch is who pays. Conservative update didn't improve the single-row sketch at all (identical numbers, as it has no minimum to be conservative about), and the rest of the items still get overcounts. The fraction of items with an exactly right count stayed small until the table was wide: at exponent 1.1 and 16,384×4, 15% of items were exact with plain update and 42% with conservative. Also, conservative update can't be merged or subtracted like plain counters can, and it needs a read of all d counters before writing, which my loop paid for (the plain version is one vectorized pass).

What I'd take from it

  • If you want "who are the heavy hitters and how big are they", use conservative update. It turns a sketch that is off by a hundred into one that's right for the items you care about.
  • Use at least two rows. One row has no protection against a collision with a giant, even when the second row costs half the width.
  • For a fixed budget, two rows if you care about the typical item, four if you care about the bad tail; eight only if the single worst answer is all that matters. One row is only competitive on the mean, and only when traffic is fairly flat.
  • More skew helps: at exponent 1.4 and 16,384×4 the sketch was exact for 96% of items (99% with conservative update) since a few items dominate the stream.

Limits. One stream length and universe size; a simple hash family rather than a production one; errors measured over items that appeared, not over queries for items that never did (those would read pure collision noise); and I didn't try deletes or merges. Counters were 64-bit integers, so overflow wasn't an issue.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: One short of a run
entry.summary: Python's list.sort does 14% more comparisons on sorted runs of 31 than on runs of 32, because runs shorter than its minimum get padded by insertion. The edge moves with the list's length, survives 3.15's new minrun, and an easy patch fixes it only by moving it.
entry.content:
Python's list.sort is built to take advantage of data that's already partly sorted. Give it 65,536 items made of sorted runs 32 long and it does 11.98 comparisons per item. Make the runs 31 long and it does 13.69, which is 14% more, even though the two inputs hold almost the same amount of order. Runs of 31 are barely better than shuffled data (14.74). The edge sits exactly at the sort's minimum run length, and it moves when the list length changes.

What the source does

CPython's sort (Timsort, with the powersort merge order since 3.11) walks the list once, left to right, looking for natural runs: stretches that are already ascending or descending (descending ones get reversed). Each run it finds goes on a stack, and runs are merged according to their lengths. Short runs are bad for merging, so in list_sort_impl in Objects/listobject.c any run shorter than minrun is padded out to minrun with a binary insertion sort that pulls in the elements that follow it:

n = count_run(&ms, &lo, nremaining);
/* If short, extend to min(minrun, nremaining). */
if (n < minrun) {
    ...
    binarysort(&ms, &lo, force, n);

minrun is picked from the list length so that the length divided by minrun is a power of two or just under one. In 3.14 it's the top six bits of the length, plus one if any lower bit is set, so for lists of 64 or more items it's between 32 and 64. For 65,536 items it's 32. For 49,152 it's 48.

On random data this is exactly right: natural runs are short, and padding them gives evenly sized chunks that merge cheaply. The design notes in listsort.txt explain it that way. But the padding doesn't look at what it pulls in. A natural run of 31 takes one element from the next run and inserts it with a binary search, about five comparisons. The next scan then starts partway through that run, finds 30 sorted items, and pulls in two more. The chunk edges drift away from the run edges, and most chunks end up being two partial runs glued together by insertion. The sort then merges 32-item chunks just as it would for runs of 32, so the insertions are pure extra work.

Counting comparisons

I built inputs by shuffling 0..N−1, cutting the result into consecutive blocks of length L and sorting each block. Then I sorted the whole list with a key object whose __lt__ counts calls, averaged over 6–8 seeds (the spread was under 0.003 comparisons per item). As a floor I used the information-theoretic minimum: log₂ of the number of ways to interleave the runs, the comparisons any comparison sort needs on average for that input.

Below 32 the stock sort sits between 13.7 and 14.7 comparisons per item. At L = 31 it is 25% above the minimum; at L = 32, 10% above. The small dips at 16 and 24 are lengths where run edges and chunk edges line up again every one or three chunks, which fits the drift explanation.

The cliff follows minrun, not the run length:

itemsminrunjust belowat minrun
65,53632L=31: 13.69L=32: 11.98
49,15248L=46: 12.98L=48: 10.99
40,00040L=38: 12.83L=40: 10.96

So data with sorted runs of 40 costs 11.73 comparisons per item in a list of 65,536 and 13.07 in a list of 49,152. Which side of the cliff you're on depends on the list's length.

Python 3.15 changed how minrun is chosen: it now produces a minrun for each run, so the run lengths add up to the list length more evenly. In the 3.15 source, the if (n < minrun) padding step is still there as before. On 3.15.0rc3 (whose sort code is the same as 3.15.0's) the 65,536-item numbers are identical, and at 50,000 items, where the minrun alternates between 48 and 49, the cliff sits at 49: 12.96 at L = 48, 10.98 at L = 49.

Does it show up in time?

Only when comparisons are expensive. With plain ints (CPython uses a fast specialised compare for lists of one simple type), runs of 31 took 149 ms against 138 ms for runs of 32 on 2²⁰ items, and with strings I couldn't see a difference. Both were measured on a busy machine, so read the int gap (about 7%) as rough. With a Python-level __lt__ that does a little work, the comparisons are the cost: 305 ms for runs of 31 against 268 ms for runs of 32 on 65,536 items, 14% slower, matching the comparison count.

A one-line patch, and what it costs

The obvious fix is to leave natural runs alone once they're reasonably long, and let the merge order handle uneven lengths, which is what powersort is for. I built CPython 3.14.0 with the condition changed to skip the padding for natural runs of at least T items, with T read from an environment variable so one binary could run both ways. With T unset, it matched the stock counts exactly.

With T = 16, runs of 31 drop from 13.69 to 12.04 comparisons per item, runs of 24 from 13.78 to 12.46, and everything from 32 up is unchanged (dashed line above). The expensive-__lt__ sort of runs of 31 went from 305 to 271 ms. Other input shapes, T = 16 against stock:

input (65,536 items)stockT = 16change
shuffled14.7414.740
runs of random length 1–4013.7713.47−2.2%
runs of random length 8–6412.3712.07−2.4%
sorted, then 1% random swaps2.192.10−4.4%
16 sorted streams dealt round-robin6.906.02−12.8%
sorted list + 1,000 new items at the end1.311.310
20 sorted, 12 shuffled, repeating13.3914.73+10.1%

The last row is the catch. Stock sorting happens to fit that input perfectly: each 32-item chunk is one sorted run of 20 plus 12 loose items. The patch keeps the run of 20, then pads the loose items by pulling sorted items from the next block, which is the same drift problem moved somewhere else. So the patch moves the cliff around rather than removing it, and I don't know which shapes real data has more of. A fix that removes it would need the padding step to notice that what it's pulling in is itself sorted, for example by merging the next natural run instead of inserting it item by item. I haven't built that.

What I'm not sure of

These are synthetic inputs with every run the same length, which is the worst case for the cliff; with run lengths that vary, the stock penalty mostly averages out (the 1–40 row is only 2% worse than the patch). Timings come from a container on one Apple M6 machine with other work running. I haven't looked through the CPython tracker for a past discussion of this exact case, so the edge may well be known and accepted as the price of keeping the merge step simple.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: A pool remembers two collections
entry.summary: Go's sync.Pool keeps objects for a number of garbage collections, not a length of time. Bursty pool users get everything back when bursts are under one GC period apart and nothing past two, so the rest of the program's allocation sets the pool's hit rate.
entry.content:
Go's sync.Pool doesn't keep objects for a length of time. It keeps them for a number of garbage collections. An object put back in the pool survives the next GC and is dropped at the one after. So whether a pool helps depends on how often the program collects, and that depends on how much everything else in the program allocates. I measured it on Go 1.27.1: code that uses a pool in bursts gets nearly every object back when the bursts come less than one GC period apart, and none when they're more than two apart. In between, the hit rate follows a straight line, 1 − (T/G − 1), where T is the gap between bursts and G is the GC period. Doubling unrelated allocation halves how long the pool remembers.

What the source does

Each pool has a primary cache and a victim cache, both split per processor (P). At the start of every GC, with the world stopped, poolCleanup in src/sync/pool.go does two things to every pool: it throws away the victim cache, and it moves the primary cache into the victim slot. Put always goes to the primary cache. Get tries the local primary, then steals from other processors' primaries, and only then looks in the victim cache.

The victim cache arrived in Go 1.13 with the commit "sync: smooth out Pool behavior over GC with a victim cache". Before it, every GC emptied every pool, and a comment on issue #22950 described a server that collected every 4 seconds or so and whose gzip-writer pool's hit rate dropped as low as 50%. The commit message says objects are now collected "within two GCs (as opposed to one)", and that in steady state there are roughly no new allocations after a GC. Both are true. The steady state is the part that has a limit.

Counting collections directly

A burst is 64 goroutines that each take a 4 KiB buffer from the pool, hold it until all 64 have one, wait 100 µs and put it back. A miss is a call to the pool's New function. First I forced exactly k collections between bursts with runtime.GC(), 100 bursts each, on an Apple M6 with the default GOMAXPROCS of 12:

GCs between burstsmisses per burst (of 64)worst burst
00.021
10.823
26464
36464

One collection costs almost nothing. Two cost everything. There's no middle ground in the mechanism itself: the gradual curve in real programs comes from where collections happen to fall.

The small loss after one GC is a detail of Get. Each processor's cache has a private slot plus a shared queue, and other processors can only take from the shared queue. When a Get finds nothing anywhere in the victim cache, it marks the whole victim cache empty, and any objects still sitting in other processors' private slots are never handed out again. With one or two processors this lost nothing in 300 bursts. With 4 it lost 0.09 objects per burst; with 12, 0.68. That's at most about 1% here.

Letting the program set the pace

Real programs don't call runtime.GC(). They collect when the heap grows enough, so the GC period is roughly the live heap (times GOGC/100) divided by the allocation rate. To model that I kept 32 MiB live and ran a background goroutine that allocates and drops 64 KiB chunks at a fixed rate, 50, 200 or 800 MB/s, while bursts fire every T milliseconds. It measured GC periods of 625, about 157 and about 39 ms, close to 32 MiB divided by the rate.

If collections are evenly spaced at period G and a gap of length T starts at a random point, the chance of two or more collections landing in the gap is T/G − 1, clipped to between 0 and 1. That's the predicted miss rate. Rows from around the switch, 60 to 300 bursts each:

background allocgap TT/Ghit rate (predicted)
50 MB/s600 ms0.960.985 (1)
50 MB/s800 ms1.280.710 (0.720)
50 MB/s1200 ms1.920.082 (0.083)
200 MB/s150 ms0.950.988 (1)
200 MB/s200 ms1.260.729 (0.737)
200 MB/s300 ms1.890.114 (0.110)
200 MB/s400 ms2.520 (0)
800 MB/s25 ms0.640.989 (1)
800 MB/s50 ms1.260.757 (0.740)
800 MB/s100 ms2.520 (0)

All 33 configurations land within 0.03 of the prediction. Once the gap is measured in GC periods, the allocation rate drops out. The same 200 ms gap is a 99% hit rate next to 50 MB/s of other allocation and a 0% hit rate next to 800 MB/s.

The GC knobs move the line the same way. At 200 MB/s with bursts every 100 ms, the default settings hit 99.2% of the time. Setting GOMEMLIMIT=44MiB, a little above the 32 MiB live heap, shortened the GC period from 158 ms to 12.6 ms, and the pool hit 0%. Going the other way, with bursts every 400 ms, the default missed every object and GOGC=400 (period 632 ms) hit 99%. A program running close to its memory limit collects so often that its pools can stop working, just when every extra allocation brings the next collection sooner.

What this means

For a busy server, where every processor uses the pool many times per GC period, this should rarely matter: the gaps are far shorter than a GC period, which is the left edge of the table, where the pool refills itself after every collection as the commit promised. The pools that quietly turn into plain allocation are the ones used now and then: a buffer pool behind a once-a-second flush, a pool of encoders for a periodic job, anything that sits idle for longer than two collections. Their hit rate isn't set by their own code. It's set by the rest of the program's garbage, and it changes when someone else's code changes. If you want objects kept for a period of time rather than a number of collections, sync.Pool can't do that, and a plain free list (a slice or a buffered channel you size yourself) can.

What I'm not sure of

This is a synthetic program on one machine (macOS, Apple M6) with other work running alongside. Its allocation is steady, so collections are close to evenly spaced. Real programs allocate unevenly, which I'd expect to blur the straight line; the rule underneath it (survive one collection, lost at the second) is what the forced-GC table shows and what poolCleanup does. I didn't test changing GOMAXPROCS at runtime, which per a comment in pinSlow throws away a pool's primary cache too, or measure on Linux.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: The fair mode was the fast one
entry.summary: Go's mutex source says normal mode is considerably faster than starvation mode. With critical sections of a few microseconds or more, forcing handoff mode got 1.25–1.8× the throughput, because a normal-mode wakeup leaves the lock idle while a thread wakes up.
entry.content:
Go's sync.Mutex has two modes. Normal mode lets a running goroutine grab the lock ahead of the ones queued for it. Starvation mode hands the lock straight to the head of the queue. The source says normal mode "has considerably better performance". I measured both on Go 1.27.1. When goroutines hold the lock for a few microseconds or more and then do some work outside it, the fair mode got 1.25–1.8× the throughput of the default on macOS (from 3 µs holds up) and 1.3–1.5× in a Linux VM (from 10 µs up). With critical sections around 100 ns, the claim holds: the two tie, or normal mode wins. The difference is where the woken waiter runs.

The two modes

Starvation mode came in with Go 1.9 ("Mutex is now more fair"), in CL 34310, as a fix for issue #13086. That issue described a goroutine that waited over 100 seconds for a lock another goroutine kept retaking. The rules, from the comment in internal/sync/mutex.go:

  • In normal mode, Unlock wakes the first waiter, but the waiter has to compete for the lock with goroutines that are already running. It usually loses, and goes back to the front of the queue.
  • If a waiter has been waiting more than 1 ms when it wakes and still finds the lock held, it switches the mutex to starvation mode. Then Unlock hands ownership directly to the first waiter, and newcomers queue at the back.
  • The mode ends when a waiter that waited under 1 ms, or the last waiter, gets the lock.

The CL's benchmarks use critical sections of about 100 ns, and there the cost of normal mode was within a few percent either way. I wanted to see longer ones.

Setup

Four goroutines, GOMAXPROCS=4. Each loops: lock, spin for h (the hold time), unlock, spin for the same h outside the lock. With four goroutines each wanting the lock half the time, the lock is oversubscribed, so ideally it's never idle and throughput is 1/h. I built Go's sync package from an overlay that makes the 1 ms threshold a variable, so one binary can run three ways: default, threshold 0 (starvation mode as soon as anyone waits), and threshold infinite (never). The overlay also counts mode switches and handoffs. Each configuration ran 8 times for 1 second with modes interleaved, on an Apple M6 (macOS) that was also running other work, so I compare modes within a batch rather than across batches.

hold hdefault (k locks/s)forced handoffGosched after Unlock
0.1 µs29410.99×1.02×
0.3 µs14001.11×1.01×
1 µs4470.99×1.22×
3 µs1591.25×1.36×
10 µs481.84×1.88×
30 µs211.41×1.51×
100 µs7.01.36×1.39×

At 10 µs the ceiling is 100k locks/s. The default reached 48k, so the lock sat idle about half the time while four goroutines were waiting for it. Forced handoff reached 89k. The "never" threshold stayed within 10% of the default at every hold time (46.5k at 10 µs): in these runs, the default spent at most about 3% of the time in starvation mode, so the 1 ms switch hardly ever fired, and the default was in effect running normal mode.

Where the time goes

The runtime's semaphore code explains it. In starvation mode, Unlock puts the waiter in the current processor's runnext slot and yields. The waiter runs right away on the same processor, and the goroutine that unlocked goes back in the run queue, where an idle processor can pick it up for its outside work.

In normal mode, Unlock also puts the waiter in runnext on the same processor, but doesn't yield. The unlocking goroutine carries on with its 10 µs of outside work, and the waiter sits behind it. To get the waiter running sooner, the runtime wakes an idle OS thread, which then has to find the waiter and steal it from the busy processor. Until one of those two things happens, nobody holds the lock.

The last column in the table is a check on that explanation. Calling runtime.Gosched() right after Unlock gives up the processor the same way handoff mode does, so the waiter in runnext runs at once. It matched or beat forced handoff at every hold time from 1 µs up, without starvation mode switching on. I'm not suggesting anyone sprinkle Gosched calls through their code; it's a diagnostic, and it would hurt in other situations.

Two more measurements narrow down the cost:

  • Before stealing another processor's runnext goroutine, the runtime sleeps 3 µs, so the owner gets a chance to run it first. On this machine that sleep takes about 7 µs. I patched it to zero, with a toggle in the same binary. At 10 µs holds, throughput rose from 36k to 41k; forced handoff got 57k in the same batch. At the other hold times it moved throughput by 7% or less, in both directions. The sleep is a small part of the cost.
  • Waking a parked thread on a pthread condition variable (what Go uses on macOS) took a median of 4–6 µs here, before the woken thread has done any scheduling work.

So each lock passed between goroutines in normal mode costs a thread wakeup, a search for work, and a steal. That's several microseconds with the lock idle. With 100 ns critical sections it doesn't matter. The unlocking goroutine comes back for the lock almost at once, and normal mode's real advantage applies: the running goroutine takes the lock again without a context switch. With 10 µs sections, the same gap costs about half the throughput.

Linux and other shapes

The same binary, built for Linux and run in a 6-CPU VM on the same machine, showed the same pattern. Forced handoff was 1.05× and 1.03× at 1 and 3 µs, then 1.41×, 1.48× and 1.34× at 10, 30 and 100 µs. Gosched after Unlock was 1.15–1.62×. A VM's thread wakeups aren't bare metal, and I haven't tested bare-metal Linux.

With 16 goroutines on 8 processors, forced handoff was 0.80× at 0.1 µs (so normal mode really is faster there), 1.20× at 1 µs and 1.65× at 10 µs. At 100 µs the default already ran the lock at its ceiling and the modes tied. A wider sweep covered 108 configurations: hold times of 0.1, 1 and 10 µs, outside work of zero, equal to or 10× the hold, 2 to 64 goroutines, and 2 to 8 processors. The median ratio of forced handoff to default was 1.00 (range 0.73 to 2.04), but it split by shape. With 0.1 µs holds the median ratio was 0.89–1.00, depending on the outside work, so normal mode was faster or equal. With 10 µs holds and equal outside work it was 1.48 (1.11 to 2.04). With 10 µs holds and no outside work it was 0.99, and with 10× outside work, 1.03. Neither of those keeps the lock busy enough for the wakeup gap to matter.

What starvation mode is for

None of this argues against the 1 ms rule; it does its job. With 10 µs holds, no outside work and 64 goroutines, the longest single wait ranged from 94 to 496 ms with starvation mode disabled, and 2–4 ms with the default. The CL's summary says unfair waits are "limited to 1ms". The waits I saw were a few milliseconds. That fits the code: the 1 ms check runs only when a waiter wakes, so a sleeping waiter can't notice it has been waiting too long until someone wakes it. Still, that's 20 to 250 times shorter than without the rule.

The surprise is the other half of the comment. Normal mode's advantage is lock reacquisition without a context switch, which is worth a lot when critical sections are a few hundred nanoseconds. When they're microseconds long and there are idle processors, normal mode pays for a cross-thread wakeup on every handoff, and handing the lock over on the same processor wins.

What I'm not sure of

This is a synthetic loop on one machine, with other work running alongside it. Absolute numbers moved between batches. Forced handoff at 10 µs got anywhere from 55k to 89k depending on the batch, which is why every comparison here is within one interleaved batch. In one early 2-second run, threshold 0 never entered starvation mode, because the switch needs a woken waiter to find the lock still held, so even "forced" isn't guaranteed. I don't know how many real programs hold a contended mutex for microseconds while processors sit idle. Before blaming the mutex, a program in that state should probably shorten its critical sections.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: Redis LFU forgets on a clock
entry.summary: A line-for-line simulation of Redis's approximate LFU: it matches exact LFU at 10,000 requests a second and does worse than LRU at 10, because counters decay by the minute. Raising lfu-decay-time drops the leftover time on every read, so often-read keys barely decay; a one-line change fixes it.
entry.content:
Redis's allkeys-lfu eviction keeps an 8-bit frequency counter per key and lets it decay with wall-clock time. I rebuilt its eviction logic in a simulator, line for line from evict.c, and ran it against exact LFU, LRU and the optimal policy. Two things came out. First, how well the approximation works depends mostly on how many requests per second the cache serves, because counters fade by the minute rather than by the request. On a fixed Zipf workload it matches exact LFU at 10,000 requests a second and does worse than plain LRU at 10. Second, raising lfu-decay-time above its default of 1 doesn't just slow the decay down. A key read a few times per decay period barely decays at all, because the leftover time is thrown away on every access.

How the counter works

Each key has 24 bits of metadata. In LFU mode, 8 bits hold a counter and 16 bits hold a time in minutes. New keys start at 5, so they aren't evicted before they get a chance. On each read, the counter goes up by one with probability 1/(10·(counter−5)+1) (10 is the default lfu-log-factor), so it grows roughly like a square root of the read count and tops out at 255. Before incrementing, Redis takes off one point per lfu-decay-time minutes since the key's stored time, then stores the current minute. To evict, it samples 5 keys, keeps the 16 best candidates seen so far in a small pool, and evicts the one with the lowest counter.

My simulator copies all of that: the counter, the minute clock, the pool's insertion rules, and the habit of evicting a pool entry without re-scoring it. The one simplification is sampling: Redis takes neighbouring keys from a random spot in its hash table, and I sample uniformly. Wall-clock time is the request number divided by a request rate. To check it, the LRU and optimal miss ratios on the standard workload (Zipf α=1, 100,000 keys, 1,000-key cache) came out at 0.495 and 0.336, matching a separate simulator I wrote for an earlier cache study.

Traffic rate decides how good it is

With fixed popularity (top panel), Redis LFU's miss ratio goes from 0.529 at 1 request a second to 0.417 at 1,000 and 0.406 at 10,000, where it matches exact LFU (0.407). Below about 10 requests a second it does worse than Redis's own LRU (0.496). Popularity hasn't changed at all. What changed is that the counters drain by one a minute whether traffic is light or heavy.

A rough rule fits this. What matters is the least popular key that ought to stay cached: if it gets fewer than about one read every ten decay periods, its counter sits near zero along with everything else, and eviction becomes close to a coin flip. With a 1,000-key cache that key gets about 0.05 reads a minute at 10 requests a second, which is where LFU and LRU cross. A 10,000-key cache pushes that key ten times further down the popularity curve, so I predicted a crossover around 100–140 requests a second. The simulator put it between 100 and 300.

The top end is fine. The counter tops out at roughly 2,500 reads a minute, and at 1 or 10 million requests a second the hottest keys all sit at 255, but the miss ratio stays at 0.407. Ties among keys that are all clearly worth keeping don't cost anything.

When popularity moves (bottom panel: every 10 minutes, all keys get new ranks), exact LFU never forgets and misses 76–93% of the time. Redis LFU with the default decay does better than LRU at every rate I tried from 30 to 30,000 requests a second, best at about 1,000 (0.433 against 0.496). The default is well chosen for that range. With a 10-minute decay it does worse than LRU everywhere, at 0.507–0.535.

The decay throws away the remainder

Here is the decay step, from LFUDecrAndReturn:

num_periods = LFUTimeElapsed(ldt) / server.lfu_decay_time;
counter = (num_periods > counter) ? 0 : counter - num_periods;

and the access path, updateLFU, writes the current minute back as ldt on every read. The division rounds down, and the remainder is never stored anywhere. With a decay time of N minutes, a key read every N−1 minutes never loses a point. For a key read at random at rate r, the expected loss per unit of time is a fraction x/(eˣ−1) of what it should be, where x = r·N is reads per decay period. At one read per period that's 58%. At three it's 16%. Monte Carlo on Redis's minute clock agrees for long decay times (0.569 and 0.158 at N=60). For short ones the minute rounding adds some decay back: at three reads per period, 19% at N=10 and 36% at N=2.

The default decay time of 1 avoids this. Stored times are whole minutes, so elapsed minutes just count minute boundaries crossed, and nothing is lost on average. The problem only shows up for anyone who raises lfu-decay-time to make counters last longer. What they get is decay that's slower than they asked for, and much slower for exactly the keys that are read often.

The fix is one line: on access, advance ldt by num_periods × N instead of setting it to now, so it means "last decrement" rather than "last access". That's apparently what the field once meant: a 2018 pull request (#4784) points out that ldt was named "last decrement time" but holds the access time. It was closed unmerged in 2023, after a separate change (#12244) updated the comments in evict.c. The behaviour stayed the same. I tested the fix as a toggle on the same simulator:

decay timeRedis todaywith the fixLRU
1 min (default)0.4200.4200.496
2 min0.4460.4210.496
5 min0.4790.4470.496
10 min0.5000.4760.496
30 min0.5100.5010.496

Miss ratio, popularity reshuffled every hour, 1,000 requests a second, 4 hours, mean of 3 seeds (spread ≤0.001).

At 10,000 requests a second the fix helps by a similar amount (0.490 → 0.457 at 2 minutes, 0.505 → 0.485 at 5). It's not a free win everywhere. At 100 requests a second the 2-minute setting is better without the fix (0.435 vs 0.454), because counters there are already draining faster than they should, and losing the remainder happens to offset that. Fixed popularity at low rates is the other case where it hurts. Over-remembering costs nothing when nothing changes, so the unfixed 10-minute decay looks better there (0.443 vs 0.468 at 10 requests a second). The fix also makes the setting mean what it says. With it, a 10-minute decay at X requests a second gives nearly the same result as a 1-minute decay at 10X from 100 requests a second up (0.4166 vs 0.4169, 0.4061 vs 0.4056). At 10 the two are 0.468 and 0.460. Without the fix, they drift further apart.

Things I expected to matter that didn't

  • Stale pool scores. A pool entry is evicted with the score it had when sampled, even if the key has been read since. That happened in 0.08% of evictions.
  • Old favourites trickling along. After a reshuffle, I kept every formerly hot key at one read every 30 seconds to 15 minutes. Every policy's miss ratio rose by at most 0.02, about the same for all of them.
  • The clock wrapping. The minute clock is 16 bits, so it wraps every 45.5 days, and a key left untouched that long briefly looks recently used with its old counter (the code also counts one minute short across the wrap). It's real, but you'd need memory to stay below the limit for six weeks for it to matter.

What I'd take from it

In my runs, Redis's LFU was a good approximation from a few hundred to tens of thousands of requests a second, with popularity that drifts over minutes to hours. Outside that range its quality depends on traffic in a way the configuration doesn't make obvious. On a quiet instance, LRU can simply be better. If you raise lfu-decay-time, expect much less decay than the number suggests, especially for keys that get regular reads.

entry.title: The GC limiter counts in its own units
entry.summary: Squeezed against GOMEMLIMIT, an allocation-heavy Go program kept GC near the limiter's 50% by the limiter's own count, and did 15–26% of its usual work. Allocation-time sweeping counts as application time, and two runtime patches show why counting it better doesn't help much.
entry.content:
Go's garbage collector has a CPU limiter that kicks in when a program runs out of room under its memory limit (GOMEMLIMIT). The comment at the top of runtime/mgclimit.go says it "sets a very conservative limit of 50%" on GC CPU. I squeezed an allocation-heavy program against its memory limit on Go 1.27.1. By the limiter's own accounting it held GC at about 55%. The program did 15–26% of the work it did with plenty of room. Most of the loss is a GC that never stops running: assists and background marking. On top of that, allocation-time sweeping counts as application time, so the limiter's 55% understates what the GC really used, which was closer to 72%.

The setup

The program builds a 256 MB live heap of small pointer-linked objects, then runs one goroutine per processor. Each goroutine does a fixed bit of arithmetic, allocates a fresh 4-object chain (256 bytes), and swaps it into a random slot, so the live heap stays the same size while the program allocates fast. After building the heap, it measures the runtime's total memory footprint, turns GOGC off, and sets the memory limit to some multiple of that footprint. Then it counts operations for 10 seconds after a 2-second warmup. I ran it on linux/arm64 with 1, 2 and 4 processors, 3 seeds each, one run at a time. "Throughput" below is relative to the same program with the limit at 8× the footprint, where the GC has lots of room.

Results

With 4 processors and little arithmetic per allocation:

Memory limit (× footprint)ThroughputGC share (runtime metrics)Peak memory / limit
81.009%0.96
no limit, GOGC=1000.8221%–
20.5334%0.99
1.50.3746%1.01
1.20.1754%1.17
1.050.2253%1.41
1.00.1855%1.40

With 4 processors the limiter turned on in every run at 1.2× and below, and in none at 1.35× and above. With 1 and 2 processors the picture was the same: across every setting where the limiter was on in all runs, throughput was 15–26% and the runtime's GC share was 53–62%. The standard deviation across seeds was up to 0.08 on the throughput column. Peak memory went 17–41% over the limit, because the limiter's response is to let the heap grow (more on that below). The limit is documented as soft, but it's worth knowing by how much.

The limiter isn't the only problem. At 1.5× the footprint, with the limiter never on in the 4-processor runs, the program ran at 37%, less than half of what plain GOGC=100 without a limit gave it. Squeezing the heap costs throughput long before the safety valve opens. With ten times more arithmetic per allocation, it was gentler: about 55% throughput at 1.0–1.05×.

Where the CPU went

A CPU profile at 1.05× with 4 processors shows where it went. The program's own arithmetic was 12% of samples; at 8× it was 66%. Mark assists, where an allocating goroutine is drafted into marking, took 35%. The background mark workers took 23%. Sweeping done on the allocation path, before a goroutine may take a new span, took 14%. I didn't break down the remaining 16%; the allocator's span refill path and write barriers are the biggest names in it.

That 14% is the interesting part.
