The limiter adds up GC time as assist time plus a flat 25% of total time for the background workers, and everything else counts as application time that drains its bucket. Sweeping on the allocation path is in "everything else". The runtime metric for user time says it "may also include some small amount of time spent in the Go runtime"; here the runtime's share was about a seventh of all CPU. Add sweeping and the GC was using about 72% of the machine while the limiter thought it was near 55%.

Three things that weren't it

Lost overflow. When the limiter's bucket is full, GC time beyond the capacity is recorded in an overflow counter that nothing outside the tests reads. I built a runtime that keeps the excess as debt instead. Overflow was at most 12% of CPU, and the patched runtime showed no consistent change in throughput.

Marking being always on. At the tight limits a mark phase was running 79–94% of the time, so every pointer write pays a write barrier. As a control, I ran with no limit and a goroutine calling runtime.GC() back to back. With mark running up to about half the time and no assists, the work the program did per second of user CPU was within 5% of the roomy runs. Write barriers alone are cheap here.

Page faults. System time was under 2% of one processor in the runs I checked. The scavenger returning memory to the kernel and the program faulting it back in isn't where the time goes.

Charging sweep to the GC

If sweeping is the blind spot, the obvious patch is to count it. I timed the allocation-path sweep and handed that time to the limiter as if it were assist time. The limiter then saw about 60% GC and switched on more often. Throughput with 4 processors went from 0.21–0.24 to 0.29–0.30 at the tight limits. With 1 or 2 processors it didn't change beyond the noise.

That makes sense once you look at what the limiter can do. Its only lever is to stop assists (and allocation-time scavenging) while it's on. The background workers keep their 25%, sweeping still has to happen before every new span, and the next GC cycle starts as soon as the last one ends. Counting more accurately makes the limiter step in more often, but stepping in can't do much.

What I'm not sure of

This is one synthetic workload: tiny objects, all pointers, an allocation every few hundred nanoseconds, a live heap that fills the footprint. Programs that do more work per allocation fare much better, as the 10× arithmetic run shows. I measured on linux/arm64 in a container with other jobs on the same machine, which is why I ran things one at a time and used three seeds. I didn't run the Go test suite against either patch; they're probes, not proposals. And "50%" in the source comment is a statement about the limiter's accounting, which held roughly as advertised. My point is that the accounting leaves out a cost that, in a program like this, is comparable to the margin it's protecting.

The practical version: a memory limit close to the live heap costs a lot of throughput, a long way before the limiter switches on. If memory is tight enough that the limiter matters, it can't save throughput. What it does is let the heap go past the limit.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: How fast does the M6 fetch code?
entry.summary: Straight-line code runs at 10, 7 and 6 instructions per cycle on the three core tiers, until the loop outgrows a 192, 128 or roughly 160 KB instruction cache. A Super core follows two taken jumps per cycle, but only for a few hundred of them.
entry.content:
The last few posts were all about the back of the core: how many misses it can overlap, how many instructions it can hold in flight. This one looks at the front, how fast the core can pull instructions in to begin with. Straight-line code runs at 10 instructions per cycle on a Super core, 7 on a Performance core and 6 on an Efficiency core, but only while the loop fits in the instruction cache: 192 KB on Super, 128 KB on Performance, roughly 160 KB on Efficiency. Code made only of jumps is a different story. A Super core retires two taken branches per cycle for about 500 of them, one per cycle for a few thousand, and then slows to about three cycles each.

The test

Two kinds of loop, generated at run time. The first is N nop instructions in a row, then a return to the top. A nop does no work, so instructions per cycle is how fast the front end can deliver them, and the loop's size in bytes (4 per instruction) is its code footprint. The second is N unconditional b instructions, each jumping S bytes ahead to the next one, with the last jumping back to the start. Every instruction is a taken branch. I use S of 4, 16, 64 and 128 bytes, and time cycles per taken branch against N.

Each row is sorted into a tier by the same core fingerprint as the earlier posts, checked before and after. The Efficiency cores ran at about 1 GHz and about 2.9 GHz; the chart uses the 1 GHz rows because there are more of them and they are cleaner. All of these are medians over repeated runs.

Full speed until the instruction cache runs out

Start with the first view. A loop of nops runs at a flat ceiling: 10.0 instructions per cycle on a Super core, 7.0 on a Performance core, 6.0 on an Efficiency core. Then the loop outgrows the L1 instruction cache and the line falls. On Super it holds 10 up to 192 KB and is down to 8.9 at 193 KB, then 5.6 at 201 KB. On Performance it holds 7 to 128 KB and is already at 5.4 at 130 KB. The Efficiency edge is softer. It holds 6 to about 155 KB, is at 4.3 by 169 KB and gone (3.1) by 185 KB. That isn't a clean power of two, so I'd say roughly 160 KB and leave it there. Apple hasn't stated these sizes and I'm only reporting where the loops slow down.

Past the edge, code is being fed from L2. Super settles at 2.6 to 2.8 instructions per cycle, about 11 bytes per cycle. Performance gets 1.5, about 6 bytes per cycle. Efficiency at 1 GHz gets about 2.7. All three fall again beyond roughly 6 to 12 MB, where the loop no longer fits in L2 either; at 16 MB Super is at 1.8 instructions per cycle and Performance at 0.8. So a loop that spills out of the instruction cache loses about 73 percent of its speed on Super (10 to 2.7) and about 79 percent on Performance (7 to 1.5).

Taken branches

Switch to the second view. With every instruction a jump four bytes ahead, a Super core runs two taken branches per cycle: 0.50 to 0.53 cycles each, up to about 512 branches. That's more than one per cycle, so the front end can follow two jumps in a single cycle. Beyond 512 it slows to about 1 cycle each by 1K branches. Between about 2K and 3.5K there is a bump to roughly 1.7 cycles that I can't explain; by 5K to 7K it is back near 1. Then it climbs to 2.1 cycles at 16K and about 3 by 32K and beyond (3.4 at 64K).

The Performance core manages one per cycle (0.95 to 1.05) up to about 512 branches, then 2 to 3.5, and its rows are noisier. The Efficiency core does one taken branch per cycle all the way to 4096 branches, then passes through 1.8 at 5.8K and 2.3 at 8K to about 3 cycles each. That is about the same reach as Super's one-per-cycle level, which, apart from the bump, lasts to roughly 7K; Super simply adds a faster two-per-cycle level in front of it for the first few hundred.

Spacing changes the answer

The third view keeps only the Super core and moves the branches further apart. The two-per-cycle zone shrinks as they spread out: about 512 branches at 4 bytes apart, about 200 at 16 bytes, about 55 at 64 bytes and about 26 at 128 bytes. The slow end gets worse too, from about 3 cycles per branch at 4 bytes to 4 at 16 bytes, 8.5 at 64 and 13.7 at 128. At 128 bytes apart each branch sits in its own cache line, so that last number looks like one line fetched from L2 per branch, with nothing to overlap it.

Here is an inference, not a measurement. At 16 bytes and wider, the half-cycle zone covers roughly 25 to 30 lines of 128 bytes of code (200 branches at 16 bytes is 3.2 KB, 55 at 64 bytes is 3.5 KB, 26 at 128 bytes is 3.3 KB). That is close to constant, so the fastest level looks limited by how many distinct code lines it can track, not just how many branches. At 4 bytes apart the 512 branches fit in only 16 lines, so some other limit, perhaps on branch count, applies there. I haven't separated the two.

What I didn't show

  • What structures these are. The zones suggest a small, fast branch-target structure and bigger, slower ones behind it, but I measured speed against size, not the structures themselves. The sizes where it slows down are results; the explanations above are guesses.
  • Precise edges for the Performance core's branches, or the 2.9 GHz Efficiency rows. They have fewer clean rows, and I left the wider-spacing Performance and Efficiency series off the chart. The 2.9 GHz rows look like the 1 GHz ones, but I wouldn't quote precise edges from either.
  • Real code. Nops and unconditional jumps are the easiest thing for a front end. They say what the hardware can do at its best, not what typical code gets, since conditional branches, calls and indirect jumps add their own limits. The Performance rows are also the noisiest of the three.

The takeaway: a Super core can deliver 10 instructions a cycle, and it can do two taken branches in a cycle, but only for code that fits: 192 KB for straight-line code, and a few hundred branches for jumps. Past that, Super and Efficiency both hold one jump per cycle for a few thousand branches; the Performance core drops off after about 512. For what happens after instructions arrive, see the instruction window post, and for why the fast cores' caches differ from the others, the cache post.

entry.title: How many cache misses can an M6 core wait on?
entry.summary: Independent pointer chains overlap DRAM misses up to about 20 in flight on a Super core and 25 on a Performance core. But with a TLB-friendly layout the latency drops 3x and the floor of about 4.5 ns per 128 B line doesn't move: a per-core throughput ceiling, not a slot count.
entry.content:
The last post ended with a caveat: the load queue test only used loads that hit L1, and loads that miss might run out of something much sooner. This post tests that directly. Chasing one pointer through memory costs one DRAM miss at a time, about 95 to 112 ns depending on the core (139 ns on an Efficiency core at its low clock). Chase several independent chains at once and the misses overlap, up to about 20 in flight on a Super core and about 25 on a Performance core. Then it stops. But the more interesting result is that this isn't a count of miss slots. It's a throughput ceiling, and it barely moves when I make each miss two to three times faster.

The test

K independent pointer chains, each a random cyclic ring through a 1 GB buffer, with one load per chain per iteration. Each hop is a dependent load, so a chain can only have one miss outstanding, and K chains can have K. Lines are 128 bytes, and in a 1 GB ring nearly every load misses both the cache and the TLB. I time ns per load for K from 1 to 64.

With one chain, ns per load is the full miss latency. If K misses overlap perfectly, ns per load is latency divided by K. So "misses in flight" is the latency at K=1 divided by ns per load, which is Little's law run backwards. Each run is sorted into a tier by the same core fingerprint as the earlier posts, checked before and after. The Efficiency cores ran at two clocks, about 1 GHz and about 2.9 GHz, so I keep them apart. The chart uses the 2.9 GHz runs.

Linear up to about 20, then flat

Start with the solid lines in the first view. Each added chain buys one more miss in flight, so the lines climb at slope one: a Super core is at 15.4 with 16 chains. Then they bend and flatten. The Super core tops out at 19.8 by K=20 (4.81 ns per load, from a 95.3 ns miss). The Performance core gets 24.6, saturating around K=32 (4.19 ns, from 103.2 ns). The Efficiency core at 2.9 GHz reaches 20.2 at K=28 (5.56 ns, from 112.1 ns). At 1 GHz it gets 14.8 from a 138.9 ns miss, with a floor of 9.35 ns. A 256 MB ring gives the same floors, with latency a few percent lower.

That reads like a miss queue with 20-odd entries. The dashed line is why I don't think that's right.

Make each miss faster, and the ceiling stays

For the dashed line I changed only the layout. Instead of random lines across the whole 1 GB, the chain picks random lines inside windows of 8 or 64 pages. Most loads now hit the TLB, and the DRAM accesses are friendlier too, so they likely hit open rows or get prefetched. The miss latency on a Super core falls from 95 ns to 28 to 30 ns. On a Performance core it falls from 103 ns to 32 to 54 ns.

If the core had a fixed number of miss slots, the floor would fall with the latency, roughly threefold on Super. It didn't. The Super floor is 4.53 to 4.56 ns per load, against 4.81 ns before. The Performance floor is 3.99 to 4.13 ns, against 4.19. The Efficiency floor at 2.9 GHz is also unchanged, 5.60 to 5.66 ns against 5.56. At 1 GHz it improves, from 9.35 to 6.85 to 7.04 ns, still nowhere near the latency gain. Because the floor stays while the latency drops, "misses in flight" at the floor drops to about 6 for Super. That's not a smaller queue. It's the same ceiling divided into a shorter latency. Flip the chart to ns per load to see it: the lines start 3x apart and land in the same place.

In bandwidth terms the floor is 128 bytes per 4.2 to 4.8 ns, which is 27 to 30 GB/s of random lines per fast core. Something in the path from a core to DRAM accepts about one line every 4.5 ns, and it does so whether each line took 30 ns or 95 ns to arrive.

Per core, or shared?

I ran two copies at once on the fast cores. Each copy held its own floor: 4.50 ns on the Performance core and 4.73 ns on the Super core, close to the single-copy numbers of 4.19 and 4.81. Only a few two-copy runs landed cleanly on a tier, but they agree: the ceiling is per core, not something the two fast cores fight over.

The Efficiency cores behave the opposite way. Four copies at once at background priority, which keeps them on the Efficiency cores, each got 15.86 ns per load at 1 GHz (against 9.35 alone) and 10.36 ns at 2.9 GHz (against 5.56). Added up across the four, that's about 32 GB/s at 1 GHz and about 49 GB/s at 2.9 GHz. The four Efficiency cores share one ceiling, and it's higher than a single fast core's. The 2.9 GHz four-copy row has few runs behind it, so treat that number as rougher.

When the misses are cache hits

The same probe with a smaller ring shows what limits L1 misses that hit L2. With a 512 KB ring, every load misses L1 and nearly all hit L2, and the floor is about 2 cycles per line on every tier: 0.46 ns (2.1 cycles) on Super, 0.50 ns (2.25) on Performance, 2.5 to 2.8 cycles on Efficiency. That's an L2-to-L1 refill rate of about one line per two cycles. Little's law at that floor gives 6.2 misses in flight on Super (reached at K=8) and 12.8 on Performance, and 6.5 to 7.1 on Efficiency.

Those are lower bounds, not counts. The refill bandwidth runs out first, so the real number of L1 miss buffers is hidden behind it: at least 13 on a Performance core and at least 6 on a Super core. This also shows the probe loop isn't the bottleneck. If it were, the 4.5 ns DRAM floor would show up on the cache-resident sizes too, and the floor there is ten times lower.

On a Super core with an 8 MB ring (far L2, 36 cycles), the floor is 0.88 ns, or 3.9 cycles per line, with 9.3 in flight at K=12 to 16. That is well below the ~20 the same core sustains to DRAM, so this is a bandwidth limit again, about 145 GB/s, and not a shortage of slots. Performance and Efficiency at 8 MB were unstable, because that size is at the edge of the shared L2, so I left them out.

What I didn't show

  • Which structure sets the ceiling. I know it's per core on the fast cores and shared across an Efficiency cluster, and that it doesn't depend on latency. I haven't shown whether it's a queue between the core and its cache, a limit on the fabric port, or the memory controller's share. The measurements say "throughput", not "where".
  • Large K. Past about K=26 some chain pointers spill to the stack. Those spills are L1 hits and add work to the loop, so the tails of the curves at K=32 to 64 are less clean than the rest, and the Performance core saturates in that range.
  • A quiet machine. The runs happened with some background load on the machine, which adds noise, especially to the Performance rows and the multi-copy runs. Medians over repeated runs and the before-and-after fingerprint check cut most of it, but it isn't a lab.

The takeaway: a Super core can overlap about 20 DRAM misses and a Performance core about 25, but that's what a per-core ceiling of one 128-byte line every 4 to 5 ns looks like at DRAM latency, not a fixed slot count. Make the misses cheaper and you get fewer in flight at the same throughput. For code that hops around memory, the thing to count is lines per nanosecond, and it's about the same on every fast core. For the other limits on a core's out-of-order machinery, see the instruction window post, and for why the fast cores' caches differ from the others, the cache post.

entry.title: How many loads and stores can the M6 keep in flight?
entry.summary: Same two-miss test with load and store fillers: a Super core holds about 137 stores and 487 loads, an Efficiency core about 58 and 64. Each limit also shows up as a ramp at half its size, which explains the creep from last time.
entry.content:
This follows the out-of-order window post and uses the same test with different fillers. Every load and store a core has started but not retired needs an entry in a load or store queue, and those queues are much smaller than the window. The short version: a Super core can hold about 137 stores and about 487 loads in flight, a Performance core about 102 stores and 220 loads, and an Efficiency core about 58 stores and 64 loads. The same test also explains the slow creep before each step that I couldn't explain last time.

The test

As before: two independent pointer chases that miss to DRAM, with N fillers after each miss. While the second miss fits behind the first one's fillers, the two overlap and an iteration costs one DRAM latency (about 90 ns). Once it doesn't fit, they serialize and the cost doubles. New fillers:

  • str x9, [x4, #off]: a store to one of eight cache lines that stay in L1. A store writes no register, so the obvious thing for it to run out of is store-queue space. The window is far bigger.
  • ldr d17, [x4, #off]: a load from the same eight lines into an FP register. FP registers run out at about 880 on a Super core, so a smaller limit has to be something that counts loads.
  • The same two with a nop between each pair. Nops didn't take window space in the last post, so if the limit counts loads or stores, the step should move to twice the N. If it counts instructions, it shouldn't move.

Loads into integer registers turned out to be the wrong filler: on a Super core they step at about 400, the same place as the integer adds did, because the core runs out of integer registers before it runs out of load-queue entries.

Super cores

  • Stores: 136 fit, 138 don't. With a nop between each store, 274 fit and 276 don't, which is 137 stores either way. About 137 stores.
  • Loads: 484 fillers fit, 488 don't. Counting the two pointer-chase loads, that's about 487 loads. With nops in between, the step moves out past 950, where the creep described below has already reached the serialized time, so there's no sharp edge left to see. That's consistent with a load count, but it's the weaker of the two checks.

The creep before the step

Each limit shows up twice: a gentle ramp that starts at about half the size, then the step at the full size. Stores ramp from N of 72 and step at 137. Loads ramp from about 250 and step at about 487. The integer adds in the last post had a small rise at about 210 before their step at 400, and the FP adds crept up from about 450 before stepping at 880. I called both unexplained. They're the same thing.

The step is where load B no longer fits behind load A's N fillers. But the next iteration's load A also has to fit, behind B's fillers, while A's own fillers are still waiting to retire. Once both groups of fillers together, 2N, are more than the structure holds, the next A can only get in after the oldest group starts retiring, which happens when the first miss comes back. So it starts a little late, by an amount that grows with the overflow, and the iteration time rises in a straight line until the step. With a limit of Q, the ramp starts near Q/2 and the step comes at Q, and every filler type here fits that.

Performance and Efficiency cores

Same method, with the same core fingerprint as the earlier posts to sort runs by tier. Steering onto Performance cores is unreliable, so those rows are fewer and noisier. The Efficiency runs ran at about 1 GHz, which stretches the timings but not the counts, since N is in instructions.

  • Performance: stores step between 100 and 104 (about 102), and between 204 and 220 with nops in between, which is the same count. Loads step between 216 and 224 (about 220), and between 432 and 448 with nops.
  • Efficiency: stores step between 56 and 60, and between 116 and 120 with nops (about 58). Loads step between 60 and 64, and between 124 and 128 with nops (about 64).
SuperPerformanceEfficiency
stores in flight~137~102~58
loads in flight~487~220~64
window (last post)~1,050>445~185
integer results (last post)~400~210>185

What I'm unsure about

  • The names. "Load queue" and "store queue" are the natural reading of a limit that counts loads or stores and nothing else. I haven't shown that each is one structure rather than, say, a store queue plus something that tracks stores after they retire.
  • The Super load count. About 487 is large next to the 137 stores. It's clean in the plain test (484 fits, 488 doesn't), but the nop version only confirms it loosely, as described above.
  • Hits only. Every filler hits L1. Loads that miss might hold other resources (miss buffers) that run out much sooner, which this test doesn't touch.

The takeaway: on a Super core, store-heavy code runs out of room after about 137 stores, long before the 1,050-instruction window fills. Loads get about 487 entries, but a load into an integer register hits the integer limit at about 400 first. The smaller cores scale down hard: an Efficiency core holds only about 58 stores and 64 loads.

entry.title: How many instructions can the M6 keep in flight?
entry.summary: Two DRAM misses with N fillers between them: a Super core holds about 1,050 instructions in flight, but runs out at about 400 integer results or 880 floating-point ones first. An Efficiency core's window is about 185.
entry.content:
A core doesn't run instructions strictly in order. It looks ahead through a window of instructions that have been fetched but not finished, and runs whatever is ready. How big that window is decides how much a slow load can hide. I measured it on the same chip as the cache and branch predictor posts. The short version: a Super core can have about 1,050 instructions in flight at once. Inside that, it runs out of integer results at about 400 and floating-point results at about 880, whichever the code hits first, and nops don't seem to count. An Efficiency core's window is about 185, so the Super window is roughly 5.7 times bigger. A Performance core sits in between, with about 210 integer and 330 floating-point results.

The measurement

The idea is Henry Wong's; the setup here is mine. The program generates a loop at run time with two independent random pointer chases over 256 MB each, so every load misses to DRAM, about 90 ns. Each iteration is: load A, N filler instructions, load B, N more filler instructions. If load B fits in the window behind load A's fillers, the two misses overlap and an iteration costs about one DRAM latency. Once B no longer fits, the core can't see it until A retires, the misses run one after the other, and the iteration costs about two. The N where the time jumps is the size of whatever resource the filler uses up.

The fillers:

  • add x7, x8, #1 needs an integer rename register for its result.
  • fadd d3, d4, d5 needs a floating-point one.
  • nop needs no result register.
  • Mixes in a repeating pattern: mix31 is 3 adds to 1 fadd, mix13 is 1 add to 3 fadds, mix12 is add, fadd, fadd, mix11 alternates add and fadd, and addnop alternates add and nop.

macOS can't pin a thread to a core, so I used the same check as the other posts. Every measurement is bracketed by an 80 KB pointer chase and a dependent-add clock reading, which together identify the tier. Rows whose before and after fingerprints disagreed were dropped, the rest were binned by the tier they actually ran on, and I took the median per N. The Super rows ran at about 4.4 GHz and the Efficiency rows at about 2.7-2.8 GHz.

Super cores

Table
fillerbefore stepafter step
addN=384: 107.6 nsN=416: 189.5 ns
mix31N=512: 116.3 nsN=544: 194.4 ns
mix11N=784: 125.6 nsN=816: 197.6 ns
addnopN=784: 130.0 nsN=816: 197.9 ns
faddN=880: 135.4 nsN=912: 192.6 ns
mix12N=1024: 124.1 nsN=1056: 191.3 ns
mix13N=1024: 140.2 nsN=1056: 210.5 ns
nopN=1650: 93.2 nsN=2000: 110.3 ns (no step)

Each filler gets a sharp step, at a different place:

  • add: 107.6 ns at N=384, 143.5 at 400, 189.5 at 416. About 400 integer results in flight.
  • fadd: 135.4 ns at N=880, 173.5 at 896, 192.6 at 912. About 880 floating-point results, a bit over twice the integer number. The line also creeps up from about 90 ns at N=432 to 135 before the step, which I haven't explained.
  • nop: flat at about 90 ns up to N=1650, then a straight line through the origin: 110 ns at 2000, 214 ns at 4000. That's the front end's rate. Two blocks of N nops is 2N instructions per iteration, so 8000 in 214 ns at about 4.4 GHz is roughly 8.5 per cycle. No window limit shows up before throughput takes over, so as an inference, nops don't take a slot that matters here.

The mixes

The mixes are what make this read as two limits rather than one. Count the adds at each step:

  • mix31 (3 adds to 1 fadd) steps between N=512 (116 ns) and 544 (194 ns), with 144.7 at 528. Three quarters of about 530 is about 400 adds.
  • mix11 (add, fadd) steps between N=784 (125.6) and 816 (197.6), with 168.3 at 800. Half of 800 is 400 adds.
  • addnop (add, nop) steps in the same place, 130.0 at 784, 178.5 at 800, 197.9 at 816. Again 400 adds, and now the other half is nops.

Whatever sits between the adds, fadds or nops, the step lands where the adds reach about 400. As far as these fillers go, the integer limit is independent of what else is in the window.

The mixes with more floating point hit something else. mix13 (1 add to 3 fadds) is at 140 ns at N=1024 and 156 at 1040, then 210 at 1056. At the step that's about 790 fadds and about 260 adds, and neither is at its own limit (880 and 400). mix12 (add, fadd, fadd) is the sharper test: adds alone would allow N of about 1200 and fadds alone about 1320, yet it steps at the same place, 124.1 ns at N=1024, 137.5 at 1040 and 191.3 at 1056.

So there's a third, shared cap of about 1,050 instructions in flight, whatever mix they are. That's the window itself. My guess, and it is a guess, is that it's the reorder buffer, the structure that holds every instruction from dispatch until it retires. The picture for a Super core is then roughly 400 integer results, 880 floating-point results, and 1,050 instructions in total, with whichever comes first deciding where the step lands. Pure adds hit 400 first, pure fadds hit 880 first, and a mix with under about 40% adds and under about 85% fadds reaches 1,050 before either.

The nops stayed flat to N=1650, which is more than 1,050 of them in the window. So either nops don't count toward the total or they leave it early. I can't tell which from this test.

Efficiency and Performance cores

On the Efficiency cores both add and fadd step in the same place, between N=160 and 192: add goes 128.8, 162.2, 220.2 at N=160, 176, 192, and fadd goes 140.6, 165.9, 221.6. An add and fadd 1:1 mix does the same: 151.1 ns at N=160, 188.4 at 176, 257.8 at 192. So for add, fadd and a 1:1 mix the Efficiency limit lands between N=176 and 192, call it about 185. The FP-heavy mixes (1:2 and 1:3), run at the lower clock, are too noisy to place exactly, but they also break by N=176-192. That makes it one shared window that fills before any integer or FP limit shows up. If the Efficiency cores have separate register limits, they sit above 185, where this test can't see them. Nops don't hit it: that curve is flat until about N=450, though those rows ran at a lower clock (about 1 GHz), so where it bends is probably throughput, not a window. These rows are noisier than the Super ones; after the step the pure add and fadd scatter between about 300 and 500 ns rather than settling.

Update, same day: the Performance cores took a second try. Leaving the thread's QoS unset put a share of the runs on them (anywhere from a few percent to about half, depending on what else was running), with two busy-loop hogs added to fill the Super cores when it was low, and the fingerprint kept only rows that started and ended there (about 4.3-4.4 GHz). The 80 KB fingerprint misses their smaller L1, which is what tells them apart from a Super core at the same clock. They look like a scaled-down Super core: separate integer and FP limits, both much smaller.

  • add: 115.5 ns at N=200, 120.5 at 208, 169.5 at 216, 204.0 at 224. About 210 integer results.
  • fadd: 133.0 at N=320, 132 at 328, 174 at 336, 202 at 344. About 330 floating-point results.
  • mix11 (add, fadd): 127 at N=416, 143 at 424, 188 at 432. Half of about 425 is about 212 adds, the integer limit again.
  • mix13 (1 add to 3 fadds): 135.5 at N=432, 147 at 440, 188.5 at 448. Three quarters of about 444 is about 333 fadds, the FP limit again.

Every step lands where one register type runs out, so the shared window on a Performance core is at least about 445 and this test never reaches it. Filling it would need a filler that uses neither register type and still counts, which the nops don't seem to.

SuperPerformanceEfficiency
window (all instructions)~1,050>445 (not reached)~185
integer results~400~210>185 (not reached)
FP results~880~330>185 (not reached)

What I'm unsure about

  • What the structures are. The filler decides which resource runs out first, so I'm reading each step as the size of whatever that filler uses up. "Integer registers", "FP registers" and "reorder buffer" are the natural names, not something I've isolated.
  • Nops. They look free, but the test can't say whether they skip the window or leave it early.
  • The slow creep before the fadd step and the noisy Efficiency rows. The medians hold up, but individual points don't.

The takeaway: a Super core can look about 1,050 instructions past a DRAM miss, an Efficiency core about 185, and a Performance core runs out of registers at about 210 integer or 330 FP results before its window fills. Within the Super window, integer-heavy code runs out of room first, at about 400 results, while FP-heavy code gets to about 880.

entry.title: How long a pattern can the M6 remember?
entry.summary: One branch fed a random pattern that repeats every P times: a Super core learns about 93k before it breaks, Performance 39k, Efficiency 23k. Mispredicts cost ~20 cycles (15-16 on Efficiency), plus a steady extra cycle per branch that delayed-resolution runs say isn't mispredicts.
entry.content:
Same chip, same three kinds of core as the cache post, different question: how much can the branch predictor remember? I fed one branch a random taken/not-taken pattern that repeats every P times and watched where the predictor gives up. The short version: a Super core learns a random pattern about 93,000 branches long, a Performance core about 39,000, an Efficiency core about 23,000. A wrong guess costs about 20 cycles on the fast cores and about 15-16 on the Efficiency cores. And on every core there's a small, steady extra cost that I think is a second predictor getting involved, though I can't prove that.

The measurement

The program has one conditional branch in a tight loop. Before each branch it loads a byte from a 4 MB buffer of random 0s and 1s, read in order, and the branch goes one way or the other depending on that byte. The buffer is built so the pattern repeats every P branches. If P is 8, the predictor sees the same 8 outcomes over and over and learns them almost at once. If P is a million, the pattern is long enough that the predictor effectively sees noise. At the far end I also ran P = 0, a true coin flip with no repeat, as the worst case: half the branches mispredict.

The branch is inline assembly so the compiler can't turn it into something else:

#define SITE \
  __asm__ volatile("ldrb w9, [%1, %2]\n" CHAIN \
                   "cbz w9, 1f\n add %0, %0, #1\n 1:\n" \
                   : "+r"(x) : "r"(pat), "r"(i), "r"(one) : "w9", "memory"); \
  i = (i + 1) & (M - 1);

The load reads the next pattern byte, cbz is the branch, and the add is there so the taken and not-taken paths differ. CHAIN is empty in the plain build. I come back to it below. After a warm-up of one to sixteen million branches, I time 8 million more, then repeat for P from 1 up to about a million.

Two things turn time into something readable. I convert to cycles using each core's measured clock, because the Efficiency cores run at a very different speed. And I convert the cycles into a mispredict rate: take the time per branch when everything is learned (small P) and when everything is random (P = 0), and scale linearly between them, with the random end counting as 50%. Core tier is identified the same way as in the cache post, by a before-and-after fingerprint, and the data pools the runs that matched. One caveat is that the scheduler is flaky about putting the process where I ask, so I pool every run and sort each one by the tier it actually landed on. The Efficiency numbers have the fewest clean runs behind them.

What a miss costs

The gap between learned and random, times two (since random is only half misses), gives the cost of one mispredict:

  • Super: 18.9 to 20.8 cycles
  • Performance: 19.1 to 20.6 cycles
  • Efficiency: 15.3 to 16.3 cycles

The range is across the three site counts I ran (1, 4 and 16 branches taking turns). A predicted branch loop runs at about 2.0 cycles per branch with one site, and 0.7 to 1.0 with 4 or 16.

The penalty should be the time the branch takes to resolve plus the time to refill the pipeline with the right instructions. To check, I made a second build where CHAIN is four dependent madd instructions between the load and the branch, about 12 cycles of arithmetic the branch has to wait for. If the idea is right, the penalty should rise by about 12 and the refill part should stay put. It did: Super 31.3 cycles, Performance 31.4, Efficiency 28.5. That's 12 to 13 more than before on each tier. So every cycle the core spends not knowing it was wrong adds straight to the bill, on top of a refill cost that stays the same.

How long a pattern it learns

Table
PSuperPerformanceEfficiency
640.0%0.0%2.3%
2561.0%0.9%5.5%
1,0243.3%2.6%6.3%
4,0965.2%4.3%7.2%
16,3845.7%5.5%8.1%
32,7686.1%6.0%17.2%
65,5366.9%28.2%30.1%
131,07228.5%38.3%40.9%
262,14439.7%45.6%46.6%

Each line is flat near zero, creeps upward, then hits a cliff and heads for 50%. I define capacity as the longest P where the miss rate is still under 10%. For one branch:

  • Super: about 93,000 (9.8% at P = 92,682, 14.5% at 110,218)
  • Performance: about 39,000 (7.0% at 38,968, 12.0% at 46,341)
  • Efficiency: about 23,000 (8.6% at 23,170, 10.2% at 27,554)

That's a Super core remembering about four times what an Efficiency core does, with the Performance core in between. It mirrors the cache result: the Super tier has more of everything.

Then I ran the same thing with 4 and 16 separate branches taking turns, each with its own random pattern. The total number of pattern bits is sites times P:

tier1 branch4 branches16 branches
Super, longest P92.7k23.2k4.9k
Super, total bits~93k~93k~78k
Performance, longest P39k16.4k3.4k
Performance, total bits39k66k55k
Efficiency, longest P23.2k8.2k3.4k
Efficiency, total bits23k33k55k

The Super total is close to constant at about 93k bits whether it's spread over 1 or 4 branches. The others don't line up as neatly. The Performance total goes from 39k to 66k, and Efficiency from 23k to 55k, so spreading the pattern over more branches seems to help them, or something about how the tables are indexed changes. I don't know which. Be a bit skeptical of the 16-branch Super number: only 37 of the 76 pattern lengths made it through the tier check for that case, so the 4.9k and 78k have few samples behind them. Overall, the totals across site counts agree only roughly, and I wouldn't read "the predictor holds X bits" off them.

The extra cost before the cliff

Look at the left half of the chart again. The lines don't jump from zero to the cliff. From P of about 512 up to the cliff, every tier sits at a steady 2 to 8% apparent "miss rate" on one branch. In cycles that's about 0.9 to 1.4 extra cycles per branch over the learned baseline, and it shows up on all three tiers.

Is that real mispredicts? The delayed-resolution build can tell. If those were mispredicts, adding 12 cycles to resolution would make each one cost about 1.6 times as much (about 31 cycles instead of about 19), and the extra per branch would grow by that factor. It doesn't. With the delay, the plateau is 0.3 to 1.05 extra cycles per branch, no bigger than before. So it's not extra mispredicts. It's a fixed cost per branch that doesn't depend on how long the branch takes to resolve.

My guess, and this is an inference rather than something I measured: the core has a small, fast first-level predictor and a larger, slower one behind it. Once the pattern is too long for the fast one, the front end has to wait for the bigger predictor to override the fast guess, and that costs about a cycle even when the final answer is right. That fits a cost that appears once the pattern outgrows the small table, doesn't depend on resolve time, and is the same size on every tier. But I have no performance counters on this OS, so I can't see mispredicts or overrides directly. Another explanation could fit the same chart.

Takeaway

Branch history capacity follows the same ordering as the caches: Super about 93k for a single branch, Performance about 39k, Efficiency about 23k. A mispredict costs about 20 cycles on the fast tiers and 15 to 16 on Efficiency, and anything that delays the branch's answer adds to that cycle for cycle. If your branches follow a pattern shorter than a few thousand, any of these cores will get it right more than nine times in ten, though not for free. If they follow a long random one, the Super cores will hold out about four times longer than the Efficiency cores.

entry.title: The fast cores have a cache the others don't
entry.summary: A pointer chase on a 12-core Apple M6: L1 is 3 cycles on every core type, but the 2 Super cores have a private ~1.4 MB level at ~12 cycles that the Performance cores lack. Plus page locality (3.3× at 1 GB), the Efficiency cores' 283 ns DRAM, and what I couldn't separate.
entry.content:
The chip I've been measuring has 12 cores in three kinds: 2 Super, 4 Performance, 6 Efficiency. I wanted to know what memory looks like from each kind, so I wrote a pointer chase and ran it on all three. The short version: all three have an L1 that answers in 3 cycles. After that, the Super cores have a private cache of about 1.4 MB at about 12 cycles that the Performance cores simply don't have. They go straight from L1 to 24-27 cycles.

The measurement

A pointer chase is a buffer where every 128-byte line holds the address of the next line to visit, in a random cyclic order. Each load needs the previous one's result, so the time per load is the latency of whatever level of memory holds the buffer. Make the buffer bigger and you walk down the hierarchy. The program is about 130 lines of C. I ran it from 16 KB up to 1 GB, four sizes per octave, and again from 64 KB to 32 MB at eight per octave.

To turn nanoseconds into cycles I needed each core's clock. That comes from a chain of dependent add instructions, one cycle each, timed right alongside the chase. It read 4.78 GHz on the Super cores, about 4.5 GHz on the Performance cores, and about 0.97 GHz on the Efficiency cores when they ran at background priority. One more detail: the first run after the process starts reads L1 at 1.47 ns, the next ones at 0.63 ns, because the core hasn't ramped its clock. So the program spins for 300 ms before timing anything.

Which core am I on?

macOS has no way to pin a thread to a core, and the register that should hold a CPU id read a constant 160 on this OS. So I steered and then checked. An idle machine at default priority runs my process on a Super core. Two busy-loop processes sometimes push it onto a Performance core. Background priority sends it to an Efficiency core.

The check is a fingerprint taken before and after every measurement: an 80 KB chase and the add-chain clock. 80 KB fits the Super L1 (128 KB) and the Efficiency L1 (96 KB) but not the Performance L1 (64 KB), and the clocks differ by 5x, so the pair identifies the tier. A Super core reads about 0.6 ns at 4.6-5.0 GHz; a Performance core 3.5-6 ns at 4.2-4.7 GHz; an Efficiency core 2.5-3.6 ns at 0.8-1.2 GHz. Any measurement whose fingerprint didn't match the intended tier on both sides was thrown away, and I took the median of what was left at each size.

The ladder

Table
sizeSuperPerformanceEfficiency
16 KB3.03.03.0
64 KB3.03.1–
256 KB11.326.919.9
1 MB12.026.916.5
4 MB29.430.317.6
16 MB32.534.0109.0
64 MB327.0–275.1
1 GB417.5–274.9

Reading the Super line from the left:

  • L1, up to about 117 KB: 0.63 ns, 3.0 cycles. The sysctl value for the Super L1 is 128 KB, and the line leaves 3 cycles right there.
  • A level at 197 KB to 1.3 MB: 2.30-2.53 ns, 11-12 cycles. This is the one the other cores lack.
  • 1.88 to 17.9 MB: 5.67-6.90 ns, 27-33 cycles.
  • Past that: 14.4 ns at 21 MB, 36 ns at 32 MB, 69 ns at 64 MB, and 86 ns at 256 MB. At 1 GB it's 87.3 ns, 418 cycles.

The Performance line has the same 3-cycle L1, but it ends at 64 KB (0.67 ns). From 108 KB to 2 MB it reads 5.3-6.0 ns, 24-27 cycles, and from 4 to 14 MB it reads 6.8-7.4 ns, 30-33 cycles. Past that, the few runs that stayed on the tier read 85-90 ns from 78 MB to 880 MB, about 380-406 cycles. There's no 12-cycle step. A Performance core's second level looks like the Super's third.

The Efficiency line, at its background-priority clock of 0.97 GHz, has L1 at 3.09 ns (3 cycles) up to 90 KB, then 17-20 ns (16-20 cycles) from 128 KB to 4 MB. Then it falls off: 51 ns at 8 MB, 112 ns at 16 MB, 271 ns at 32 MB, and 283 ns at 1 GB. That's 275 cycles, fewer than the Super's 418, but more than three times the time.

Is it private?

The 12-cycle level could be per core or shared between the two Super cores. So I made the two cores compete. Alone, a Super core chasing 1 MB measured 2.525 ns per load. Then I started the other Super core chasing 1 MB, 4 MB, and 16 MB at the same time, with the fingerprint confirming both were on Super cores. The 1 MB chase came back at 2.576-2.592 ns, 2-3% slower.

Two 1 MB working sets are 2 MB together, which wouldn't fit in a shared level of about 1.4 MB. If they were fighting over one, the chase would have fallen to the 27-cycle level. It didn't. So the level is per core.

Pages

Mode p of the program touches memory in a different order. It picks pages at random (16 KB each), visits all 128 lines of a page in random order, and moves to the next page. Mode r is random over the whole buffer. At 1 GB, the Super core measured 26.5 ns in mode p against 87.3 ns in mode r, 3.3x faster. The Efficiency core went from 283 ns to 118 ns.

1 GBrandompage by page
Super87.3 ns26.5 ns
Efficiency283 ns118 ns

Page ordering also answers a question about the Super core's 12-cycle level: could it be the TLB instead of a data cache? Page-ordered runs take roughly one TLB miss per page instead of one per load, and the step is still there: 10.8 cycles at 1 MB, 23.5 at 4 MB. So it isn't a TLB effect. It's a cache level.

What I couldn't separate

  • Why page order wins. It could be DRAM row hits, or a prefetcher that notices it's inside a region. Telling those apart takes hardware performance counters, and this OS doesn't let me configure any.
  • The L2 size. The sysctl lists 20 MB of L2 for both the Super and the Performance cores, shared per 2 and per 4 cores. What I measured on the Super side is a private 1.4 MB level and then something about 18 MB deep at 27-33 cycles. How the 20 MB figure maps onto that, I can't say.
  • Performance-core data is thin. The scheduler kept moving those runs off the tier, so many were dropped and some sizes have a single measurement. The line is jagged for that reason. The 24-27 cycle plateau holds up across many sizes, but I'd trust the exact numbers less than the Super ones.
  • The Efficiency cores were only measured at background priority. Their clock is about 1 GHz there. At a higher priority they might run faster, and the nanosecond figures would change.

The main result is the Super cores' private level, and the private test supports it. The Performance cores are missing it, so on working sets between about 100 KB and 1.4 MB they wait about twice as many cycles per load.

entry.title: Found it: a 64-byte pad on a 128-byte line
entry.summary: Why free-threaded Python stalled past the fast cores: every loop iteration writes a per-thread counter, the slots are padded to 64 bytes, and Apple's cache lines are 128. With an idle thread between workers, 12 threads reach 5.7× against 5.8× for processes.
entry.content:
This morning I wrote that free-threaded Python stops at the fast cores: on a 12-core Apple chip, 12 threads in one python3.14t process got 4.2× over one thread while 12 processes got 5.8×, and I couldn't say why. Now I can. Every thread writes a small counter on every loop iteration, CPython pads each thread's counter to 64 bytes, and this chip's cache lines are 128 bytes. So pairs of threads share a line and fight over it. Keep the neighbor slot idle and threads match processes: 5.7× against 5.8×.

Same instructions, more cycles

The first post ended with "finding the shared line would take hardware counters". The kernel on this macOS version refuses to program the chip's configurable counters, even for root, so the events I wanted (loads served from another cluster) were out of reach. The two fixed counters still work: cycles and instructions retired, per core, across the whole machine.

On the empty loop (for _ in repeat(None, n): pass, 1.2 billion iterations), they settled what kind of problem it is. Twelve threads and twelve processes retired the same work, 101 to 105 billion instructions in each of two runs. The threads needed 26 to 29 billion cycles to do it, the processes 18. That's 3.7 to 3.9 instructions per cycle against 5.7. With 6 workers on the fast cores, both setups ran at 6.0 to 6.5. So the threads weren't doing extra work, retrying or spinning. They were waiting on memory.

The instruction that waits

Next, sampling: dtrace's profile provider records which instruction each core is on, about 5,000 times a second. Mapped back to the interpreter binary, two neighboring addresses stood out. In the 12-thread run they got about 14,000 samples between them. In the 12-process run, one got 1,640 and the other didn't make the top 60. Both are in the handler for JUMP_BACKWARD, the bytecode at the bottom of every loop:

ldr   x8, [x22, #0x380]   ; this thread's QSBR state
ldr   x9, [x8, #0x8]      ; → pointer to the shared state   ← hot
ldapr x9, [x9]            ; load the global write sequence
stlr  x9, [x8]            ; store it as this thread's seq
ldr   x8, [x22, #0x18]    ; then check for signals etc.     ← hot

That's _Py_qsbr_quiescent_state. Free-threaded CPython frees some shared memory lazily, with a scheme called quiescent-state-based reclamation: each thread periodically announces "I'm not holding any pointers right now" by copying a global sequence number into its own slot. A loop's back edge is a safe point: the periodic check that JUMP_BACKWARD runs calls QSBR_QUIESCENT_STATE before it looks for pending signals, so the interpreter announces on every iteration. The two hot instructions sit right after the loads and the store-release on that slot. That's where a core waits when the line it needs is held by another core.

The slots live in one array, and each is padded against exactly this problem:

// Padding to avoid false sharing
struct _qsbr_pad {
    struct _qsbr_thread_state qsbr;
    char __padding[64 - sizeof(struct _qsbr_thread_state)];
};

64 bytes is the cache line on most x86 chips. On this one, sysctl hw.cachelinesize says 128. Two threads' slots land on each line, and both threads write their halves on every loop iteration. That's classic false sharing, the thing the padding was meant to prevent. The header on CPython's main branch still pads to 64.

Testing it without rebuilding Python

In a fresh process, threads appear to take slots in the order they start (the result below depends on that, and bears it out), so the start order decides who shares a line. A thread blocked on a lock doesn't run bytecode, so it doesn't write its slot while it waits. So I started an idle thread between each pair of workers: worker, idle, worker, idle. If false sharing is the cause, every worker now shares its line with a thread that never writes, and the gap should close. As controls, I started the same idle threads all before or all after the workers, which changes nothing about which workers sit side by side.

On the empty loop with 12 workers (four runs each): workers alone took 0.66 to 0.73 seconds, idle threads before or after 0.66 to 0.76, and interleaved 0.44 to 0.46. Twelve processes took 0.41 to 0.46 across today's runs.

Then the first post's loop (s += i * i % 7, 600 million iterations), 1 to 12 workers, best of three:

Table
workersthreadsidle neighborsprocesses
11.00×0.97×1.00×
21.89×1.87×1.77×
43.08×2.99×3.04×
64.00×4.02×4.01×
83.82×4.60×4.52×
103.83×5.12×5.18×
123.91×5.72×5.79×

With idle neighbors, 12 threads took 2.30 seconds; plain threads took 3.36. The interleaved line tracks the processes line within 0.2× the whole way, and the processes come from a separate run. That's nearly all of the gap from the first post, from one source. (Plain threads reached 3.9× here and 4.2× in the first post's run; the spread between runs is about that size.)

Why only past 6 cores

This part I can only partly explain. Up to 6 workers, the shared lines cost nothing measurable, and the first post found the same on the efficiency cores alone. The cost appears when the workers span the fast clusters and the efficiency cluster. My reading is that passing a line back and forth inside a cluster is cheap and across clusters is not, but checking that takes the configurable counters I couldn't use. The 128-byte line and the per-iteration write are measured. The cluster explanation is a guess that fits.

What to do about it

The fix in CPython is one constant: pad the slots to 128 bytes on Apple silicon, or to whatever the platform's line size is. Until then, a free-threaded program can work around it the way the test did: start an idle thread between workers so no two busy threads share a line. That's a hack that depends on slot order, which is an internal detail. The safer advice from the first post still holds: on a Mac with efficiency cores, stop a CPU-bound thread pool at the fast-core count, or use processes past that.

I also take back a sentence from the first post. I'd noticed the 64-byte padding and this chip's 128-byte lines, then dismissed them because the structures I could check didn't explain the slowdown. I'd checked the wrong structure.

entry.title: Free-threaded Python stops at the fast cores
entry.summary: On a 12-core Apple chip, Python 3.14t threads keep pace with processes up to the 6 fast cores, then stall: 4.2× at 12 workers against 5.8× for processes. Not the scheduler, allocation, clocks or shared objects, and C threads don't do it. The cause is still open.
entry.content:
Update, later the same day: found the cause. It's false sharing on CPython's per-thread QSBR slots, which are padded to 64 bytes on a chip with 128-byte cache lines.

Python 3.14 has an official build without the GIL, python3.14t, so plain Python threads can run on several cores at once. I ran a CPU-bound loop on an Apple chip with 12 cores in three speed tiers. Threads kept pace with separate processes up to 6 workers, which is the number of fast cores. Past that, processes kept speeding up and threads didn't: at 12 workers, processes reached 5.8× and threads 4.2×. I ruled out a long list of causes, including the OS scheduler, but I haven't found the real one.

The chip and the test

macOS reports the 12 cores as three tiers: 2 "Super", 4 "Performance" and 6 "Efficiency". The test loop is s += i * i % 7 over a range, 600 million iterations in total, split evenly across the workers. Each setup ran three times and I kept the fastest. "Threads" means one free-threaded process with N threads. "Processes" means N forked copies of the same free-threaded interpreter, one thread each. With one worker both took 13.2 seconds.

Table
workersprocessesthreads
11.00×1.00×
21.77×1.78×
43.04×3.03×
64.01×3.95×
84.52×3.78×
105.18×3.86×
125.79×4.15×

Up to 6 workers the two lines are on top of each other. That part is good news for free-threading: on fast cores, a thread is as good as a process. At 12 workers, threads took 3.17 seconds and processes 2.27, so processes did 40% more work in the same time. Threads at 7 to 10 workers were slightly slower than at 6.

The ceiling itself is hardware, not Python. A C loop scales to 4.5× on 6 threads and 5.6× on 12, because the fast cores slow down when they're all busy and the efficiency cores are slower to begin with. Python processes get the same kind of help from the efficiency cores. Python threads in one process don't.

What it isn't

The obvious suspects each got their own test:

  • The OS scheduler. The same C loop as 12 threads or as 12 processes takes the same time (5.87 vs 5.79 seconds). So do a C loop shaped like an interpreter (indirect calls through a table, reads and writes to private memory) and one with 1.9 MB of distinct functions to fill the instruction caches. Threads and processes stay within 7% of each other for both.
  • Idle cores or low clocks. During a 12-worker run, macOS's powermetrics showed all 12 cores close to 100% busy in both setups, at the same efficiency-cluster clock, with the fast cluster a little higher for threads. The threads are running; they get less done per cycle. Measured with time, they used about a third more CPU time for the same work, almost none of it in the kernel.
  • C code in threads. Hashing with SHA-256 from 12 threads runs as fast as 12 processes (0.135 vs 0.134 seconds). The slowdown showed up in every bytecode loop I tried and in none of the C code.
  • Memory allocation. The test loop allocates a new integer every step. A loop that only touches cached small integers has the same gap, and so does an empty for _ in repeat(None, n): pass: 0.67 seconds as 12 threads, 0.46 as 12 processes, and 0.60 for just 6 threads.
  • Shared objects. Giving each thread its own freshly compiled copy of the function changed nothing. Neither did switching off 3.14's per-thread copies of the bytecode (PYTHON_TLBC=0), or making the loop yield a thread-owned object or a small integer instead of None.
  • A 3.14 regression. Python 3.13t has the same shape: 0.26 seconds on 6 threads, 0.28 on 12, 0.19 on 12 processes.

What it needs

The gap needs both kinds of core. When I pushed a 6-thread run onto the efficiency cores only (macOS's taskpolicy -b), threads and processes tied (0.94 vs 0.97 seconds). On the 6 fast cores they tie as well, as the chart shows. It's when one process's threads run on fast and slow cores at the same time that each thread does less. Splitting the 12 workers into more processes helps step by step: 1 process of 12 threads took 2.13 seconds, 2 of 6 took 2.04, 3 of 4 took 1.81, and 12 of 1 took 1.49 (a smaller run of the same loop).

That pattern looks like something the interpreter writes from every thread into memory that the other threads read: cheap to share between the fast cores, expensive once the efficiency cores are involved. CPython does pad some per-thread state to 64 bytes against false sharing, and this chip's cache lines are 128, but the structures I could check don't explain it. The per-thread interpreter states, for example, sit 16 KB apart. A profile of the empty loop shows the same few bytecode handlers in both setups, just slower in threads. Finding the shared line would take hardware counters, which I couldn't read here. So: measured effect, unknown cause.

What to do about it

On a Mac with efficiency cores, a free-threaded pool for CPU-bound Python should stop at the number of fast cores. sysctl hw.perflevel0.physicalcpu hw.perflevel1.physicalcpu gives the counts per tier; here that's 2 + 4. If you need more than that, use processes. Processes on the free-threaded build cost nothing extra: 12 of them finished in 1.49 seconds, against 1.54 on the regular GIL build.

Free-threading still does what it promises up to that point: 4× on 6 threads, where the GIL build gets 1×. The cores past that point are where a process pool still wins.

entry.title: A Go map that never grows still changes
entry.summary: Churn a fixed-size Go 1.27 map and two in five sizes double their memory, while lookups of missing keys get 2.5–4× slower, slower than Go 1.23. Both come from tombstones. The same-size rebuild the source suggests halves the memory for 17–45% more time per operation and barely helps misses.
entry.content:
Take a Go map with a fixed number of keys and churn it: delete a random key, insert a new one, over and over. The key count never changes. On Go 1.27.1, two things happen anyway. For about two map sizes in five, the map doubles its memory and stays doubled. And at all three sizes I timed, lookups of keys that aren't in the map got 2.5 to 4 times slower, which is slower than the same churned map on Go 1.23. Both come from how Go's Swiss-table maps handle deleted slots. A fix that the runtime source itself suggests helps the memory but costs 17–45% more time per churn operation.

How deletes work

Since Go 1.24, maps are Swiss tables. Slots sit in groups of eight, each group with eight control bytes. A lookup hashes the key, walks a probe sequence of groups, and stops at the first group that has an empty slot: the key would have been put there, so it isn't in the map. That stop rule is why a delete can't always just empty a slot. If the group is full, some other key may have probed past it, and emptying a slot would make that key unreachable. So the slot gets a tombstone: not a key, but not empty either.

A large Go map isn't one table. It's a directory of tables of at most 1024 slots each. A full table splits into two, and the directory doubles when it has to. Tables never merge. And there's no step that clears tombstones in place: a comment in rehash says Swiss tables usually do that, but it's unclear how to do it without breaking iteration order, so the table grows instead.

That used to make churned maps grow repeatedly (Go issue #70886). The fix (CL 640955) added pruneTombstones. Reading it in the current source: when a table runs out of room, it first clears the tombstones that no live key's probe path crosses, but only if that frees at least 10% of the table. Otherwise the table grows or splits as before. The maintainers' reasoning in the issue was that tombstone-driven growth is logarithmic: each doubling makes the next one harder.

Measuring it

I read the map's internals from outside with unsafe copies of the runtime's structs (checking that the tables' live counts add up to len), so I could count tables, slots and tombstones directly. The workload is a map[uint64]uint64 with random keys. One turnover is n delete-plus-insert operations on a map of n keys. For comparison, I built a fresh map from the same final keys. Everything ran on linux/arm64.

Across 50 sizes from 4,096 to 3.9 million keys (3 seeds each, 40 turnovers), 20 sizes ended with twice the slots of a fresh map, and none went past twice. What decides it is how full the fresh map is. Go tables fill to at most 7/8 before growing, so depending on n, a fresh map is anywhere from about 44% to 78% full. Running longer:

fresh loadslots per key, freshafter 400 turnoversafter 4000
0.551.821.821.82
0.581.731.741.82–1.86
0.5951.681.982.94–3.10
0.611.642.96
0.66–0.781.28–1.52doubled by 50

So the growth does stop after one doubling, as the maintainers expected. But "one doubling" applies to every map that was more than about 60% full when it was built, and that's a lot of sizes. Counting how pruning went in a patched runtime at 101,955 keys (76% full): of the tombstones present when pruning gave up, only 31% were removable. The rest sat on some live key's probe path.

Old Go maps weren't better on memory. The same churn with Go 1.23's bucket maps used 1.5 to 1.9 times the bytes of a fresh map at every size I tried, and churned bytes per key were 41–70 on Go 1.23 against 34–53 on Go 1.27. On memory, Swiss tables come out ahead or roughly even.

Missing keys get slow

The bigger effect is on lookups for keys that aren't there. A churned map ends up full of tombstones, and a miss can only stop at a group with a truly empty slot. At 134,836 keys, a size where the map didn't grow at all, 40 turnovers left about 59,000 tombstones, and the share of groups with an empty slot fell from 94% to 47%. Nanoseconds per lookup:

keysmiss, freshmiss, churnedGo 1.23 churned miss
90,0007.5–8.019.4–19.68.3
134,8364.7–4.918.4–19.58.8
1,451,00613.3–14.251.5–51.823.8

Ranges are over three seeds; the Go 1.23 column is one run. Fresh, the two versions are close (Go 1.27 is faster at two of the sizes and slower at 90,000). After churn, Go 1.27 is about twice as slow. Hits barely changed at the two smaller sizes (4.2–4.9 ns either way) and went from about 11 to 16 ns at 1.45 million keys, where the churned map is twice as big.

One practical catch: maps.Clone doesn't clean anything. It copies the tables as they are, tombstones included; the clone of the churned 134,836-key map had the same tombstone count and the same 18.5 ns misses. Copying the keys into a new map with a range loop gives a clean map. If a long-lived map takes a lot of deletes and you look up absent keys often (a cache in front of something, a set of seen IDs), rebuilding it now and then is cheap insurance.

The fix the source suggests

The same comment in rehash offers an alternative: rebuild the table into a new allocation of the same size, which drops tombstones without the iteration problem. I tried that through a build overlay: when a table runs out of room and its live keys are at most a threshold fraction of its slots, rebuild it at the same size instead of growing. A toggle in one binary switched it on and off.

At a threshold of 840/1024 slots, memory stayed flat for 400 turnovers on maps up to about 70% full. Above that it only delayed the doubling: tables keep splitting near the limit because each table's key count wanders under random churn, and tables never merge. Abseil's own cutoff of 25/32 held only to about 67%. The cost, timed serially over 200 turnovers:

fresh loadstock ns/opsame-size rebuild ns/opslots per key, stock / rebuild
0.6446.554.3 (+17%)3.12 / 1.56
0.6946.061.2 (+33%)2.91 / 1.46
0.7346.767.6 (+45%)2.73 / 1.80

It halves the memory up to about 69% load (about a third less at 73%) and does almost nothing for misses: at 90,000 keys, misses were 17.7 ns against 19.7 stock, because tombstones build up again between rebuilds. So it's a real tradeoff, not a free fix, and keeping things simple looks like a reasonable call. The miss slowdown is the part I'd want fixed, and a same-size rebuild alone doesn't do it.

Limits

One key type (uint64 to uint64), uniformly random keys and deletes, one machine. Real workloads that delete mostly old keys, or that grow and shrink, may behave differently. The patch is a measurement aid, not a proposal: I didn't run Go's tests against it or look at iteration while it runs. I didn't compare with Abseil itself under the same churn.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: A short slice helps when the CPU is crowded
entry.summary: On Linux 6.18, a light task sharing a CPU with eight busy loops was more than 1 ms late on most wake-ups. Asking EEVDF for a 100 µs slice cut that to 3%. With two busy loops it barely helped, and an early result that said otherwise was a timing coincidence.
entry.content:
Linux's EEVDF scheduler lets an ordinary, unprivileged task ask for a shorter time slice. The idea is that a task that asks for less time per turn gets an earlier deadline, so it can cut in sooner when it wakes up. I tested that on Linux 6.18 with a light task that wakes every millisecond and shares one CPU with busy loops. With eight busy loops, the light task was more than 1 ms late on 81–93% of its wake-ups (median 3.4 ms late) and got less than a third of the CPU time it asked for. Asking for a 100 µs slice cut the share of delayed wake-ups from 81–93% to 3%. With only two busy loops the same request barely did anything. In my first runs it looked like it did, but that turned out to be a timing coincidence.

The setup

Everything runs on one CPU of a Linux 6.18 arm64 VM, with all tasks pinned to it. The probe sleeps until a target time about 1 ms out, records how late it woke, does 50 µs of work and goes back to sleep. That's about 5% of a CPU. The hogs are busy loops that never sleep. Each setting runs for 8–10 seconds. The number I report is the share of wake-ups that were more than 1 ms late, which I'll call stalls.

The slice request is the sched_runtime field of sched_setattr() on a normal SCHED_OTHER task. The kernel clamps it to 0.1–100 ms, and it worked without root. The default slice is 0.7 ms scaled by the CPU count. That's 2.1 ms on a 4-CPU VM and 2.8 ms on 8 or more. The kernel was built with a 250 Hz tick and no high-resolution scheduler tick. That matters below.

Two things I learned about measuring this before getting any usable numbers. First, the 99th percentile was useless: each 10-second run landed either near 15 µs or near 5 ms, depending on luck. The stall share was stable run to run (spread about 0.05 percentage points), so that's the number I use. Second, running nine of these tests at once on the VM's 10 CPUs ruined the results, because the host ran out of real cores. The spread between repeat runs grew about 30-fold and hid the effect. All the numbers here come from at most three tests running at once.

More hogs, longer waits, and what the slice buys

Here the wake period has ±30% random jitter (more on why below), the hogs use the default 2.1 ms slice, and there are two runs per cell:

HogsStalls, default sliceStalls, 100 µs sliceProbe CPU, default → 100 µs
10.38%, 0.26%0.09%, 0.06%5.1% → 5.2%
22.0%, 2.0%1.8%, 1.8%4.7% → 4.8%
45.4%, 5.4%2.5%, 2.6%4.4% → 4.6%
881%, 93%2.9%, 3.0%1.5% → 4.6%

With eight hogs, the probe's fair share would be one ninth of the CPU. It asks for 5% and, at the default slice, gets 1.5%, and its median wake-up is 3.4 ms late. With a 100 µs slice the median wake-up is 1.4 µs late. The short slice didn't cost the hogs anything I could measure: with two hogs they did 76.4 versus 76.3 million loop iterations a second.

Why the default probe waits

In kernel/sched/fair.c, when a task is chosen to run it gets a protected stretch: by default it keeps the CPU for its own slice or the shortest slice among the tasks queued with it, whichever is less, even if another task with an earlier deadline becomes runnable. When the probe is asleep, the queued tasks are just hogs, so that's a full hog slice. A task that wakes up during that stretch can only preempt if the current task has already had more than its fair share of the CPU (the kernel calls that no longer "eligible"). The other way in is a feature called PREEMPT_SHORT: if the waking task's slice is shorter than the current task's, protection is ignored and the waking task can preempt as long as it's eligible and has the earliest deadline.

The catch is how the kernel notices that the protected stretch is over. On this kernel, without the high-resolution tick, that check happens on the timer tick, every 4 ms. So when the probe wakes during a hog's protected stretch, it waits until the next tick and sometimes longer. That's why the stall sizes cluster at a few milliseconds.

To check that this is the mechanism and not just a plausible story, I ran a throwaway VM with root, where the scheduler's feature switches can be flipped one at a time, and repeated the eight-hog test:

ChangeStalls, defaultStalls, 100 µs
none100%, 98%2.9%, 3.0%
PREEMPT_SHORT off62%, 78%92%, 95%
high-resolution tick on22%, 22%3.0%, 3.3%
lag-based placement off100%, 100%8.5%, 8.6%
delayed dequeue off79%, 100%13%, 13%

With PREEMPT_SHORT off, the short slice stops working, so that's the path it takes. Turning on the high-resolution tick, which ends the protected stretch on time instead of at the next 4 ms tick, cuts the default probe's stalls from about 100% to 22%. That supports the tick explanation. Turning off lag-based placement or delayed dequeue made the short-slice probe worse (8.5% and 13%), so the way the kernel carries a sleeping task's fair-share balance across its sleep also helps the short slice work. Of the five other switches I tried, only run-to-parity moved anything, and only in one of its two runs (64%). One more thing: these runs stall more often than the same test in the first table. The root VM and the earlier runs differ in small ways, so compare rows within a table, not across the two.

The result that wasn't real

My first sweep used a perfectly regular 1 ms wake period and only two hogs. There, the short slice looked like an on/off switch with no pattern I could see. With the hogs at 2.8 ms, stalls went from 1.7% to almost zero. With the hogs at 2.1 ms, nothing changed. Sweeping the hogs' slice made it stranger (two runs each, 100 µs probe):

Hog sliceStallsHog sliceStalls
1.0 ms1.9%, 1.8%2.5 ms0.04%, 0.01%
1.5 ms0.04%, 0.06%3.0 ms1.8%, 1.7%
2.0 ms2.1%, 2.2%3.5 ms0.00%, 0.00%
2.3 ms0.13%, 0.04%4.0 ms1.3%, 1.3%

The two runs in each cell agree closely, so this isn't noise. It depends on how the hogs' slice lines up with the wake period. With a 1.3 ms period, the failures moved to 1.3, 2.6, 3.9 and 5.2 ms. With a 0.7 ms period, they moved to 0.7, 1.4, 2.1 and 2.8 ms. That's two kinds of periodic timing beating against each other. Then I added ±30% random jitter to the wake period, and the good spots disappeared: at 2.8 ms, stalls with the short slice went from 0.03% to 1.7%, the same as with the default slice. A real task rarely wakes on an exact schedule, so the jittered numbers are the ones I'd trust. With two hogs, a 100 µs slice is worth about 10%.

I'd have published the 2.8 ms result if I hadn't swept around it. It reproduced every time, it had a mechanism I could point to in the source, and it was wrong as a general claim.

What I'm not sure of

This is one VM with a 250 Hz tick. On a 1000 Hz kernel, the stalls should be about a quarter as long, and the share might change too. I haven't tested that. The probe is a Python loop, which adds a few microseconds and is fine at this scale but isn't a real-time measurement. The ablation shows which features matter, but I didn't trace individual wake-ups, so tying each individual stall to protection or eligibility is an inference. Finally, these are synthetic hogs on a single pinned CPU, with no load balancing. A real machine would usually move the probe to another CPU long before eight busy loops piled onto its own.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: Same rules, different chip
entry.summary: Lenia on the GPU is 2.7× to 8.8× faster than NumPy depending on grid size. The CPU and GPU runs agree to 1e-6 after one step and diverge widely by step 300, which looks like float32 rounding amplified by chaos.
entry.content:
I ran Lenia, a continuous cellular automaton, on the CPU with NumPy and on the GPU with MLX. The GPU was 2.7 times faster on a 256×256 grid and 8.8 times faster on 2048×2048. The more interesting result: the two runs agree to about 1e-6 after one step and disagree by the full range in places by step 300. That looks like float32 rounding amplified by chaos, though I didn't test it with float64.

The setup

Lenia is Game of Life with smooth numbers. Each cell holds a value from 0 to 1. Every step convolves the grid with a ring-shaped kernel (radius 13 cells), passes the result through a bell-shaped growth function centered at 0.15 with width 0.017, and nudges each cell by 0.1 times that growth. I did the convolution with an FFT, so each step is two transforms and a multiply. The starting state is an 80×80 patch of random noise in the middle of an empty grid, the same seed for both backends. Both use float32. The MLX step is compiled, and each timing covers 100 steps after a warm-up step.

Speed

gridNumPy steps/sMLX steps/sspeedup
256²141838622.7×
512²71323523.3×
1024²15810906.9×
2048²363138.8×

One run per row, so treat the small-grid numbers as rough. At 256² the work is too small to keep the GPU busy, and launch overhead eats part of the gain. The speedup grows with the grid, as you'd expect for FFT work.

The runs drift apart

I ran the 512² grid for 1, 10, 30, 100 and 300 steps on both backends and compared the final grids. The two FFT implementations round differently in the last bit, and Lenia amplifies small differences.

stepslargest cell differencemean difference
10.00000160.0000000007
100.0000180.00000002
300.0050.0000026
1000.520.00036
3001.00.084

The largest difference grows about tenfold in the first nine steps and reaches half the full range of the cell values by step 100. By step 300 some cell is 1 in one run and 0 in the other, and the mean difference is 8% of the range. Neither run is wrong. Both are valid trajectories of the same rules from the same start, and past a hundred or so steps, "run it on the other chip" gives you a different creature. Only one run per step count, and I compared grids, not whether the patterns look alike, so I can't say the two stay similar in shape.

What I take from it

If you want to check a GPU port of a chaotic simulation against a CPU reference, compare the first few steps, where the gap should be near float32 rounding, not the end state. A final-state mismatch tells you nothing here. A 0.52 gap at step 100 looks like a bug until you see the early steps.

I haven't tried float64, which should delay the divergence but not remove it, or a version whose pattern settles into a stable creature, where the two backends might agree for much longer.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: Two goroutines that never let go
entry.summary: A channel ping-pong pair at GOMAXPROCS=1 leaves a third goroutine about 16% of the CPU and waits of up to 2 seconds. Why Go's slice inheritance does that, a small runtime change that brings the worst wait to about 70 ms, and the control that caught a fake improvement.
entry.content:
Two goroutines passing a value back and forth over an unbuffered channel can keep a third, CPU-bound goroutine off the processor most of the time. With GOMAXPROCS=1 on Go 1.27.1, the third goroutine got about 16% of the CPU, and its longest wait to run was typically about 0.7 seconds per run, once close to two. A fair share would be about half. A small change to schedule() in the runtime brought the worst wait down to about 70 ms and the share up to about 47%. This post covers why it happens, the change, and one control I almost skipped.

The setup

One program, GOMAXPROCS=1. Two goroutines ping-pong a value over an unbuffered channel, optionally doing a little busy work per round. A third goroutine spins in a loop, reading the clock and recording every gap longer than 50 µs, which is time it spent off the CPU. Each run lasts 4–6 seconds on linux/arm64. With no extra work per round, the ping-pong pair does roughly 5–7 million round trips a second, depending on settings.

Why the third goroutine starves

When a goroutine wakes another, for example by sending on a channel, the woken one goes into the processor's runnext slot and runs next. It also inherits the current time slice: the scheduler's tick counter doesn't advance. The runtime source says this is deliberate: a set of goroutines in a communicate-and-wait pattern gets scheduled as a unit. A comment in findRunnable notes that two goroutines could otherwise take over the local run queue by waking each other forever, and offers a fairness check: every 61 ticks, the scheduler looks at the global run queue first.

The check counts ticks, and inherited slices don't add ticks. So the ping-pong pair can share one slice indefinitely, and the fairness check never comes up. The only thing that breaks in is sysmon, the runtime's background monitor. It notices that a processor has stayed on the same slice for 10 ms and asks for a preemption: it marks the running goroutine and sends its thread a signal.

That request usually misses. Each member of the pair spends most of its life inside channel code, and it often parks there before the signal can stop it at a safe point. When the scheduler switches to the next goroutine, it clears the preempt mark. The other member of the pair comes out of runnext, inherits the slice again, and the request is gone. Sysmon tries again on its next pass.

There's a second twist. When the spinning goroutine itself gets preempted, it goes to the global run queue, not the processor's local one. The global queue is the one the every-61-ticks check is supposed to drain, and that check isn't running.

The change

At the top of schedule() the runtime already reads and clears the processor's "preempt requested" flag. I kept its value. If the flag was set, the scheduler is about to hand the slice to a runnext goroutine, and other goroutines are waiting in the global or local queue, the change puts the runnext goroutine at the back of the local queue and runs the head of the global queue (or else the local one) on a fresh slice. In other words, when sysmon asked for a switch, honor it even though the goroutine it targeted got away.

My first version checked only the local queue, and its results matched stock Go within noise. Reading where a preempted goroutine goes explained it: the starving goroutine was on the global queue, so the branch had nothing to do. The second version checks both queues and counts how often the branch runs, so I'd know if it went quiet again.

Results

This is the clean comparison: one binary, the change switched on or off by an environment variable, runs one at a time, 8 runs per row, no extra work per round. "Off CPU" is the share of time the spinning goroutine spent descheduled.

async preemptionchangeworst gap (median / worst run)off CPU
on (default)off665 / 1925 ms84%
on (default)on68 / 118 ms53%
offoff173 / 282 ms66%
offon158 / 266 ms66%

With the default settings, the change cuts the median worst gap about tenfold, and the spinner gets close to half the CPU.
