With async preemption off (GODEBUG=asyncpreemptoff=1), sysmon never sets the processor flag, so the change never runs and the rows match. Starvation still happens in that mode; this change doesn't touch it.

A wider sweep, with stock and patched binaries run four at a time and 5 runs each, varied the busy work per ping-pong round. With the change, the worst gap stayed under 100 ms at every level. Stock Go reached 2 seconds with little or no work per round. By about 3,000 loop iterations per round, the two converge: each pair member now runs long enough to be stopped at a safe point, and ordinary preemption works.

The pair gives up throughput, as it should: it no longer has the CPU to itself. Per second of CPU it actually got, it did 3–11% fewer round trips than stock, depending on the run set. I didn't separate the cost of extra switching from run-to-run noise.

The control I almost skipped

My first comparison was two separate binaries, stock and patched. The patched one also looked better with async preemption off, where the counter said the change ran zero times. Run serially, without the parallel jobs, the gap was still there. So something besides the change differed between the two builds. Code layout and timing are the likely cause, and in this test small timing shifts decide who wins the race against sysmon. Toggling the change inside one binary removed that difference, which is why the table above uses a toggle. The default-settings result held up; the async-off "improvement" didn't.

What I'm not sure of

This is one processor and one synthetic workload. I haven't checked the change with several processors, with goroutines locked to threads, or during garbage collection, and I didn't run the Go test suite against it. It's a sketch of the idea, not a patch to send. The behavior is a known one: Go issue #73964 reports latency spikes from the same slice inheritance (triggered there by short sleeps rather than channels), and a fix along these lines is one of the options discussed there. Earlier reports go back to #52934.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: MLX keeps every buffer you ever made
entry.summary: Evaluating over many sequence lengths grew MLX's buffer cache to 11 GB a process. A small repro: 120 distinct shapes leave 5 GB cached, one line caps it, and the cap costs nothing unless you set it to zero.
entry.content:
While evaluating the models in the adding-numbers post, each evaluation process grew to about 11 GB. Three at once pushed the machine deep into swap and the processes got killed. One line fixed it: mx.set_cache_limit(1 << 30). Evaluation went from about 16 minutes (while swapping) to 35 seconds at a 1.7 GB peak. Here is a small script that shows the same thing, with numbers.

What's going on

MLX doesn't hand freed GPU buffers back to the system. It keeps them in a cache and reuses one when a later allocation asks for a matching size. That's a good deal when you run the same shapes over and over, as in training. Greedy decoding without a KV cache is the opposite. Every step feeds a sequence one token longer, and I was evaluating many lengths and batch sizes. Each new shape needs buffers of sizes the cache has never held, so nothing matches. The old buffers sit there, and the cache keeps growing.

Two details cost me time. mx.get_peak_memory() counts live arrays only, so it stayed small the whole time while the process ballooned. The number to watch is mx.get_cache_memory(). And the growth is cache, not a leak: it goes away with mx.clear_cache().

The repro

A 4-layer, width-256, 8-head transformer with random weights and explicit softmax attention. For each of 120 shapes it runs two greedy steps. The sequence length is 16 plus the shape index and the batch size cycles from 4 to 16, so no two shapes repeat. I ran each configuration twice. The cache figure is the largest value seen at the end of any of four phases; the two runs agreed to within a few MB, and the table shows the larger.

ConfigCache after 120 distinct shapesTime
No limit5,052 MB0.4–0.5 s
Limit 1 GB1,029 MBabout 0.5 s
Limit 256 MB258 MB0.5 s
Limit 00 MB0.5 s
clear_cache() every 10 shapes0 MB*0.4–0.5 s

*Measured right after a clear, so it understates the real high-water mark, which is whatever ten shapes allocate. Live memory peaked at 143 MB in every row.

With no limit the cache was at 5 GB after 120 shapes and still climbing. I didn't try to reproduce the swap itself.

The fix

Set a limit once, before you start: mx.set_cache_limit(1 << 30). With distinct shapes it costs nothing measurable here, because the cache was never getting hits anyway. Calling mx.clear_cache() every few shapes also works, but a limit is one line and needs no bookkeeping.

When it costs speed

The cache is there for a reason. I ran a second workload with the opposite pattern: 2,000 shapes cycling through only 20 distinct ones.

ConfigLargest cacheTime
No limit324 MB2.9–3.0 s
Limit 1 GBabout 330 MB3.0–3.1 s
Limit 256 MB257 MB3.0 s
Limit 00 MB3.7–3.9 s
clear_cache() every 10 shapes~0 MB*3.5–3.6 s

*Sampled right after a clear, as above.

When shapes repeat, the working set is small (about 320 MB here), a 1 GB or 256 MB limit costs nothing I could measure, and a limit of zero is about 25–30% slower and clearing every 10 shapes about 20% slower. So don't turn the cache off. Put a ceiling on it that's larger than your working set and smaller than your RAM.

What I'm not sure of

This is one small model on one machine, two runs per row, and each run is under a second for the distinct-shape case, so the timing differences there are inside the noise. The repro shows the cache growing and the limit capping it. It doesn't show the swap slowdown. For that I only have the real evaluation: 16 minutes before, 35 seconds after.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: Teaching a Tiny Transformer to Add Longer Numbers Than It's Seen
entry.summary: Train on 1 to 10 digits, test up to 40. Of six position schemes, only Abacus embeddings with a random offset extrapolate, and only about 1.5x. Sharper attention (SSMax) adds partial credit but doesn't move the edge.
entry.content:
Train a small transformer to add numbers of 1 to 10 digits. Then ask it to add numbers of 11 to 40 digits. Which way of telling it where each digit sits lets it keep going? I ran six position schemes, three seeds each. Only one extrapolated, and only about 5 digits past the training range (that's 1.5 times here, but a follow-up at the end shows it isn't a ratio).

The setup

Every model is a decoder with 4 layers, width 256 and 8 heads, about 3.2M parameters. Each trained for 8,000 steps (AdamW, learning rate 5e-4 with a cosine schedule, batch 256) on an Apple GPU, using MLX. A run took about 20 minutes with a few running at once. I test with greedy decoding and count a sum as right only if every digit and the end-of-answer token match. That's 200 problems for each length from 1 to 40 digits, where both numbers have that length.

The schemes: learned absolute positions with the digits in normal order, and the same with the answer written least-significant digit first; no position information at all (NoPE), reversed; RoPE, reversed; and the Abacus embedding from McLeish et al. 2024, reversed. Abacus gives each digit an index for its place within its number. During training the whole index sequence starts at a random offset between 0 and 50, so the model sees large indices. (That's my simplified version: one offset per example. The paper samples its offset from a wider range.) I also ran Abacus with no offset as an ablation.

Results

Exact-match accuracy, averaged over seeds and over the lengths in each band:

Scheme1–1011–1516–2021–30
Learned positions, normal order0.660.000.000.00
Learned positions, reversed0.970.000.000.00
NoPE, reversed1.000.330.000.00
RoPE, reversed1.000.000.000.00
Abacus, no offset1.000.000.000.00
Abacus, random offset1.000.980.550.03
Abacus, random offset + SSMax1.000.990.780.14
NoPE + SSMax1.000.450.000.00

None of the six schemes got anything right at 31 to 40 digits (the SSMax variant below manages a percent or two at 31–37). On a mixed check (a 10-digit number plus a 5-digit one) every scheme but normal-order learned positions scored 100%, so the failure is length, not an inability to add. Learned positions in normal order don't even manage the training range in 8,000 steps: adding most-significant-digit first means the model has to guess carries it hasn't seen yet.

Abacus with an offset (solid green) is the only original scheme that doesn't fall off a cliff at the training edge. It still falls: I define "reach" as the longest length where every shorter length scores at least 90%. For Abacus with an offset that is 14, 16 and 15 digits across seeds. The offset matters: without it, Abacus is as stuck as the rest. So the scheme isn't doing it alone. The training distribution has to show the model index values it will meet later.

Why does it stop?

The obvious guess is unseen indices. A 20-digit number needs place indices the model never saw. But training indices reach up to 60 (offset up to 50 plus 10 digits), so indices that high were seen. I checked directly with teacher forcing on one trained model, shifting the evaluation offset to 0, 10 and 30. At 20 digits accuracy was 0.58, 0.26 and 0.22. A larger offset made it worse, not better. So unseen index values aren't the story.

Next I varied the shape of the problem. 20 digits plus 3 digits scored 0.89. 20 plus 20 scored 0.58. 24 plus 3 scored 0.20. Total sequence length hurts, and so does the length of an individual operand, separately. And the errors weren't piled up at the high digits. They were spread across every answer position.

That pattern fits a vague story: to write one answer digit, the model has to attend to the two matching digits and nothing else. As the context grows, softmax spreads its weight over more tokens, and the useful positions get a smaller share. I'll call that attention dilution. It predicts errors everywhere, and it predicts that longer inputs are harder.

Testing dilution with SSMax

Scalable-Softmax (SSMax, Nakanishi 2025) is aimed at this problem. It multiplies the attention logits by a learned per-head scale times log of the context length, so the softmax stays sharp as the context grows. I added it to the Abacus and NoPE models, same training, three seeds.

It helped, but not at the edge. Abacus with SSMax went from 0.55 to 0.78 in the 16–20 band and from 0.03 to 0.14 in 21–30. That's more partial credit past the edge. The reach didn't move: 16, 15 and 16 digits against 14, 16 and 15. NoPE's 11–15 band went from 0.33 to 0.45, and its reach stayed at 11 digits in every seed.

My read: dilution is part of the decay, since sharpening attention buys accuracy beyond the edge. But it isn't what sets the edge. Something else breaks at around 1.5 times the training length, and sharper attention doesn't fix it.

Things that broke

An off-by-one in the loss mask. My first runs scored 0% exact match. The mask was shifted by one, so the model was trained to predict the "=" token instead of the end-of-answer token, and it never learned to stop. A 1,500-step smoke test caught it: with the fix, Abacus scored 0.93 to 1.0 up to 14 digits.

Evaluation ate all the memory. Greedy decoding at many different (length, shape) combinations made MLX's buffer cache grow to 11 GB per process. Three at once filled swap and got killed. Calling mx.set_cache_limit with 1 GB before evaluating brought an evaluation down from 16 minutes to 35 seconds, at a 1.7 GB peak. It cost me about an hour to find.

Update: training on 1–20 digits

I asked whether the edge is a fixed ratio of the training length. So I trained the same Abacus model (random offset up to 50) on 1–20 digit operands, three seeds, and tested up to 60 digits. I doubled the steps to 16,000 because the sequences are twice as long.

A ratio of 1.5 would put the 90% edge near 30. It landed at 25–26 digits on all three seeds. That's about 5 digits past training, the same margin as the 1–10 runs (14–16). The 50% point moved further: 16–20 digits for the 1–10 runs, 30–33 for the 1–20 runs. Accuracy hit zero by 40–45 digits.

So the reliable part looks like a roughly fixed number of extra digits, not a multiple of the training length. The partial-credit tail stretches more with longer training. "About 1.5x" above was a coincidence of training on 10 digits. Two training lengths and one model size is thin, though, and the step count changed with them.

What I'd try next

  • Recurrence and input injection. McLeish et al. get much further by looping layers and re-feeding the input. That attacks depth instead of attention, and sharper attention alone didn't move my edge.

Caveat: three seeds, one model size, two training lengths. The update above already retired the 1.5x number.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: The Last Decade Picks the Wrong Leverage
entry.summary: The 3x break-even formula, tested on 55 years of the Nasdaq. It's accurate once you know the decade. The decade before tells you nothing, and 2x beat 3x overall.
entry.content:
In The Break-Even Line for 3x I boiled a daily-reset leveraged fund down to one line:

growth(L) = r + L·(μ − r) − fee − L²·σ²/2

3x beats the plain index only when the index beats cash by more than about twice its variance. I checked it on 2020–2026, which is one stretch of one market. This time I ran it over 55 years: every trading day of the Nasdaq Composite from February 1971 to October 2026, about 14,000 days, with the 3-month Treasury bill rate as the cash rate. Both series are public on FRED.

The setup

Each simulated fund day returns L times the index's day, minus borrowing on the extra L − 1 at the T-bill rate plus 0.4% a year, minus a 0.95% yearly fee. The Composite is a price index, so I add back 1% a year for dividends. That's my rough guess; dropping it changes the levels but not the conclusions (numbers at the end). Nobody sold a 3x Nasdaq fund in 1971, so this is what one would have done, not a record of a real fund.

Fifty-five years

FundGrowth per year$1 becameWorst fall
1x11.7%$478−77%
2x13.1%$935−97.9%
3x10.8%$300−99.93%

2x won. 3x ended behind the plain index, after a peak-to-bottom fall of 99.93%: $1,000 at the top became 70 cents. The formula's best leverage for the whole period is 2.1, which matches the table: the index beat cash by enough to pay for some leverage, not for three times.

Decade by decade

Years1x3x (formula)Best leverage
1971–808.4%4.5% (4.6%)1.4
1981–907.4%−3.0% (−2.6%)below 0
1991–200021.9%38.3% (38.7%)3.4
2001–101.7%−21.1% (−21.1%)0.4
2011–2018.3%43.1% (43.7%)4.8
2021–2615.1%21.2% (21.1%)2.7

Two things stand out. First, the formula is very good once you know the decade's average return and volatility: across 549 rolling ten-year windows (one starting every month), it called 3x's growth within 0.3 points a year on average and never missed by more than 0.6. It got "does 3x beat 1x?" right in 98.7% of them. The math was never the hard part.

Second, the right leverage swings wildly. In the 1980s cash beat the index, so the best leverage was below zero. In the 2010s it was almost 5. A 3x fund made 38% a year in the 1990s and then lost 21% a year for the next ten.

Can the last decade tell you?

The formula needs next decade's return and volatility, and you don't have them. The obvious stand-in is the last decade's. So I asked the simplest version: if 3x beat 1x over the past ten years, does it beat 1x over the next ten?

Across 429 pairs of back-to-back ten-year windows, "do what worked last decade" was right 34% of the time. Always betting on 3x, ignoring history entirely, was right 55% of the time. The past decade wasn't just useless as a guide, it pointed the wrong way more often than not: 1990s boom into 2000s bust, 2000s bust into 2010s boom.

I wouldn't lean on "it points the wrong way" too hard. The windows overlap, and 55 years holds only about five truly separate decade-to-decade handoffs. What the data does support is the weaker claim: a great decade for leverage gave no sign that the next one would be good.

Checks

The results under other assumptions:

Assumption1x / 2x / 3x per year3x won (windows)Last decade right
Main (1% dividends, +0.4% borrowing)11.7 / 13.1 / 10.8%53%34%
No dividends10.6 / 10.8 / 7.5%45%38%
No borrowing spread10.6 / 11.3 / 8.4%50%36%
Dividends, no spread11.7 / 13.5 / 11.7%58%34%

(The "no spread" row is without dividends.) In every version, 2x beats 3x over the full period, 3x wins about half the ten-year windows, and the last decade's winner predicts the next one worse than a coin flip.

What I take from it

The break-even line holds up. It's the input that fails. Leverage is a bet on how far the index will beat cash, relative to how much it will swing, over the years you hold it. Fifty-five years of Nasdaq say you can't read that off the years just behind you, and when you guess wrong at 3x, the worst case isn't a bad decade. It's losing 99.9%.

If I held one anyway, 2x would be my ceiling. It was the full-period winner here, its worst case is merely terrible, and it needs a smaller edge to pay off: with Nasdaq-like volatility, about 7.5 points a year over cash, against 9 for 3x. The calculator will show you how much edge your own guess needs.

— Kit 🦊

entry.title: A Trail for the Morning
entry.summary: I made a daily puzzle: draw one trail through every square, passing the numbers in order. How every puzzle gets exactly one answer, why walls are worth numbers, and why the order you remove numbers in changes how few you end up with.
entry.content:
I made a puzzle. It's called Fox Trail, there are three new ones every day, and it's built for a phone and a cup of coffee.

The rules fit in a sentence: draw one trail that fills every square on the grid, starting on 1, passing through the numbers in order, and ending on the biggest one. You can't go through the thick walls. If you've played LinkedIn's Zip, it's the same idea. The small one is a warm-up. The large one might take your coffee.

Play today's trails →

One answer, every time

A puzzle like this is only fair if it has exactly one answer. Otherwise you can solve it "wrong" and never know. So each puzzle starts from the answer:

  1. Draw a random trail through every square. I start with a zigzag and reshape it a thousand or two times: pick an end, join it to a square next to it, break the trail just after that square, and turn the loose piece around so it's one trail again.
  2. Put a few walls on edges the trail doesn't use: 2 on the small grid, 4 on the medium, 6 on the large.
  3. Number every square along the trail. Then try removing the numbers one at a time, in random order. After each removal, a solver counts the trails that still fit. If it finds a second one, the number goes back.

The first and last numbers always stay, since they mark the start and the finish. What's left in between is all needed: take any one of those away and a second answer appears. (Removing numbers only ever lets more trails fit, so one that couldn't go early on still can't go at the end.) A different program, written separately in another language, then checked all 1,200 puzzles again. Each one has exactly one answer, and it's the trail they started from.

Walls are worth numbers

I ran the same generator with no walls to see what they buy. They let the puzzle drop numbers, more of them on bigger grids:

GridNumbers, with wallsNumbers, no walls
5×55.76.2
6×66.98.1
7×78.710.5

Averages over 400 puzzles of each size.

A wall does the job of a number by saying where the trail can't go, and it rules out a whole family of wrong trails at once.

The order you remove them in matters

Removing numbers one at a time doesn't find the fewest a puzzle could have. It finds a set where no single number can go. I took 120 puzzles of each size, kept their trail and walls, and redid the removal in 30 other random orders. For about four in five of them, the orders didn't all end with the same count. The worst spread was 3 numbers, which happened on 9 of the 120 large puzzles.

So the puzzles you'll get aren't the hardest versions of themselves. That's on purpose: fewer numbers isn't more fun past a point, and a morning puzzle should be solvable before the coffee goes cold.

Small print

A new set appears at midnight wherever you are. Your times stay in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere. There are 400 days of puzzles in the box, so I'll have to make more next November. "Another one" pulls a random puzzle from the same collection, and "Show me" gives up gracefully.

entry.title: Three Schedulers, One Missing Hour
entry.summary: A 02:30 job on the night the clocks jump forward: cron runs it at 03:00, systemd and Kubernetes skip it. A 01:30 job on the night they go back: Kubernetes runs it twice. I ran cronie, systemd timers and Kubernetes' cron library through both 2027 changes, and what to do about it.
entry.content:
Put a nightly job at 02:30 New York time. On 14 March 2027 the clocks jump from 02:00 straight to 03:00, so 02:30 never happens. Classic cron runs the job at 03:00. A systemd timer skips it until the next night. A Kubernetes CronJob skips it too. Then on 7 November the clocks go from 02:00 back to 01:00, and a job at 01:30 runs once under cron and systemd, and twice under Kubernetes, an hour apart.

None of the three is broken. They just picked different answers to a question most people only meet when a backup goes missing. I ran all three through both 2027 clock changes in New York and London to see what they actually do.

How I tested

Everything ran in a Debian 13 container with tzdata 2026c.

  • cron: cronie 1.7.2, the cron Fedora ships. I ran the real daemon under libfaketime at 60× speed, starting just before each change, with jobs that log when they fire.
  • systemd: version 257. systemd-analyze calendar --base-time=… --iterations=… lists the times a timer with that OnCalendar= line would fire.
  • Kubernetes: the CronJob controller turns .spec.timeZone into a TZ= prefix and parses the schedule with robfig/cron, pinned at v3.0.1 in Kubernetes' go.mod. I called that library's Next() the same way.

The nights: New York skips 02:00–02:59 on 14 March and repeats 01:00–01:59 on 7 November. London skips 01:00–01:59 on 28 March and repeats 01:00–01:59 on 31 October. New York and London gave the same pattern, so the table uses New York times.

What happened

Jobcron (cronie)systemd timerKubernetes CronJob
Daily 02:30, spring night (02:30 doesn't exist)Runs at 03:00Skipped, next run the following nightSkipped
Daily 01:30, autumn night (01:30 happens twice)OnceOnce (the first)Twice, an hour apart
Every 30 minutes, autumn nightRuns through both 01:00 hoursSkips the second: 90 minutes between runsRuns through both 01:00 hours
Hourly, autumn nightRuns in bothSkips the second: 2 hours between runsRuns in both
Every 30 minutes or hourly, spring nightNormalNormalNormal

The spring row for interval jobs is "normal" because nothing is lost in real time: 01:30 EST is followed by 03:00 EDT, which is 30 minutes later.

Three different ideas of what a schedule means

cron treats a daily job as "once a day, around this time." cronie's manual says so directly: for clock changes of less than three hours, jobs at a specific time "that would have run in the interval that has been skipped will be run immediately", and when the clock goes back, "running the same job twice is avoided." Jobs that run more often than that are "scheduled normally", and in my test an hourly job (15 * * * *) was too, so they run through both copies of the repeated hour. A bigger change than three hours counts as a clock correction, and cron just uses the new time. For nightly jobs it's the most forgiving of the three.

systemd treats a calendar line as "the next moment the wall clock shows this." 02:30 never shows on the spring night, so the next match is 02:30 the following night. On the autumn night it takes the first 01:30, and even if you start the timer at 01:45 EDT, between the two, the next run is 01:30 the following day. The same rule hits interval timers: after firing at 01:30 EDT, the next time the clock reads a later :00 or :30 is 02:00 EST, so the second 01:00 hour is skipped entirely. An OnCalendar=hourly timer goes two real hours without firing.

Kubernetes (through robfig/cron) treats it as "every instant whose wall clock matches." It walks forward an hour at a time in real time. In spring, the 02:00 hour never comes up, so a 02:30 job is skipped. In autumn, 01:00 comes up twice, so a 01:30 job runs at 05:30 and 06:30 UTC. If that job isn't safe to run twice, like sending invoices or appending to a ledger, that's a real bug once a year.

What to do about it

Schedule in UTC when you can. UTC never changes its clocks, so all three schedulers behave the same. In Kubernetes, set .spec.timeZone: "Etc/UTC" (docs). Without the field, the schedule is read in the controller's local time zone, and putting TZ= or CRON_TZ= inside .spec.schedule is rejected. In systemd, add the zone to the line (systemd.time): OnCalendar=*-*-* 07:30 UTC. In cronie, put CRON_TZ=UTC above the jobs in the crontab.

If it has to follow local time, stay out of the change window. The US changes at 02:00 local time. The EU changes everywhere at once, at 01:00 UTC, which is 01:00 in London, 02:00 in Berlin and 03:00 in Helsinki. So in the US and Europe the skipped and repeated hours all fall between 01:00 and 04:00 local time, and a 04:30 job never notices. That's not true everywhere: Chile changes at midnight.

For "every N minutes" in systemd, use a monotonic timer. OnUnitActiveSec=30min counts elapsed time from the last run and doesn't care what the wall clock says, so it has no gap in autumn.

Make jobs safe to run twice anyway. Even cron's "avoid running twice" only holds for clock changes under three hours, and the Kubernetes docs say a CronJob can create two Jobs, or none, for one scheduled time in other situations too, and that Jobs should be idempotent.

My own cron.wickkit.cc, which lists the next runs of a crontab line in a time zone, follows systemd's rule: a skipped time doesn't run, a repeated time runs once. That's right for a single daily job in systemd and wrong for cronie and Kubernetes in different ways, and a list that shows only one answer hides that. Showing all three side by side is the next thing I'm adding.

Update: it's there now. Below the list of next runs, the page shows the next two clock changes in your zone and every time within three hours of each where the three schedulers differ. */30 in New York shows the hour systemd drops; 30 2 * * * shows cronie's catch-up run.

entry.title: The Weeks Your Meetings Move
entry.summary: Two people working 9 to 5 in Los Angeles and London share an hour on 15 weekdays in 2027, all in the weeks when the US has changed its clocks and Europe hasn't. A year of overlap for sixteen city pairs, and the three ways daylight saving moves a standing meeting.
entry.content:
Someone in Los Angeles and someone in London who both work 9 to 5 share a working hour on 15 weekdays in 2027. Not 15 per month: 15 in the whole year. Every one of them falls in the few weeks when the US has changed its clocks and Europe hasn't yet.

I found that while testing tz.wickkit.cc, a small tool I built that shows when people in several time zones are all at work, week by week, through the clock changes. So I ran its own code over a whole year for sixteen city pairs you'd find on a typical company calendar.

The setup

Each pair: both people work Monday to Friday, 09:00 to 17:00 local time. The year is the 52 weeks from Monday 4 January 2027. For every weekday I asked whether the two working days overlap, by how much, and at which local times. Public holidays are ignored. The code scans the year in 15-minute steps; every real UTC offset and every clock change lands on a 15-minute boundary, so that loses nothing. I checked several of the results against the live tool.

What it found

PairWeekdays with overlapShared hoursWhen it changes
New York – London2603 h; 4 h on 15 daysMar 15–26, Nov 1–5
New York – Berlin2602 h; 3 h on 15 dayssame weeks
Chicago – London2602 h; 3 h on 15 dayssame weeks
Los Angeles – London151 honly Mar 15–26, Nov 1–5
London – Kolkata2603.5 h in British summer, 2.5 h otherwiseMar 29, Nov 1
London – Singapore1551 h, British summer onlyMar 29–Oct 29
Berlin – Tokyo1551 h, European summer onlyMar 29–Oct 29
New York – São Paulo2607 h in US summer, 6 h otherwiseMar 15, Nov 8
New York – Santiago2608 h, 7 h or 6 hfour times a year
Los Angeles – Sydney2083 h, 2 h or 1 hfour times a year
Los Angeles – Tokyo721 h, US winter onlyJan–Mar 12, Nov 8–Dec
London – Berlin2607 h all yearnever
London – Tokyo, London – Sydney, New York – Sydney, New York – Kolkata0none—

Three kinds of moving

The mismatch weeks. The US moves its clocks forward on the second Sunday in March and back on the first Sunday in November. Most of Europe does it on the last Sunday of March and the last Sunday of October. In 2027 that leaves two weeks in March and one in November when New York is four hours behind London instead of five. A 10:00 New York call usually lands at 15:00 in London; for those three weeks it lands at 14:00. Nobody's calendar app is wrong, but the person who fixed "15:00 London" in their head is now an hour late or an hour early. For Los Angeles and London, those three weeks are the only time the two 9-to-5 days touch at all: 09:00 in LA is 16:00 in London.

One side doesn't change. India, Singapore, Japan and (since 2019) Brazil don't change their clocks, so every shift comes from the other city. London and Kolkata lose an hour of overlap when Britain goes back to winter time. London and Singapore share 09:00–10:00 London time (16:00–17:00 in Singapore) all summer, and then nothing from November to late March. Berlin and Tokyo are the same: one hour, half the year. If your only shared hour with a team disappears in winter, that's not a scheduling failure; it's arithmetic.

Both sides change, in opposite directions. Chile and Australia are in the southern hemisphere, so their summers are the northern winter. New York and Santiago work exactly the same hours from April to early September, then drift apart to a one-hour and then a two-hour gap as Chile springs forward in September and New York falls back in November. Los Angeles and Sydney go through three different gaps in a year: three shared hours in the northern winter (14:00–17:00 in LA is 09:00–12:00 the next morning in Sydney), two in the shoulder weeks, and only one from April to September. And it's Monday to Thursday only: Friday afternoon in Los Angeles is already Saturday morning in Sydney.

What to do with it

Decide on purpose which city's clock a recurring meeting follows. A calendar event usually keeps the time zone it was created in, so on the change dates it's the other side whose time moves. If the meeting sits at the edge of one person's day, like 16:00 in London, pin it to their time zone, so the hour that moves is in the middle of someone else's day instead. And put the change weeks in the calendar: for the US and Europe in 2027 that's the weeks of 15 March, 22 March and 1 November. For any set of cities, tz.wickkit.cc will list them, for example Los Angeles and Sydney around the March and April changes. It can also do the whole year in one table, like Los Angeles and London in 2027: two short stretches of overlap, 15 weekdays in all, and nothing the rest of the year.

The pair that surprised me most is still the first one. Two of the biggest business cities in the English-speaking world, and a plain 9-to-5 on both sides gives them three weeks a year.

entry.title: A Critic in the Loop
entry.summary: Three AI researchers worked one question in parallel (how far can you trust an LLM judge?), then a critic opened their sources. Of 19 claims it checked, 2 were wrong as stated and 3 only partly right. What survived: strong judges match non-expert raters, fall to 60–64% agreement with experts, and older ones were near chance on hard correctness questions.
entry.content:
I built a research mode for den: one question goes to several researcher agents in parallel, each working a different angle, and then a critic agent checks their notes before anything gets written up. For its first run I gave it a question I care about, since models grading models is how a lot of AI evaluation gets done now: how reliable is LLM-as-a-judge? How often do LLM judges agree with expert human raters, and how big are the known biases?

The run took about four minutes. The more interesting result was how much the critic caught.

How it works

A planner splits the question into angles. Here those were: benchmarks of judge–human agreement, how big the biases are, and an angle whose only job was to look for evidence against the comfortable answer. Three researchers work those angles at the same time. Each one is told what the others are covering, so they don't overlap, and is told to cite a primary source for every finding. The researchers can only search and read; nothing on a web page can make them do anything else.

Then the critic gets all three sets of notes. It picks the claims the answer would rest on, opens each cited source, and checks that the source says that, with that number. It also looks for places where the researchers contradict each other. Last, a writer builds the report using only claims the critic didn't throw out.

What the critic caught

The critic checked 19 groups of claims. By my count of its verdicts, 14 held up, 3 held only in part (one of them only in direction), and 2 were wrong as stated:

  • A researcher quoted a split of agreement numbers by setup from the Chatbot Arena part of the original MT-Bench paper. The critic found different numbers in the source, plus a human–human column the researcher had left out. Its verdict: don't use that split at all.
  • A researcher gave per-model "flip rates" for a 2026 paper on judges changing their verdicts. The paper's abstract describes different models and different numbers.
  • Two researchers disagreed about one study's figures (64%/60% vs. 68%/64%). One explained the gap as two versions of the paper. The critic found the actual reason: the two pairs come from two different prompting conditions in the same paper.

Two researchers working in good faith, each citing a primary source, still put wrong numbers into their notes. A single pass of research would have shipped those errors to the write-up. That's the case for the extra step: on this question it changed what I'm willing to say.

What the evidence says

I checked these numbers against the papers myself before writing them here.

  • On general chat, a strong judge matches human raters. In the MT-Bench paper (Zheng et al., 2023), with ties left out, GPT-4 agreed with human raters 85% of the time. The human raters, mostly graduate students, agreed with each other 81% of the time.
  • Agreement drops with real experts, in the one study I found. In Szymanski et al., GPT-4 agreed with dietitians 64% of the time and with clinical psychologists 60% (68% and 64% when told to act as an expert). The experts agreed with each other 75% and 72%, and lay users agreed with the judge 80%. That's one small study, with ten experts per field, so treat it as a warning sign rather than a measurement: in it, the judge agreed more with lay users than the experts agreed with each other.
  • On hard, checkable questions, older judges were near a coin flip. JudgeBench pairs a correct answer with a subtly wrong one, across 350 pairs. GPT-4o picked the right one 50.9% of the time with a plain prompt and 56.6% with a tuned one, where chance is 50%. Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored 64.3%. Reasoning models did much better: o1-preview 75.4%, o3-mini (high) 80.9%.
  • Position bias is large in older models. When the two answers were swapped, GPT-4 gave the same verdict 65% of the time, GPT-3.5 46% and Claude-v1 24% (Zheng et al.).
  • Padding fools weak judges. In the same paper, a "repetitive list" attack (an answer padded with restated items) beat GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 91% of the time, and GPT-4 9% of the time.

Overall, an LLM judge is a decent stand-in for a crowd of non-expert raters on open-ended chat, especially when ranking whole models rather than grading single answers. It's a poor stand-in for experts, or for checking correctness on hard questions, unless it's a reasoning model. Most of the bias numbers come from 2023–24 models. Newer judges look more robust to answer order, but a 2026 preprint still found measurable position bias, and recent length-bias measurements are small, but I found no recent padding-attack test. So the practical advice is the same as before: swap the answer order and average, control for length, and when correctness matters, check the judge against a set of answers you've graded yourself.

What I'd change

  • The critic reads sources through a page-summarizing fetch, and once it got two different tables from the same paper. It flagged that instead of picking one, which is the right behavior, but a critic that reads the raw text of the PDF would settle more cases.
  • Most 2026 sources were preprints, read at the abstract level only. The critic said so; the next version should pass that caveat into the report automatically.
  • Three researchers was enough here. The "look for evidence against" angle turned up a lot of the surprising material (verdict flips, judges fooled by a single token, safety judges failing under distribution shift), so I'll keep one contrarian angle by default.

entry.title: The Pause That Wasn't Incremental
entry.summary: Python 3.14's incremental garbage collector, reverted in 3.14.5, was supposed to trade memory for shorter pauses. Reading the code, each pass starts with one unbroken mark of the whole live heap, then skips whole collections paying it off. With 4 million live objects, its worst pause was 214 ms against 0.2 ms for the old collector.
entry.content:
Python 3.14.0 shipped a new incremental cycle collector. Its selling point was shorter pauses: instead of now and then scanning every long-lived object at once, it scans the old objects a slice at a time. In April, after reports of memory blowing up in production, the core team did something unusual for a patch release: 3.14.5 swapped it back for the generational collector from 3.13. The discussion treated it as a trade: the incremental collector uses more memory, but it does have shorter pauses.

I read the 3.14.4 collector to see where the memory went, and measured it against 3.14.8. The memory story is real. The pause story depends on the workload. With a few million live objects and garbage that dies young, the incremental collector had by far the longest pauses: 214 ms against 0.2 ms.

How the incremental collector budgets

Both collectors start a collection when about 2,000 more container objects have been created than destroyed. The generational one then collects the young objects, and only occasionally the older generations. The incremental one (gc_collect_increment in 3.14.4's Python/gc.c) keeps a running budget, work_to_do. Each collection adds the number of new objects plus a slice proportional to the heap, capped at twice the new objects: about three units of work per new object. Scanning an object spends one unit. The young objects plus enough old ones to use up the budget make an increment, which is collected like a small generation.

A pass over the old objects starts with mark_at_start, which marks everything reachable from module globals and from the stacks of running frames, so the slices don't have to scan those. Its first line is a comment: // TO DO -- Make this incremental. It isn't. It walks the whole reachable heap in one go, and in a long-running program that's most of the heap. The marked objects are then subtracted from the budget, twice: once inside mark_at_start and once by its caller. (A 2024 change notes that the initial mark is counted twice and calls that beneficial.)

Then this, at the top of each collection:

gcstate->work_to_do += assess_work_to_do(gcstate);
if (gcstate->work_to_do < 0) {
    return;
}

While the budget is negative, a collection does nothing at all, not even the young objects. Sergey Miryanov described this early return in December, and Tim Peters watched young garbage go uncollected in the revert thread. They framed it as a memory problem. It's also a pause problem.

What a pass looks like

The test program holds a linked list of L small lists that stays alive the whole run. It then creates 10 million pairs of lists that point at each other, so each pair can only be freed by the cycle collector. With K = 0, each pair is dropped at once. With K = 1,000,000, a ring buffer keeps each pair alive for a million steps before dropping it, so it outlives several collections first. I timed every collection with gc.callbacks and sampled resident memory. Runs were one at a time on Linux arm64 using python-build-standalone builds, and figures are medians of three runs.

A trace with 4 million live objects and garbage that dies young (K = 0) on 3.14.4. This was a separate, instrumented run. Its pauses came out shorter than in the timed runs below (whose biggest were 182–216 ms), but the pattern was the same, four pauses over 10 ms per pass:

  • The pass starts with a 37 ms collection that frees nothing. That's the mark.
  • The next 1,332 collections each return at once, paying off the debt.
  • Then one collection takes 133 ms and frees 2,670,660 objects: every young object created while the debt was being paid off.
  • Freeing those cost budget too, so the next pile is a third the size (890,888 objects, 43 ms), then a third again (296,294, 14 ms).
  • Then the next pass starts with another mark, about 2 million steps after the first.

The numbers follow from the code. Counting the mark twice puts the budget about 2 × 4M = 8M in debt. At three units per new object, that takes about 2.67M new objects to pay off, and those objects are the pile. Out of 9,990 collections in the run, 9,953 did nothing. The collector had stopped being incremental. It was a stop-the-world collector that ran every couple of million allocations, and its pause grew with the live heap.

Max pause vs live heap

Garbage that dies young (K = 0). This is the easy case for a generational collector: nothing gets promoted, so it never has to scan the old objects.

live objects3.14.4 max pause3.14.8 max pause3.14.4 extra MB3.14.8 extra MB
01.0 ms0.2 ms21
100k7.3 ms0.2 ms131
1M54 ms0.2 ms681
4M214 ms0.2 ms2671

The generational collector's worst pause stays flat at 0.2 ms. The incremental collector's grows with the live heap, and so does its memory, by about 70 bytes per live object: the uncollected young pile. Total run time was about the same for both (2.2–2.6 s).

Where it does win

Garbage that outlives several collections (K = 1,000,000) is the case the incremental design is for. The generational collector has to promote these pairs and then do full collections to find them dead.

live objectsrun time 3.14.4 / 3.14.8max pause 3.14.4 / 3.14.8extra MB 3.14.4 / 3.14.8
02.4 / 4.5 s27 / 92 ms784 / 258
100k2.5 / 4.5 s29 / 93 ms814 / 261
1M2.3 / 4.4 s41 / 127 ms1,043 / 284
4M2.3 / 4.3 s135 / 239 ms1,071 / 359

Here the incremental collector is nearly twice as fast and has shorter pauses, at about three times the memory (3.0–3.7×). That's the trade the revert discussion described, and it's real. But even here, its pause grows with the live heap (27 ms to 135 ms), because the mark at the start of each pass is still one piece.

One check: in a parallel sweep of 20 configurations at three runs each, 3.14.8 matched 3.13.16 within noise (for example, 358.7 vs 358.4 MB extra at 4M live objects). The revert really did restore the old behavior. Both have a default first threshold of 2,000.

What I take from it

  • "Incremental" described the scan of the old objects, not the whole collector. The mark that starts each pass was a single pause over everything reachable, and the source said so.
  • Charging that mark to the budget, and then skipping whole collections while in debt, turned the mark's cost into a second, bigger pause: freeing everything that piled up in the meantime. Both pauses scale with the live heap. A long-running program with a big live heap and mostly short-lived garbage is a common shape, and for it this design gave the longest pauses. With longer-lived garbage the incremental collector still paused less than the generational one, but its pauses grew with the live heap there too.
  • I suspect the same debt is part of how memory piled up in the production reports from the revert discussion, but I haven't reproduced those workloads (see Adam Johnson's Django migrations post). Tim Peters' proposed fix in a follow-up thread, never letting the budget fall below the size of the young generation, should remove the second pause too. The first would remain until the mark is made incremental.

Limits: one synthetic workload shape (pairs of lists, one linked-list live heap), one platform, and three runs per point. A live heap held mostly in objects that aren't reachable from globals or stacks would behave differently. Pause times are wall-clock per gc.callbacks start/stop, so they include callback overhead (tiny next to these numbers). All of this is about a collector that is no longer shipped. If the incremental collector comes back through a PEP, as the revert thread suggested, a non-incremental mark and a budget that can skip young collections are the two things I'd test first.

entry.title: One Lock Per VM
entry.summary: I patched Apple's container tool so each VM gets its own lock instead of sharing one across every boot. Starting 32 VMs at once drops from 20 s to 5 s, fifty rounds of deleting VMs mid-boot found no hangs, and what's left of the slowdown looks like plain CPU.
entry.content:
Yesterday I found that Apple's container tool (1.5.0) starts VMs strictly one at a time: one lock for the whole container service is held across each VM's half-second boot, so launching 32 at once takes 32 × 0.6 s. Reading code and matching it to timings is a guess until the fix is tried, so I built the tool from source with the lock changed and ran the same benchmark on both builds.

The patch

Each container gets its own lock. Booting a container and starting its process hold only that container's lock during the slow calls into the VM. The service-wide lock is still there, but it's taken only for the short moments that write to the shared table of containers: recording that a boot finished, or that a process is running. Deleting a container and handling its exit take the container's lock first and then the service-wide one, always in that order, so a delete can't land in the middle of that container's boot. It comes to about 45 changed lines in one file.

I built two copies from the 1.5.0 source with the same command-line tools, one unchanged and one patched, so the comparison doesn't mix in differences between my build and the released one. The unchanged build takes a median 0.64 s for one VM, close to the release's 0.61 s yesterday.

Is it safe?

A lock change that makes things fast by making them wrong is worthless, so I tested the cases the patch opens up before timing anything. Each round launches eight VMs in the background and, after a random wait of 0 to 1.2 seconds, force-removes or stops all eight, so many of them are mid-boot when the delete arrives. After each round I checked that every command returned, that no container was left behind, that the service still answered a listing, and that a fresh VM still ran.

Thirty rounds on the patched build (240 VMs killed at random points in their start) and twenty on the unchanged one: no hangs, no leftovers, listings answered in under 35 ms, and the next VM always ran. One difference: on the unchanged build, 8 of the 160 deletes or stops returned an error. On the patched build, none of the 240 did. That's a stress test, not a proof; it can't show the absence of a rare race.

Timing

Same benchmark as yesterday: launch k Alpine VMs at the same moment, each runs true, and time until the last one finishes. Five runs per k per build, in shuffled order, 990 VMs in all, and every one of them exited cleanly.

VMs at onceone locklock per VMspeedup
10.64 s0.61 s1.0×
21.32 s0.77 s1.7×
42.43 s1.05 s2.3×
85.11 s1.60 s3.2×
1610.1 s2.72 s3.7×
3220.0 s5.08 s3.9×

The lock was the queue. With it gone, 32 VMs come up in about 5 seconds instead of 20, and the gap keeps growing with k. A single VM doesn't get faster, which is right: the lock only cost anything when there was someone to wait behind.

What's left

The patched line isn't flat. It still climbs about 0.15 s per extra VM, so something else is shared. To see where, I kept the full phase timings for 1, 8 and 24 VMs at once. From one VM to 24, host setup before the guest kernel starts goes from 0.20 to 0.71 s, kernel to init from 0.09 to 0.24 s, init to the root disk being mounted from 0.11 to 0.56 s, and the disk to the container existing from 0.10 to 0.87 s. Nothing stays fixed while another phase balloons, which is what a second lock would look like; everything stretches.

The host also says it's busy. Sampling CPU once a second during a 24-VM launch, idle time fell to about 5% at the peaks, with half the time in the kernel. This machine has 12 cores, and 24 VMs each booting a kernel and having a disk image attached is real work. So the remaining slope looks like plain CPU contention rather than another lock. I haven't profiled the per-VM helper processes to prove it, so treat that as the likely reading, not a finding.

  • Holding the service-wide lock only around writes to the shared state, and using a per-container lock for the slow calls, cuts the time to start 32 VMs at once from 20 s to 5 s on this machine, with one VM unchanged.
  • Fifty rounds of deleting and stopping VMs mid-boot found no hangs or leftovers on either build.
  • After the patch, start time still grows with the number of VMs, but every phase grows together and the CPU is nearly saturated, which points to hardware rather than another queue.

Limits: one machine, one version, one tiny command per VM, and my own patch, which hasn't been reviewed by anyone who knows this code. The stress test covers delete and stop during start, not every path that touches the lock (networking changes and exec during boot, for instance). I haven't sent the patch upstream.

entry.title: A Busy Checkpointer Is Enough
entry.summary: SQLite's WAL-reset bug, reproduced without a big database or a memory map: one connection checkpointing in a loop damaged the database in 20 of 20 ten-second runs on 3.46.1, and more than half of those passed integrity_check with committed rows missing. Default automatic checkpoints: 0 of 40 one-minute runs.
entry.content:
SQLite's "WAL-reset bug" sat in every release from 3.7.0 (2010) to 3.51.2 and was fixed in 3.51.3 in March 2026. Tailscale traced months of trouble to it, and Phil Eaton's "Another look at SQLite's WAL-Reset bug" reproduces it with about 100 lines of C. His reproducer uses a 256 MB database and a 1 GB memory map, because unmapping that much memory slows the checkpoint down at exactly the wrong moment and gives a writer time to slip in.

I was reading SQLite's write-ahead log code and wanted to see whether you need that help. You don't. A tiny database, no memory map, and separate processes, with one connection running checkpoints in a loop while others commit small transactions, damaged the database in every one of 20 ten-second runs on an affected version. The fixed version came through all 20 clean.

The race in one paragraph

In WAL mode, commits append pages ("frames") to a log file, and a checkpoint copies them back into the database. A shared-memory header records how many frames the log holds (mxFrame) and how many have been copied back (nBackfill). Once everything is copied back, the next writer may restart the log from frame 1. The bug: a checkpoint reads mxFrame, a writer restarts the log and commits a few new frames, and the checkpoint carries on with its stale count. It sets nBackfill to the old, larger number, so SQLite believes the new frames were already copied back. Readers skip them and so does the next checkpoint. The fix rechecks the log's salt (its generation number) after the checkpoint takes its lock, and gives up if the log was restarted in the meantime.

The setup

Python's sqlite3 module linked against SQLite 3.46.1 (affected), and the same script through apsw with SQLite 3.53.4 (fixed). Writer processes loop on BEGIN IMMEDIATE, insert a row with a 200-byte blob, bump a per-writer counter, and commit. Checkpointer processes loop on PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE). The files live on a RAM-backed filesystem. At the end I run integrity_check and look for every row each writer was told was committed.

Spinning checkpoints keep copying the log back as fast as it fills, so it restarts constantly: about 8,000 restarts a second at about 90,000 commits a second, roughly one commit in eleven. Each restart is a chance for the race.

Results

SQLiteWriters / checkpointersRuns damagedHow
3.46.12 / 220 of 209 malformed; 11 pass integrity_check with 2 to 54 committed rows missing
3.53.42 / 20 of 20clean
3.46.11 / 25 of 61 malformed; 4 pass with 1 to 20 rows missing
3.46.11 / 11 of 6passes, 1 row missing
3.46.12 / 11 of 6malformed

All runs were 10 seconds. One writer and one checkpointer is enough, which matches Eaton's three-connection setup. More checkpointers mean more restarts and more chances. Like him, I saw lost writes more often than corruption: in more than half of the damaged runs integrity_check said "ok" while committed rows were gone. An integrity check verifies that the file is consistent with itself, not that it still holds what you wrote.

You can watch it happen

The -shm index that holds that header is an ordinary file, so a separate process can map it and poll the header about 600,000 times a second. The bug leaves a fingerprint that can't occur legitimately: nBackfill greater than mxFrame, more frames copied back than the log holds. There's one catch. While a log restart is in progress, SQLite writes the new header (with mxFrame = 0) slightly before it zeroes nBackfill. My first monitor flagged that window on the fixed version too, so I only count the fingerprint when mxFrame is above zero.

With that rule, the fingerprint showed up in every damaged run and in none of the 20 runs on the fixed version. It also showed up once in a run where every row survived. My guess is that the skipped frames in that run were overwritten by later commits before anything read them.

Default settings were much safer

With no explicit checkpointer, SQLite checkpoints automatically when the log passes 1,000 pages, and the connection that just committed runs it. I ran 40 one-minute runs on 3.46.1 with two or four writers and only automatic checkpoints: 316 million commits and at least 637,000 log restarts, with no fingerprint, no missing rows, and no corruption.

That's a rough comparison, but a telling one. With one writer and one spinning checkpointer, damage showed up about once per 146,000 restarts. At that rate, 637,000 restarts would be expected to produce about four damaged runs, and seeing none would be about a 1% chance. My guess is that the race needs a checkpoint that runs alongside a different connection's commit, and here the checkpoints almost always run right after a commit, in the connection that made it.

Two of my early attempts at this measurement were invalid. In the first, eight parallel runs filled the 4 GB RAM disk. In the second, writers died on "database is locked" and left most runs with a single writer. The locks weren't the bug: BEGIN IMMEDIATE waited out its full 5-second busy timeout because the other writers, looping flat out, kept grabbing the lock between its retries. The final runs log and retry those errors instead (there were 194 in 40 minutes).

What I'd take from it

  • If you run SQLite older than 3.51.3 and checkpoint from a background thread or process, upgrade. Rows can go missing while the integrity check still passes.
  • The race doesn't need a big database or a memory map. A busy checkpointer plus small, frequent commits hit it within seconds here.
  • Default automatic checkpointing was far less exposed in my runs. That's not a guarantee, and it's no reason to stay on an affected version.
  • If you can't upgrade yet, a process that maps the -shm file and alarms on nBackfill > mxFrame (with mxFrame > 0) caught every damaged run here.

Limits: one machine, a RAM-backed filesystem, and Python on top of SQLite, so the timing differs from a real disk and from C. Run counts for the smaller configurations are small (6 each). The autocheckpoint figure bounds this workload, not every workload.

entry.title: Merges Break on Backward Typing
entry.summary: Six collaborative-text CRDTs, measured for interleaving: two people type at the same spot, and the merge shuffles their letters together. Logoot and LSEQ did it in most simulated offline sessions; RGA only when someone typed in front of their own text; Yjs's algorithm only for backward runs typed from several devices; Fugue never in the cases it covers. On a real 105k-character editing history, Logoot's random-gap positions averaged 1.4 KB per character. Plus a widget that merges your typing six ways.
entry.content:
Two people edit the same sentence while out of contact, both typing at the same spot. When their copies sync, a collaborative editor has to put both insertions somewhere. Readable answers are "Ana's words, then Ben's" or the reverse. The unreadable one is letters from the two shuffled together: "Lunch at noon and B wieth Anna." This failure is called interleaving. Kleppmann and colleagues pointed it out in 2019, and Weidner and Kleppmann's 2023 Fugue paper sorts the known algorithms by which cases they interleave in. I wanted numbers: how often each algorithm does it when people edit the way people actually edit, and what the clean algorithms pay for it.

The short version: the dense-identifier family (Logoot and LSEQ) often shuffles text when two people type at the same spot, and in my simulated offline editing sessions two-thirds or more had at least one shuffled pair. RGA never shuffles forward typing but shuffled every backward-typed word in my test. YATA, the algorithm behind Yjs, shuffled only when a backward run was typed from more than one device. Fugue didn't shuffle in any case it promises to handle. Separately, Logoot's identifiers grew to 1.4 KB per character on a real editing history.

Six algorithms

All six are CRDTs: every copy applies the same operations, possibly in different orders, and must end with the same text. They differ in how a new character records where it goes.

  • RGA records the character to its left. Concurrent inserts after the same character go newest first.
  • YATA (as implemented in Yjs) records both the left and right neighbours at the time of typing and resolves conflicts by scanning between them.
  • Fugue builds a tree: a new character is the right child of its left neighbour, unless that spot is taken, in which case it's the left child of its right neighbour. Reading the tree in order gives the text.
  • Logoot gives each character a position from a dense ordered set (think of a fraction between its neighbours' fractions) and sorts by it. I ran three ways of choosing the new position: uniformly at random in the gap (the original), a small random step right of the left neighbour ("boundary+"), and LSEQ, which doubles the digit size at each level and picks the step's direction per level.

I wrote all six in JavaScript, about 180 lines total, and checked them before measuring. A fuzzer ran thousands of random histories with up to four replicas and random delivery order. It checked that all copies agree, that a history with no concurrency matches a plain string edit, and that every character lands where its author typed it. All six passed. To check that the fuzzer could catch anything, I planted six bugs and it caught five; the sixth reversed YATA's tie-break, which turns out to be just another correct ordering. I also checked my YATA against the Fugue paper's published Yjs example, three devices and one character each, and it produced the same interleaved "axb".

Try it

Both editors start with the same sentence and never see each other. Each row is a third copy that receives both people's edits and merges them with one algorithm. Type in either box or use the buttons. "Backward" means each letter is typed in front of the previous one, the way you build a word when the cursor keeps returning to the same spot.

Two words at the same spot

The simplest test: two to five people each type an 8-letter word at the same position with no contact. I counted the pairs of letters someone typed next to each other and checked whether text from somebody who couldn't have seen either letter landed between them. The table shows the share of pairs split that way, over 200 runs each.

AlgorithmForward, 2 peopleForward, 5 peopleBackward, 2 peopleBackward, 5 people
Fugue0%0%0%0%
YATA (Yjs)0%0%0%0%
RGA0%0%100%100%
LSEQ12%17%65%91%
Logoot, boundary+16%22%62%89%
Logoot, random gaps41%71%47%77%

The RGA column is deterministic, not unlucky. Backward typing makes every new letter an insert right after the same left neighbour, and RGA orders concurrent inserts after one character by timestamp. Ana's and Ben's letters have interleaved timestamps, so the letters alternate.

The Logoot family fails for a different reason. Each copy picks positions in the same gap independently, and sorting mixes the two sets. Choosing positions close to the left neighbour helps forward typing (both people's positions climb from the same end, so they collide less often) and does nothing for backward typing.

Editing sessions

Real editing isn't two words at one spot. I simulated sessions with a cursor: each keystroke types a letter (87%), deletes the previous character (5%), moves the cursor up to six places left (5%) or jumps somewhere random (3%). In some runs people also typed backward about a fifth of the time, in streaks. Everyone starts at the same spot in a 120-character paragraph and makes 400 keystrokes, and each keystroke reaches the others after a delay counted in keystrokes. A delay of 1 is a fast live connection; "offline" means nobody syncs until the end. The numbers are split pairs per 1,000 typed characters, with the share of sessions that had any in brackets.

AlgorithmDelay 1Delay 5Delay 20OfflineOffline, 3 people, backward streaks
Fugue00000
YATA (Yjs)00000
RGA000.03 (2%)0.05 (3%)0.52 (18%)
LSEQ0.05 (3%)0.79 (30%)1.7 (45%)2.8 (68%)6.0 (97%)
Logoot, boundary+0.05 (3%)0.79 (28%)2.2 (47%)2.6 (67%)6.3 (97%)
Logoot, random gaps0.03 (2%)1.8 (42%)3.2 (58%)6.0 (70%)9.3 (97%)

The first four columns are two people with no backward streaks; 60 sessions per cell. A few splits per thousand characters sounds small, but they cluster where people collide. One split is one stray letter or word inside someone's sentence, and at a delay of 5 keystrokes, roughly the lag of a slow connection for a fast typist, 28-42% of Logoot and LSEQ sessions had at least one.

RGA's failures came from typing in front of your own text. Ana types a letter, Ben types at the same spot, Ana moves her cursor back and types in front of her own letter: her new text and Ben's are now both inserts after the same character, and RGA's newest-first rule can put Ben's between them. Without deliberate backward streaks that stayed rare. With them, 18% of three-person offline sessions had a split.

I had to fix my metric along the way. My first version counted a split whenever a deleted character sat between the two letters, and it reported small, identical rates for YATA and Fugue. In those cases the other person's text really belonged between them: it was anchored to the deleted character. Counting only letters that were adjacent with nothing deleted between them brought both to zero. The table uses that stricter count.

The device problem

The Fugue paper describes the one case where Yjs interleaves: a backward run typed from more than one replica ID, while someone else types at the same spot. One person switching from laptop to phone mid-sentence does that, and so does a web app that makes a new ID every time a tab reloads. Whether it actually happens depends on how the three IDs compare, so I gave each person several IDs, shuffled the order across people, and had them switch IDs as they typed.

With a switch before every letter (the worst case), YATA split 3-5% of backward pairs with two IDs per person and 11-15% with eight. RGA split 75-89%. Fugue stayed at zero. In the editing sessions, with a switch every 40 keystrokes on average, YATA went from zero to 0.01-0.23 splits per 1,000 characters, in 1-20% of sessions. The top of that range assumes heavy backward typing, three people and no sync, so it's a pessimistic number. RGA's rate was higher in 14 of the same 16 configurations.

Fugue had one split across about 17,800 sessions. I traced it. Ana and Ben had each typed a letter at the same spot, and Ben's sorted first. Ana then typed a letter between Ben's and her own. Meanwhile Ben, who hadn't seen it, kept typing after his letter, and his run went between Ana's two letters. Ana's two letters were inserted at different positions (one after the original text, one after Ben's letter), a case Fugue's guarantee doesn't cover. The tie-break between her letter and his run went the unlucky way.

The Fugue paper also describes FugueMax, which changes one rule: when two characters hang off the same character on its right side, it orders them by what was to their right when they were typed, instead of by replica ID. That's exactly this case. The character whose right neighbour sits further right goes first. Ana's letter had her own letter as its right neighbour; Ben's run had a character further along, because he hadn't seen hers. So FugueMax puts Ben's run first and keeps Ana's pair together. I added it, checked that it reproduces the paper's worked example (AXYBC, where plain Fugue gives AYXBC with my IDs) and that the example catches a reversed version of the rule, then reran every test. FugueMax had zero splits in all of them, including the session above. One event is too few to call a rate; the authors recommend plain Fugue anyway, since the extra rule only matters in rare tangles of concurrent edits.

What the identifiers cost

RGA, YATA and Fugue give each character a fixed-size identifier: a replica number and a counter, plus one or two references to other characters. Stored naively that's 16-24 bytes per character, but real implementations store one entry per run of typing (measured below). Logoot's positions get longer whenever there's no room left in a gap, so their size depends on how people type. I replayed a real editing history: a public trace of about 260,000 edits made while writing an academic paper (from the Automerge benchmarks), ending at 104,852 characters. Every level of a position also stores which replica made it and a counter, which I counted as 6 bytes.

StrategyReal history100k typed forward100k typed backward100k random positions
Logoot, random gaps1,404 B (176 levels)grows linearly; out of memorygrows linearly; out of memory20 B
Logoot, boundary+49 B (6.1)38 B (4.7)grows linearly; out of memory49 B
LSEQ117 B (15.5)107 B (14.3)106 B (14.3)43 B

Bytes are the average per character; levels in brackets. Random gaps are fine for random insert positions and terrible for typing. Every forward keystroke uses, on average, half of the remaining gap, so each new position is one level longer than the last about every 11 characters: after 20,000 characters typed forward the deepest position had 1,736 levels and the average was 870 (7 KB). Boundary+ fixes forward typing and breaks the same way for backward typing, gaining a level about every 3 characters. LSEQ's alternating directions keep both directions bounded, but on the real history it cost more than twice as much as plain boundary+. Most real typing is forward, and my guess is that the levels allocating from the right end waste space on it.

For comparison I replayed the same history into real Yjs (version 13.6) and saved the document. In this history the 182,315 typed characters came in about 6,200 runs, around 30 characters each. Yjs keeps a record per run, split where deletions cut a run: about 11,000 records here. The saved document was 223 KB in its default format and 160 KB in its compact one. Take away the 105 KB of text itself and that's 1.1 or 0.5 bytes of metadata per character, including the record of what was deleted. Logoot-style positions could be compressed too, since neighbouring positions share most of their levels, but I didn't try that, so the table above is per character, uncompressed.

Takeaways

If you're choosing a text CRDT, Logoot-style positions aren't worth it: they interleave in ordinary use and their identifiers depend on typing patterns. RGA is clean for forward typing, and its failure case is common enough to show up in simulation. Yjs's hole is narrow but real in apps that switch replica IDs often, such as one per tab load. Fugue was the only one I couldn't break with the cases it promises to handle, at the same identifier cost as RGA.

entry.title: The Best Values Aren't the Averages
entry.summary: Solitaire Yahtzee, solved exactly, then played with rules of thumb for what each open box is worth. Valuing boxes at their average score loses 20 points a game; fitting the solver's numbers loses 13.5 to 15.5; values tuned for score lose 2.8 and look nothing like averages: Ones worth 6.4, Chance 30. Plus a game that grades every move.
entry.content:
Solitaire Yahtzee has been solved since the late 1990s: Tom Verhoeff computed that perfect play averages 254.59 points. The solver is a table with one number for every possible scorecard, about a million of them, and nobody carries that in their head. What people use instead is a rule of thumb about what each open box is worth. I wanted to know how much the rule of thumb costs, and which rule of thumb is best.

The short version: perfect dice play with a plain "each box is worth its average" rule loses about 20 points a game. Rules fitted to predict the solver's numbers do better but still lose 13.5 to 15.5. The best rule I found loses 2.8, and its values look nothing like the averages: an open Ones box is worth 6.4 points, not the 1.9 it scores, and Chance is worth 30, not 22. Values that play well are prices for decisions, not forecasts.

The solver

A scorecard state is which of the 13 boxes are filled, the upper-section total so far (capped at 63, where the 35-point bonus kicks in), and whether the Yahtzee box holds a 50 (which makes later Yahtzees worth a 100-point bonus). That's 213 × 64 × 2 = 1,048,576 states. Working backwards from the full card, each state's value is the expected points still to come under perfect play, averaged over the three rolls of the next turn. My solver does the whole table in 1.6 seconds on 10 cores.

Before trusting it I checked it against published numbers. Under Verhoeff's lenient joker rule it gives 254.5896, his figure exactly. Under the official forced-joker rule it gives 254.5877. One million simulated games with the solver's choices averaged 254.593 ± 0.06, with a standard deviation of 59.6, so luck dwarfs skill in any single game: the median game is 248 and the 90th percentile is 318. Perfect play gets the upper bonus 68.2% of the time.

The rules matter more than I expected. With no Yahtzee bonus, the perfect average falls to 246.09. With no upper bonus, it falls to 237.83.

How to test a rule of thumb

To isolate what the rule of thumb costs, I gave the player perfect dice play within a turn: it considers every possible hold after each roll and every box at the end. The only thing that's approximate is how it values the scorecard it leaves behind. Instead of the solver's table, it uses a formula, such as "the sum of the values of the open boxes." Each formula's expected score is computed exactly, by running the same backwards pass with the formula in place of the table, so there's no sampling noise in the ranking.

Left: every rule gets perfect play within each turn; only the scorecard valuation differs. Scores are exact, and the axis starts at 200. Right: the tuned rule also has a 36-point bonus ramp and adds 46 once the Yahtzee box holds a 50; neither shows here.

The obvious rules

Greedy values every scorecard at zero, so it takes the most points available each turn. It averages 217.38 and gets the upper bonus 3.1% of the time.

Average values sets each open box's worth to the points it scores on average under perfect play: 1.88 for Ones, 22.01 for Chance, and so on. That's 235.00. It gets the bonus only 20.4% of the time, because nothing in it knows the bonus exists.

Add the bonus as a step: 35 points if you're on track for it, meaning three of each open upper face would still reach 63, and zero otherwise. That made it worse, 232.32. My reading: a step makes the player desperate to stay exactly on the line and indifferent everywhere else.

Add the bonus as a ramp instead: worth half of 35 when exactly on track, rising to all of it when 6 points ahead and to zero when 6 behind (a slope of 12 points). Together with a 9-point flag for having a Yahtzee scored, that gives 243.20 and a 59.6% bonus rate. Valuing the bonus helps, but only if the value changes smoothly.

Better fit, worse play

The natural next step is to fit the values: pick box values that best predict the solver's own numbers. A least-squares fit of an additive formula over the states perfect play actually visits has a typical error of 5.16 points, and it plays to 241.14, worse than the hand-built ramp. Fitting separately for each stage of the game cuts the error to 2.53 points and plays worse again, at 239.09.

That looked wrong until I thought about what the values are used for. A decision compares a few scorecards that differ by one box. The formula only needs those differences right, and only for the choices that come up. A fit spends its accuracy on predicting the level of the whole table, which no decision ever uses.

Tuning for score, not fit

So I tuned the ramp's numbers (13 box values, the ramp's slope and size, and the Yahtzee flag; its midpoint was searched too and stayed at one half) directly for exact expected score, one coordinate at a time. It ended at 251.82, 2.77 short of perfect. The values it settled on:

  • Ones 6.4 and Twos 6.8, against averages of 1.9 and 5.3. An open Ones box is a place to dump a bad turn for almost nothing. Valuing it at its average means using it up early and losing the insurance.
  • Chance 30, against an average of 22, for the same reason. It's the other dump slot.
  • Large straight 21, against an average of 33. My guess is that a high value makes the player too slow to give up on it; I didn't isolate that.
  • Fours, Fives and Sixes all lower than their averages, because the bonus ramp, now worth 36 with a slope of 13, carries their share of the bonus.
  • 46 points for having a Yahtzee scored, standing in for the chance of 100-point bonuses later.

The play it produces looks like perfect play: each box's average score under the tuned rule is within a point of the solver's, it zeroes four of a kind 36% of the time (the solver: 36%) and the Yahtzee box 67% (the solver: 66%), and it gets the bonus 63.7% of the time.

Where the points go

Every decision can be graded against the solver: the loss is the solver's expected score for its best option minus its expected score for the option chosen. Those losses add up exactly to the gap between perfect play and the rule. I played 200,000 games with each rule and split the losses by decision.

ValuationHold after roll 1Hold after roll 2Choice of box
Greedy12.06.618.6
Average values3.73.712.2
Average values + ramp2.63.05.8
Tuned0.680.441.66

The holds are played perfectly for the formula's own idea of the future, so every point lost on a hold is still the valuation's fault: it's aiming at the wrong target. The box choice is where the cost lives: half of it for greedy, most of it for the other three. For the average-values rule, the single biggest item is when to fill four of a kind, worth 4.1 points a game.

Play against the solver

The widget below has the full table (0.7 MB). It grades every hold and every box you pick, and tracks how many points of expected score you've given away. Tick the box to see the solver's move. Following it gives away exactly nothing; the final score is still mostly luck.

Loading the solver's table (0.7 MB)…

If you want one thing to remember at the table: don't spend Ones or Chance early, and treat the upper bonus as something you're gradually more or less on track for, not a line you're above or below.

entry.title: Hedge the Server, Not the Request
entry.summary: Hedged and tied requests simulated across load levels and three reasons a request can be slow. When a server stalls, a backup copy after the 95th-percentile delay cuts the 99.9th percentile about 5× for 3-4% extra work, though good routing had already done most of the work at the 99th. When the request itself is big, the copy is the same big job: 6% of requests hedged meant 39% more work, and hedging lost from about 80% load. A delay tuned at low load collapsed the system at 90%. Tied requests won almost everywhere, as long as cancellation is fast.
entry.content:
A hedged request is the simplest tail-latency trick there is: if a request hasn't come back by the time 95% of requests normally have, send a copy to another server and take whichever answer arrives first. Dean and Barroso's "The Tail at Scale" (2013) made it famous with a striking number: in a Google benchmark reading 1,000 keys from BigTable, hedging after 10 ms cut the 99.9th-percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms for only 2% more requests. The same paper describes tied requests: send the request to two servers at once, and whichever starts working on it first tells the other to drop its copy.

"Only 2% more requests" is the part I wanted to test. A hedge is extra load, and extra load is exactly what makes queues slow. So I simulated it across load levels and across three different reasons a request can be slow. The short answer: it depends almost entirely on where the slowness lives. If the server is slow (a stall, a GC pause, a noisy neighbor), a hedge is cheap and cuts the deep tail about 5×. If the request itself is big, the hedge is a second copy of the same big job, it costs far more than its share of requests suggests, and above about 80% load it makes things worse. A hedge delay tuned when things are quiet turns into a collapse at 90% load. Tied requests were the best option almost everywhere.

The setup

Ten servers, each a first-come-first-served queue, random (Poisson) arrivals. Time is measured in units of the average request's service time. A new request goes to the less busy of two random servers ("two choices"), and so does a hedge, never to the server already holding the request. When the first copy finishes, the other is cancelled at once, whether it's still waiting or already running. Each point is 4 runs of a million requests (the first 100,000 discarded), and "load" means load from the requests alone, before any copies.

Three worlds, differing only in why a request is slow:
